column3: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
column11: Proof-of-concept demonstrations rather than quantitative benchmarks: synthetic LLM-integrated chat applications built on text-davinci-003 (LangChain, ReAct) and GPT-4 with search, view, retrieve-URL, email, address-book and memory tools; real-world Bing Chat (GPT-4) in creative/balanced/precise modes; code-completion engines; a multi-modal injection on LLaVA. Attacks are instantiations of the taxonomy (information gathering, fraud, intrusion, malware/worming, manipulated content, availability) plus hiding techniques such as Base64-encoded and multi-stage injections. No ASR table or baseline comparison.
column12: We reveal new attack vectors, using Indirect Prompt Injection, that enable adversaries to remotely (without a direct interface) exploit LLM-integrated applications by strategically injecting prompts into data likely to be retrieved. (Abstract)
column14: Registry lists this as 'mechanism: Indirect Prompt Injection' with origin None; it should be marked as the originating paper (origin=proposed/invents) since this is where the term and taxonomy come from. Evaluation is demonstrative, not quantitative: there is an Evaluation section but it reports case-study demonstrations on synthetic apps and Bing Chat, with no attack-success-rate measurement, so anyone citing this paper for numbers should be flagged.

column3: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
column11: NQ, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO knowledge databases; retrievers Contriever, Contriever-ms, ANCE; LLMs PaLM 2, GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, LLaMA-2, Vicuna; metrics ASR, Precision/Recall/F1, #Queries, runtime; 5 baselines including Naive Attack, Prompt Injection Attack, Disinformation attack, and Corpus Poisoning Attack (Zhong et al.); several defenses (paraphrasing, perplexity-based detection, duplicate-text filtering, knowledge expansion).
column12: Based on this attack surface, we propose PoisonedRAG, the first knowledge corruption attack to RAG, where an attacker could inject a few malicious texts into the knowledge database of a RAG system to induce an LLM to generate an attacker-chosen target answer for an attacker-chosen target question. (Abstract)
column14: DISAGREE with current_registry_entry, which records this as 'mechanism: PoisonedRAG'. It is a deliberate adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial failure mode; contribution should be proposes_attack / invents. Evaluation matches the claim (ASR against RAG under injected texts).

column3: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
column11: Closed-set tasks PubHealth and ARC-Challenge; short-form QA PopQA and TriviaQA-unfiltered; long-form Bio generation (FactScore) and ASQA (str-em, MAUVE, citation precision/recall); baselines are LLMs with and without retrieval (ChatGPT, Llama2-chat, Alpaca, Llama2-FT etc.); training-scale ablation and a 50-sample human evaluation of plausibility/support and reflection-token reliability.
column12: We introduce a new framework called Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (S ELF -R AG) that enhances an LM’s quality and factuality through retrieval and self-reflection. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH relative to the registry: current_registry_entry labels this 'defense: Self-RAG', but the paper evaluates NO attack, no poisoned or corrupted context, and no adversarial condition at all - it measures QA accuracy, factuality (FactScore) and citation precision on standard capability/factuality benchmarks. It is a non-adversarial fix (irrelevant/unhelpful retrieved passages, unsupported generation), not a defense. It is also borderline for the corpus: the untrustworthy-context aspect is only 'retrieved passages may be irrelevant or unsupported', which is adjacent to but weaker than context poisoning; belongs_in_corpus marked unsure for that reason. Close call between proposes_fix and improves_existing (it is a new named framework but squarely an extension of RAG). RULING: kept in corpus per screening decision.

column3: Neural Exec: Learning (and Learning from) Execution Triggers for Prompt Injection Attacks
column11: 100 held-out prompt/payload pairs against Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, OpenChat3.5 and Mixtral-8x7B, measured by Execution (Top-1) Accuracy, compared against 12 handcrafted execution triggers from prior work and blog posts (including the separators of Liu et al.); plus persistence through a RAG preprocessing pipeline and cross-model transferability (Appendix E).
column12: We introduce a new family of prompt injection attacks, termed Neural Exec. (Abstract)
column14: Registry lists Neural Exec as a mechanism with origin None; it should be an attack with origin=invents. The paper also contributes the notion of "robustness to pre-processing" for indirect prompt injection, evaluated on a RAG pipeline. Baseline comparison is against handcrafted triggers such as "Ignore previous instructions and...", i.e. it explicitly positions itself as a learned replacement for those.

column3: From Prompt Injections to SQL Injection Attacks: How Protected is Your LLM-Integrated Web Application?
column7: mechanism: P2SQL injection (prompt-to-SQL); defense: UNNAMED: P2SQL mitigations (DB permission hard
column11: A purpose-built Langchain 0.0.189 + PostgreSQL job-marketplace testbed with SQL chain and SQL agent chatbot variants, seven representative P2SQL attacks (U.1-U.3, RD.1-RD.2, RI.1-RI.2) each repeated 30 times for success rate, replicated across 7 state-of-the-art LLMs; the four proposed Langchain defense extensions are validated on a real-world use-case application.
column12: In this paper, we present a comprehensive examination of prompt-to-SQL (P2 SQL) injections targeting web applications based on the Langchain framework. (Abstract)
column14: Paper names both a new attack class and seven named attack variants in Table 1, plus four unnamed defense extensions, so names_registry_technique=yes with the attacks listed. Quote retains the paper's rendering "P2 SQL" (superscript 2 lost in extraction). Registry origin=needs_read should become invents. Includes indirect attacks via poisoned database records, directly in scope for context poisoning.

column3: Prompt Injection attack against LLM-integrated Applications
column11: 36 real-world LLM-integrated applications (10 from a pilot study plus 26 from SUPERTOOLS), five exploit queries each repeated five times, manually verified, across five exploit scenarios (Prompt Leaking, Code Generation, Content Manipulation, Spam Generation, Information Gathering); 31 of 36 applications found vulnerable, 86.1% success rate, 10 vendor confirmations including Notion; plus an ablation study over the attack strategies and a pilot comparison against existing handcrafted prompt injection techniques, which succeeded only partially on 2 of 10 targets.
column12: Prompted by these limitations, we subsequently formulate H OU Y I, a novel black-box prompt injection attack technique, which draws inspiration from traditional web injection attacks. (Abstract)
column14: Registry lists HOUYI as a mechanism with origin None; it is an attack technique with origin=invents. Quote preserves the extraction artifact "H OU Y I" (small caps in the PDF). Named component vocabulary (pre-constructed prompt / injection prompt inducing context partition / malicious payload) and the five exploit scenarios are the parts later work cites. Claim and evaluation are aligned.

column3: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases
column11: Three agents (Agent-Driver autonomous driving, ReAct QA agent on StrategyQA, EHRAgent healthcare) with poisoned RAG/memory bases; baselines GCG, AutoDAN, Corpus Poisoning Attack (CPA) and BadChain; metrics ASR-r, ASR-a, ASR-t and benign accuracy, plus transferability across embedders (REALM, ORQA, DPR, ANCE, BGE, OpenAI-ADA).
column12: To uncover such vulnerabilities, we propose a novel red teaming approach AGENT P OISON, the first backdoor attack targeting generic and RAG-based LLM agents by poisoning their long-term memory or RAG knowledge base. (Abstract)
column14: Quote reproduces the PDF's OCR spacing of the small-caps name ('AGENT P OISON'). Registry lists it as 'mechanism: AgentPoison' with no origin; I would record it as a proposed attack (invents). Claims and evaluation match: the abstract's poisoning claim is exactly what the experiments measure.

column3: Breaking ReAct Agents: Foot-in-the-Door Attack Will Get You In
column7: mechanism: Foot-in-the-Door (FITD) attack; defense: UNNAMED: Reflection-based defenses against Foo
column11: The InjecAgent benchmark of Zhan et al. (2024): 510 direct-harm and 544 data-steal IPI attacks, with vanilla IPI as the baseline, across Mixtral, Llama-3.1, Llama-3 and GPT-4o-mini, using familiar and unfamiliar distractor tools and combined with thought injection (TI) and harmless thought injection (HTI); a self-reflection defense is then evaluated on the same setup.
column12: We introduce a novel technique called "Foot in the Door" (FITD) attack, building upon existing IPI attacks by adding a distractor phase before the main attack. (Section 3, The Foot in the Door Attack)
column14: The quoted sentence says the attack builds upon existing IPI attacks, which could argue for origin=improves; I coded invents because FITD is a newly named attack with its own mechanism (a benign distractor request preceding the malicious instruction) rather than a modification of a specific prior named technique. The paper also proposes an unnamed reflection-based defense, evaluated on the same benchmark, matching the registry entry.

column3: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation
column11: PopQA, Biography (FactScore), PubHealth, Arc-Challenge; baselines without retrieval (LLaMA2-7B/13B, Alpaca-7B/13B, CoVE65B, LLaMA2-chat13B, ChatGPT), standard RAG, and advanced RAG (SAIL, Self-RAG, Ret-ChatGPT, Ret-LLaMA2-chat, perplexity.ai); ablations on the Correct/Incorrect/Ambiguous actions.
column12: To this end, we propose the Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG) to improve the robustness of generation. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: CRAG; Self-CRAG. In scope as a non-adversarial pipeline failure (retriever returns irrelevant or inaccurate documents that mislead the generator), not an attack, so proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense; the current registry entry labels it 'defense', which I disagree with - there is no adversary and no attack is evaluated. Evaluation measures downstream QA accuracy/FactScore rather than any direct measure of how much irrelevant context was removed, but the datasets are the standard ones for this failure, so I do not treat this as a claim/evaluation mismatch.

column3: Parameters vs. Context: Fine-Grained Control of Knowledge Reliance in Language Models
column11: NQ (standard QA), ConFiQA (long-context QA) and MQuAKE (multi-turn QA) under counterfactual contexts, measuring memory recall (MR), context reliance (ConR) and parametric reliance (ParaR) across LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B, Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B; six general RAG tasks for adaptive control; ablation on the conflict-detection module (ConD) by hit rate.
column12: To address this, we propose CK-PLUG, a plug-and-play method for controlling LLMs’ reliance on parametric and contextual knowledge. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: CK-PLUG; Confidence Gain (the novel knowledge-consistency metric it introduces). In scope: the motivating case is retrieved context that is unreliable, noisy or 'potentially adversarial' conflicting with parametric knowledge. The failure mode it works on (parameter-context knowledge conflict) is named by prior work (Xu et al. 2024), not by this paper, so no registry-naming credit. Like row 42, the current registry entry calls it a 'defense'; it is a fix for a non-adversarial conflict - no attack is evaluated, only counterfactual contexts.

column3: AgentFold: Long-Horizon Web Agents with Proactive Context Management
column11: BrowseComp (36.2%), BrowseComp-ZH (47.3%), WideSearch-en Item-F1 (62.1%) and GAIA text-only (67.0%), against open-source agents (WebThinker, WebDancer, WebSailor, ASearcher, MiroThinker, WebExplorer, DeepDive, DeepDiver-V2, Kimi-K2, GLM-4.5, DeepSeek-V3.1) and proprietary agents (Claude-4-Sonnet/Opus, o4-mini, o3, OpenAI Deep Research); plus a context-dynamics analysis of 200 BrowseComp trajectories measuring average context token count and block count per turn.
column12: Addressing these, we introduce AgentFold, a novel agent paradigm centered on proactive context management, inspired by the human cognitive process of retrospective consolidation. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. this is one of the papers the screening brief warns about. The framing is 'context saturation as they accumulate noisy, raw histories' and 'critical signals become buried in noise', but nothing in the evaluation measures context degradation or context-induced error: the results tables are pure capability scores on information-seeking benchmarks (BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, WideSearch, GAIA) and the only context-specific measurement is a token-count / block-count growth curve, i.e. an efficiency statistic. There is no ablation isolating noise or distraction. I therefore left contribution unsure (it would be proposes_fix if context saturation counts as an in-scope failure mode, and out_of_scope if, as the capability-only evaluation suggests, this is an agent-performance paper using 'context' in the capacity sense) and left technique_name/origin/parent_technique blank per the blank-means-no-decision rule. I disagree with the current registry entry, which records it as a proposed 'defense' - no adversary and no attack appear anywhere in the paper. Recommend a second pass decide between proposes_fix and out_of_scope. RULING: coded proposes_fix and kept in corpus per screening decision; the mismatch warning stands - nothing in the evaluation measures context degradation.

column3: Astute RAG: Overcoming Imperfect Retrieval Augmentation and Knowledge Conflicts for Large Language Models
column11: NQ, TriviaQA, BioASQ and PopQA with 10 Google-Search passages each, ASQA for long-form QA, and RGB (English refined subset, five top negative passages as a worst case); baselines No RAG, RAG, USC, GenRead, RobustRAG, InstructRAG, Self-Route, plus a CompAct context-compression comparison and a passage-ordering study; models Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Mistral-Large 128B, Mistral-Nemo 12B; metric string-match accuracy.
column12: To render LLMs resilient to imperfect retrieval, we propose A STUTE RAG, a novel RAG approach that adaptively elicits essential information from LLMs’ internal knowledge, iteratively consolidates internal and external knowledge with source-awareness, and finalizes the answer according to information reliability. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: ASTUTE RAG. Close call between proposes_fix and measurement_study: the paper also contributes a controlled analysis of how often imperfect retrieval occurs and how often it triggers knowledge conflicts (Figs. 2 and 3), but the abstract and title lead with the method. Also a close call with proposes_defense - the abstract mentions 'irrelevant, misleading, or even malicious information' - but the evaluation contains no attack, only naturally imperfect retrieval and worst-case negative passages, so the 'defense' label in the current registry entry overstates it. The names (imperfect retrieval, knowledge conflicts) are inherited from prior work. Quote is rendered with the small-caps artifact 'A STUTE RAG' exactly as the extracted text shows it.

column3: MEM1: Learning to Synergize Memory and Reasoning for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents
column11: Multi-objective multi-hop QA composed from HotpotQA and Natural Questions (exact match, F1), open-domain web QA, and WebShop navigation (environment reward); accuracy baselines Search-R1, DeepResearcher, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Agent-FLAN, Agent-R, AgentLM; efficiency baselines a prompt-only agentic truncation variant and A-MEM; metrics peak token usage, average dependency length and inference time; RL vs SFT and format-reward ablations.
column12: We introduce MEM1, an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that enables agents to operate with constant memory across long multi-turn tasks. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. the same pattern as row 47. The introduction lists three motivations and only the third is in scope ('Overloaded and inefficient context. The accumulation of irrelevant or redundant content dilutes the model's attention.'); the other two, and the entire abstract, are inference cost, memory usage and out-of-distribution length generalisation. Every reported metric is task capability (EM, F1, environment reward) or efficiency (peak tokens, dependency length, inference time) - nothing measures attention dilution, distraction or any context-induced error. I left contribution unsure: out_of_scope is the reading the evaluation supports (agent capability/efficiency, 'long-horizon' in the capacity sense), proposes_fix only if the single dilution sentence is accepted as the paper's subject. technique_name/origin/parent_technique left blank per the blank-means-no-decision rule. I disagree with the current registry entry, which records MEM1 as a proposed 'defense' - the paper contains no adversary, no attack and no untrusted-content threat model. RULING: coded proposes_fix and kept in corpus per screening decision; the mismatch warning stands - every reported metric is capability or efficiency.

column3: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
column11: FaithEval, RealtimeQA, MuSiQue, SQuAD (plus MuSiQue-golden / SQuAD-golden non-conflict settings); baselines: origin model w/o and w/ context, Self-RAG, ChatQA-1.5, ChatQA-2.0, Opin(Instr), ATTR, KRE, CAD, COIECD; metrics ACC and Memorization Ratio (MR)
column12: To this end, this paper proposes FaithfulRAG, a novel framework that resolves knowledge conflicts by explicitly modeling discrepancies between the model's parametric knowledge and retrieved context. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: FaithfulRAG; self-fact mining; Self-Think. Non-adversarial failure (context-memory knowledge conflict / unfaithfulness), so coded proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense; registry entry says 'defense: FaithfulRAG' which I'd amend to a fix for a non-adversarial failure mode. Claim and evaluation are aligned (knowledge-conflict QA datasets). The paper does not name a new failure mode; 'knowledge conflict' is pre-existing terminology it inherits.

column3: Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents
column11: MetaTool and ToolBench benchmark datasets, 8 LLMs and 4 retrievers, gradient-free and gradient-based variants; baseline attacks: naive attack, escape characters, context ignoring, fake completion, combined attack, JudgeDeceiver, PoisonedRAG; defenses tested: StruQ, SecAlign, known-answer detection, DataSentinel, perplexity detection, perplexity windowed detection
column12: We propose ToolHijacker, the first prompt injection attack to tool selection in LLM agents. (Section I, contributions list)
column14: Disagree with current_registry_entry, which codes this as 'mechanism: ToolHijacker'. ToolHijacker is a deliberate adversarial attack (malicious tool document injected into the tool library), not a non-adversarial failure mechanism; it should be proposes_attack. Claim and evaluation align.

column3: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
column11: NQSwap and Macnoise knowledge-conflict open-domain QA datasets on Llama3-8B, Llama2-7B, Gemma2-9B; baselines: no control, TaskVec, ActAdd, SEA (linear and SqExp), DoLa, CAD, ICL; metrics EM_C and EM_M
column12: In this work, we propose S PARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to control the knowledge selection behaviour of LLMs. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: SpARE (Sparse Auto-Encoder Representation Engineering). Coded proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense because the target failure is non-adversarial context-memory knowledge conflict, not a deliberate attack; registry says 'defense: SpARE'. Close call on origin: SpARE is a new method but sits in the existing representation-engineering family (TaskVec, ActAdd, SEA); I coded invents because the paper presents SpARE as a new method rather than a modification of a specific prior one. Claim and evaluation align (knowledge conflict is actually measured, via EM under steering).

column3: Automatic and Universal Prompt Injection Attacks against Large Language Models
column7: mechanism: UNNAMED: automatic universal gradient-based pr
column9: M-GCG (momentum-enhanced Greedy Coordinate Gradient); the attack itself is left unnamed
column11: Seven NLP user tasks (MRPC duplicate sentence detection, Jfleg grammar correction, hate content detection, NLI, sentiment analysis, spam detection, Gigaword summarization) on victim Llama2-7b-chat; three attack objectives (static, semi-dynamic, dynamic); baselines: combined prompt injection attack (Liu et al.), repeated characters attack, naive attack; defenses: paraphrasing, retokenization, external data isolation, instructional prevention, sandwich prevention; ablation GCG vs M-GCG; metrics keyword ASR and LLM-evaluation ASR
column12: We introduce an automatic prompt injection attack method demonstrating strong universality across various user interactions and datasets. (Section 1, Introduction - contributions list)
column14: The attack itself is unnamed (matching current_registry_entry 'UNNAMED'); the only proper names the paper coins are M-GCG (its optimizer) and the three attack-objective categories (static / semi-dynamic / dynamic objective), which are objective taxonomies rather than attack names. Later work cites this as 'Universal Prompt Injection' from the repo name, not from a name the paper assigns. Hence names_registry_technique=unsure rather than a confident no. Note also a scope gap: the title and abstract claim 'universal' attacks against LLMs generally, but the evaluation uses a single victim model (Llama2-7b-chat), so universality is demonstrated across tasks/instructions, not across models.

column3: Meta SecAlign: A Secure Foundation LLM Against Prompt Injection Attacks
column11: 9 utility benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, BBH, GPQA Diamond, AlpacaEval2, SEP utility, AgentDojo utility, WASP utility) and 7 security benchmarks (AlpacaFarm ASR incl. basic-adaptive and GCG-adaptive, SEP ASR, TaskTracker, CyberSecEval2, InjecAgent, AgentDojo ASR, WASP intermediate/end-to-end ASR); six PI techniques (straightforward before/after data, ignore before/after data, completion, completion-ignore); compared against SecAlign-70B, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-3-Pro
column12: Our most comprehensive evaluation to date reveals previously-unrecognized shortcomings in the SoTA SecAlign: it significantly hurts utility and security in a few domains not evaluated in prior work. (Section 4, Experiments)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Meta-SecAlign; SecAlign++. Close call between proposes_defense and improves_existing: Meta-SecAlign is a new named released model, but the defense technique is explicitly SecAlign++, a fixed/extended SecAlign recipe, and the paper's own framing is that it repairs shortcomings in SecAlign. I coded improves_existing and flag the alternative. The attack names in the evaluation (ignore / completion / completion-ignore, GCG) are inherited from prior work, not coined here. Claim and evaluation align and the evaluation is unusually broad.

column3: Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge
column11: MT-Bench and LLMBar (restructured into 10 target questions / 10 target responses / 500 clean responses each); victim LLMs Mistral-7B-Instruct, Openchat-3.5, Llama-2-7B-chat, Llama-3-8B-Instruct; baseline attacks: naive attack, escape characters, context ignore, fake completion, combined attack, fake reasoning, and jailbreaks TAP, PAIR, AutoDAN, GCG; three application case studies (LLM-powered search, RLAIF, tool selection); defenses: known-answer detection, perplexity detection (PPL), perplexity windowed detection (PPL-W)
column12: We propose JudgeDeceiver, the first optimization-based prompt injection attack to LLM-as-a-Judge. (Section 1, contributions list)
column14: Disagree with current_registry_entry, which codes this as 'mechanism: JudgeDeceiver'; it is a deliberate optimisation-based prompt injection attack, so proposes_attack. The paper also coins a second named attack, Fake Reasoning ('We propose a novel manually crafted injected sequence against this defense'), used as a baseline in its own evaluation; I listed it under named_techniques. Claim and evaluation align.

column3: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
column11: TriviaQA, Natural Questions, PopQA with Contriever-MSMARCO top-1 retrieved Wikipedia context, split into gold-context and noisy-context subsets plus Known-noisy / Unknown-gold analyses; models Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B; baselines regular greedy decoding closed-book and open-book, CAD, MICD_F, MICD_D; metrics Exact Match and AUROC of alpha vs context noisiness
column12: We extend the scope of previous studies to encompass noisy contexts and propose adaptive contrastive decoding (ACD) to leverage contextual influence effectively. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: adaptive contrastive decoding (ACD). Coded proposes_fix because noisy retrieved context is a non-adversarial pipeline failure, not a deliberate attack; registry says 'defense: ACD'. origin=improves because the paper explicitly extends the existing contrastive-decoding family (CAD/MICD) with an entropy-based adaptive weight. Claim and evaluation align: noisy context is actually isolated and measured (Subset_Noisy, Known-noisy).

column3: Preemptive Answer "Attacks" on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
column7: mechanism: preemptive answer attack (CoT short-circuiting; defense: UNNAMED: two preemptive-answer mitigations
column11: GSM8K, MathQA, MATH, HotpotQA, CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA; ChatGPT and GPT-4; Zero-Shot and Few-Shot CoT (plus self-consistency); accuracy and attack success rate under Unintentional Preemptive Answer (UPA) and Malicious Preemptive Answer (MPA), with problem restatement and self-reflection as mitigations; an appendix section also evaluates alternative advanced prompt-injection attacks.
column12: In this paper, we introduce a novel scenario termed preemptive answers, where the LLM obtains an answer before engaging in reasoning. (Abstract)
column14: Straddles attack and failure mode: UPA is a non-adversarial self-inflicted variant, MPA is delivered by prompt injection; the title brackets 'Attacks' in scare quotes. Registry calls it a mechanism, which is defensible for UPA, but the paper's framing and the MPA experiments are adversarial, so coded proposes_attack. The two mitigations are named descriptively (problem restatement, self-reflection / Self-Reflect) and are not branded defenses.

column3: Agent Skills in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Security Vulnerabilities at Scale
column11: 42,447 agent skills crawled from skills.rest and skillsmp.com, 31,132 analyzed after filtering; a 1,218-skill categorized sample; SkillScan validated against 200 manually annotated ground-truth skills (86.7% precision, 82.5% recall, Cohen's kappa 0.83); odds-ratio comparison of script-bundling versus instruction-only skills.
column12: We develop a taxonomy of 14 vulnerability patterns across four dimensions: prompt injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, and supply chain risks. (Contributions)
column14: Disagrees with current_registry_entry (defense: SkillScan): the paper's own contributions list leads with the first large-scale study and the vulnerability taxonomy; SkillScan is the third listed contribution, a detection pipeline built to enable the measurement rather than a defense evaluated against attacks. named_techniques are the taxonomy's pattern labels (the four prompt-injection and four data-exfiltration patterns printed in the excerpt); the privilege-escalation and supply-chain pattern labels were not in the retrieved text. No attack experiments are run - the evaluation is prevalence measurement plus detector precision/recall.

column3: Scaling Long-Horizon LLM Agent via Context-Folding
column11: BrowseComp-Plus (150 eval instances) and SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances); Pass@1, number of tool calls, peak context length and max token cost; baselines are ReAct agents at 32K/65K/131K/327K context, a Summary Agent with 10 summarization sessions, GRPO-trained variants, and reference systems GPT-5, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, GLM-4.5-Air, Qwen3-235B-A22B.
column12: We introduce Context-Folding, a framework that empowers agents to actively manage their working context. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper motivates itself with degraded performance from long accumulated context (citing lost-in-the-middle style findings) but measures only task capability and efficiency: Pass@1 on BrowseComp-Plus and SWE-Bench Verified, tool-call counts, active context size and token budget. No measurement of context degradation, distraction, or any trustworthiness property of the context itself. Also contributes FoldGRPO, the RL algorithm with Unfolded Token Penalty and Out-of-Scope Penalty. Registry labels it a 'defense', which is wrong - there is no adversary; it is a non-adversarial context-management fix.

column3: To Trust or Not to Trust? Enhancing Large Language Models' Situated Faithfulness to External Contexts
column9: Self-Guided Confidence Reasoning (SCR) and Rule-Based Confidence Reasoning (RCR)
column11: FreshQA, NaturalQA, TriviaQA, PopQA, ConflictQA, ClashEval and the newly created RedditQA, each paired with a correct retrieved context and an LLM-synthesized or human-written incorrect context; metrics are accuracy with correct context (TR), accuracy with wrong context (FA) and overall; baselines closed-book, direct input augmentation (DIA), TACS, ActiveRAG, ContextEval/InternalEval and confidence-threshold variants; GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3-8B, plus CR-DPO fine-tuning and a robustness study over six wrong-context styles.
column12: To enhance situated faithfulness, we propose two approaches: Self-Guided Confidence Reasoning (SCR) and Rule-Based Confidence Reasoning (RCR). (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Self-Guided Confidence Reasoning (SCR); Rule-Based Confidence Reasoning (RCR); Confidence Reasoning Direct Preference Optimization (CR-DPO). Squarely about untrustworthy context: incorrect, misleading or disinformation-bearing retrieved context. The named concept 'situated faithfulness' is a desired property, not a failure mode, so names_registry_technique=no; the underlying failure mode (knowledge conflict / over-reliance on external context) is pre-existing. Also contributes the RedditQA dataset of in-the-wild incorrect contexts, which the registry entry omits. Unlike rows 5 and 10 there is no claim/evaluation mismatch - the evaluation directly measures accuracy under incorrect contexts.

column3: Can Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks Be Detected and Removed?
column7: defense: UNNAMED: IPI detection + post-detection remova
column11: Inj-SQuAD and Inj-TriviaQA, the paper's own benchmarks (900 samples each, injected instructions crafted with GPT-4o for phishing, advertising and propaganda goals, placed at head/middle/tail); detection evaluated via true positive rate on injected documents and false positive rate on clean documents for existing LLMs, open-source detectors (ProtectAI, Meta Prompt Guard) and newly trained detection models; removal evaluated by removal rate for a segmentation removal method and an extraction removal method; combined pipeline measured by attack success rate.
column12: In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of detecting and removing indirect prompt injection attacks, and we construct a benchmark dataset for evaluation. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: segmentation removal method; extraction removal method (both described rather than branded). Partly disagrees with current_registry_entry (defense: UNNAMED IPI detection + removal): the paper's leading contribution is the Inj-SQuAD / Inj-TriviaQA benchmark plus training datasets, with the detection models and the two removal methods evaluated on top of it; the removal methods are called 'two intuitive methods' by the authors. origin left as none because no named technique is claimed; the benchmarks themselves are new.

column3: HiAgent: Hierarchical Working Memory Management for Solving Long-Horizon Agent Tasks with Large Language Model
column11: Five long-horizon agent tasks from AgentBoard - Blocksworld, Gripper, Tyreworld, Barman, Jericho - with GPT-4-turbo; metrics are progress rate, success rate, average steps, context efficiency (tokens) and run time; the only baseline is the STANDARD full-history prompting strategy, plus task-decomposition and module ablations (w/o Observation Summarization, w/o Trajectory Retrieval).
column12: Experimental results across five long-horizon tasks demonstrate that H I AGENT achieves a twofold increase in success rate and reduces the average number of steps required by 3.8. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames the problem as redundant, overlong working memory that hinders coherent strategies and accurate predictions, but the evaluation measures only capability and efficiency: success rate, progress rate, average steps, context token count and run time on Blocksworld/Gripper/Tyreworld/Barman/Jericho. Nothing measures context degradation, distraction, or any property of context trustworthiness. Registry calls HiAgent a 'defense'; there is no adversary - it is a non-adversarial working-memory management fix. Note the evidence quote reproduces the extractor's small-caps spacing of the system name.

column3: ACON: Optimizing Context Compression for Long-horizon LLM Agents
column11: AppWorld (task completion score), OfficeBench (accuracy), Multi-objective QA / 8-objective QA (EM, F1); efficiency metrics are steps, average peak input tokens and dependency. Baselines: No Compression, FIFO, Retrieval, LLMLingua, naive Prompting compression. Agents/compressors: gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, and distilled Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-8B, Phi-4 compressors.
column12: We introduce Agent Context Optimization (ACON), a unified framework that optimally compresses both observations and history into concise, informative representations. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames the problem as context dilution and 'reasoning degradation due to irrelevant information' / 'context distraction', and claims up to 46% improvement 'by mitigating context distraction', but nothing in the evaluation measures distraction, dilution or context rot directly. Section 4 measures only (a) task capability scores - AppWorld completion score, OfficeBench accuracy, 8-objective QA EM/F1 - and (b) efficiency - number of steps, average peak input tokens, dependency (KV cost), and compressor size after distillation. The distraction claim is inferred purely from accuracy going up when context is compressed for small models; there is no distractor-controlled experiment, no position/noise sweep, and no ablation isolating irrelevant content. Also disagrees with current_registry_entry: ACON is labelled 'defense' there, but there is no adversary anywhere in the paper - it is a non-adversarial fix (proposes_fix), so the registry entry should be reclassified.

column3: ParamMute: Suppressing Knowledge-Critical FFNs for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
column9: Parametric Knowledge Muting through FFN Suppression (ParamMute)
column11: CoFaithfulQA (their own new benchmark built from HotpotQA, NQ, NewsQA, SearchQA, SQuAD, TriviaQA), ConFiQA (out-of-domain) and FaithEval; baselines Vanilla-RAG, Attrprompt, O&Iprompt, COIECD, SFT, KAFT, C-DPO, DDR; metrics ConR (context reliance), MemR (memory reliance), MR; plus ablations over suppressed sublayers and FFN-selection strategies.
column12: Building on this insight, we propose Parametric Knowledge Muting through FFN Suppression (ParamMute), a framework that improves contextual faithfulness by suppressing the activation of unfaithfulness-associated FFNs and calibrating the model toward retrieved knowledge. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: ParamMute (Parametric Knowledge Muting through FFN Suppression). Non-adversarial failure mode: unfaithful generation / internal-knowledge dominance over accurate retrieved context, so this is a fix rather than a defense; the failure mode itself ('unfaithful generation', knowledge conflict) is inherited vocabulary, not coined here. Secondary contribution is the CoFaithfulQA benchmark, but the contributions lead with ParamMute. Evaluation genuinely measures faithfulness to context (ConR/MemR), not merely task accuracy, so no claim/evaluation mismatch. Registry entry 'defense: ParamMute' is close but it mitigates a non-adversarial failure, not an attack.

column3: WebInject: Prompt Injection Attack to Web Agents
column11: Ten webpage datasets (five real collected via SingleFile and five GPT-4-Turbo-synthesized, across blog, commerce, education, healthcare, portfolio); five MLLM-based web agents (UI-TARS-7B-SFT, Phi-4-multimodal, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-4b); baselines Naive, Context Ignoring, Fake Completion, Combined, and screenshot-based perturbation attacks; metric Attack Success Rate; ablations over monitor count, perturbation bound epsilon, prompt categories, target actions, and compute cost.
column12: In this work, we propose WebInject, a prompt injection attack that manipulates the webpage environment to induce a web agent to perform an attacker-specified action. (Abstract)
column14: Registry entry says 'mechanism: WebInject' - disagree: this is a deliberate adversarial attack (optimized raw-pixel perturbation injected via webpage source code), not a non-adversarial failure mechanism; it should be classed as an attack.

column3: PISmith: Reinforcement Learning-based Red Teaming for Prompt Injection Defenses
column11: 13 PIArena benchmarks across QA (SQuAD v2, Dolly Closed QA, Dolly Info Extraction, Dolly Summarization), RAG (NQ, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO) and long-context (LongBench: HotpotQA-Long, Qasper, GovReport, MultiNews, Passage Retrieval, LCC); 8 defenses including Meta-SecAlign-8B; 7 attack baselines (naive/direct, combined, TAP, PAIR, Strategy, vanilla GRPO, RL-Hammer) plus EPO and DAPO ports; agentic settings on InjecAgent and AgentDojo with GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-nano; metrics ASR@1, ASR@10 and benign Utility.
column12: In this work, we propose PISmith, a reinforcement learning-based red-teaming method for evaluating prompt injection defenses. (Introduction)
column14: Registry says 'mechanism: PISmith' - disagree: PISmith is an adaptive black-box prompt-injection attack / red-teaming method, not a failure mechanism. Origin coded 'improves' because the method is GRPO fine-tuning of an attack LLM in the RL-Hammer line, with two new components (adaptive entropy regularization, dynamic advantage weighting); the paper itself frames these as fixes to GRPO's reward sparsity. Paper also contributes a 13-dataset red-teaming evaluation suite as a secondary contribution.

column3: Memory-R1: Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning
column11: LoCoMo (152/81/1307 train/val/test QA, adversarial subset excluded), MSC and LongMemEval; baselines LoCoMo RAG, A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS and a Memory-SFT behaviour-cloning variant; backbones LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (3B-14B scales); metrics token-level F1, BLEU-1 and LLM-as-a-Judge on single-hop, multi-hop, open-domain and temporal questions.
column12: We present Memory-R1, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that equips LLMs with the ability to actively manage and utilize external memory through two specialized agents: a Memory Manager that learns structured operations, including ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, and NOOP; and an Answer Agent that preselects and reasons over relevant entries. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper is framed around noisy and corrupted context - retrieval that floods the model with irrelevant entries so it is 'prone to distraction by noise', and vanilla memory managers that issue wrong DELETE+ADD operations and fragment/overwrite stored facts - but the evaluation measures only QA capability: F1, BLEU-1 and LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy on LoCoMo, MSC and LongMemEval against memory-system baselines (Mem0, A-Mem, MemoryOS, Memory-SFT). There is no measurement of distraction, noise tolerance, memory corruption rate or any adversarial/poisoned-memory condition, and the LoCoMo adversarial subset is explicitly excluded. DEFENSE-NAMES-style note: the only named artifact is the Memory-R1 framework (Memory Manager, Answer Agent, Memory Distillation). Registry entry 'defense: Memory-R1' is wrong in kind - it is a non-adversarial memory-management fix, not a defense against an attack.

column3: AgentVigil: Generic Black-Box Red-teaming for Indirect Prompt Injection against LLM Agents
column11: AgentDojo (personal-assistant agents, o3-mini and GPT-4o backbones; 71% success) and VWA-adv (web agents; 70%), with AgentDojo's handcrafted adversarial prompts as the baseline attack; transferability across unseen tasks and unseen internal LLMs; AgentDojo defenses pi_detector (ProtectAI), repeat, and delimit (Spotlighting-style); ablation over seed corpus, MCTS seed selection and mutators; plus real-world web deployments redirecting agents to arbitrary/phishing URLs.
column12: In this work, we propose a generic blackbox fuzzing framework, AGENT V IGIL, designed to automatically discover and exploit indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities across diverse LLM agents. (Abstract)
column14: Registry says 'mechanism: AgentVigil' - disagree: it is an automated black-box red-teaming/attack framework for indirect prompt injection, not a failure mechanism. technique_name copied as the source text renders it (small-caps artifact 'AGENT V IGIL'); the paper's plain spelling is AgentVigil. Origin coded 'invents' since the paper claims the first automated black-box agent-attack framework, though it adapts fuzzing and MCTS and explicitly contrasts itself with GPTFuzzer.

column3: Backdooring Instruction-Tuned Large Language Models with Virtual Prompt Injection
column11: Alpaca 7B/13B victim models poisoned at 1% rate; baselines Alpaca (clean), Alpaca w/ Clean, Alpaca w/ AutoPoison (Shu et al. 2023), and text-davinci-003 with explicit injection as upper bound; evaluation data: WizardLM 218-instruction general test set, 200 ChatGPT-generated trigger instructions per sentiment-steering topic (Joe Biden, OpenAI, abortion), HumanEval 164 problems for code injection, contrast instructions for targetedness; defense evaluated = quality-guided data filtering
column12: In this paper, we formalize such a steering risk with Virtual Prompt Injection (VPI) as a novel backdoor attack setting tailored for instruction-tuned LLMs. (Abstract)
column14: Agrees with current_registry_entry naming VPI, but the registry calls it a 'mechanism'; it is an adversarial attack (data-poisoning backdoor), so contribution is proposes_attack and origin is invents. Attack is at the instruction-tuning-data level rather than the inference-time context, i.e. the untrusted content enters via training data, not the agent's context window — worth flagging for scope boundary discussion. Paper also names a defense (quality-guided data filtering), but attacks lead the contributions so names_registry_technique is yes.

column3: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
column7: defense: UNNAMED: six composable agent design patterns
column11: no evaluation
column12: In this work, we propose a set of principled design patterns for building AI agents with provable resistance to prompt injection. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: The Action-Selector Pattern; The Plan-Then-Execute Pattern; The LLM Map-Reduce Pattern; The Dual LLM Pattern; The Code-Then-Execute Pattern; The Context-Minimization Pattern. DISAGREES with current_registry_entry 'UNNAMED: six composable agent design patterns' — the six patterns ARE individually named in Section 3 and are cited by name in later work. Coded position_or_conceptual because there is no implementation and no quantitative evaluation: the paper argues qualitatively via ten case studies (OS assistant, email assistant, SWE agent, etc.), discussing utility/security trade-offs per design. The Dual LLM Pattern is attributed to Willison, not invented here; Plan-Then-Execute and Context-Minimization are also restatements of existing ideas, so the systematization rather than the patterns is the novelty.

column3: ToolSafe: Enhancing Tool Invocation Safety of LLM-based agents via Proactive Step-level Guardrail and Feedback
column11: TS-Bench (step-level tool invocation safety detection, strict and loose modes) over AgentHarm-Traj, ASB-Traj and AgentDojo-Traj splits; guardrail baselines GPT-4o, Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-Guard-3-8B, Qwen3Guard-8B-Gen, ShieldAgent-THU, Safiron; guarded-agent evaluation on AgentDojo, ASB (Agent Security Bench) and AgentHarm with ASR/Utility and Refusal Rate/Task Completion; defense-framework baselines sandwich defense and LlamaFirewall (PromptGuard2 + Alignment Check)
column12: • Benchmark: We introduce TS-Bench, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for step-level tool invocation safety detection. (Contributions)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: ToolSafe; TS-Guard; TS-Flow. Coded benchmark_or_dataset because the paper's own three-fold contributions list leads with 'Benchmark: We introduce TS-Bench', with 'Method' (TS-Guard + TS-Flow) second — per the tie-break rule. proposes_defense is an equally strong fit by evaluation weight, and technique_name was left blank only because benchmark_or_dataset requires it; the defense names are recorded above. TS-Bench does label four unsafe patterns — MUR (Malicious User Request), PI (Prompt Injection), HT (Harmful Tools), BTRA (Benign Tools with Risky Arguments) — but these are taxonomy categories rather than named attacks other papers test against, so names_registry_technique is no. Agrees with current_registry_entry's 'ToolSafe (TS-Guard + TS-Flow)' as the defense names.

column3: RL Is a Hammer and LLMs Are Nails: A Simple Reinforcement Learning Recipe for Strong Prompt Injection
column11: InjecAgent dataset (Zhan et al. 2024) split 310 train / 100 val / 100 test; target models Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Meta-SecAlign-8B, Meta-SecAlign-70B, GPT-4o and GPT-5 with the Instruction Hierarchy defense (98% ASR on GPT-4o, 72% on GPT-5); comparison attacks Default Prompt, Enhanced prompt, GCG; detector evasion against perplexity, Llama-Prompt-Guard, ProtectAI-Guard and an LLM judge; diversity metrics BLEU, BERTScore, embedding distance, LLM judge; ablations on KL coefficient, joint training, soft vs hard reward, format reward
column12: To this end, we introduce RL-Hammer, a simple recipe for training attacker models that automatically learn to perform strong prompt injections and jailbreaks via reinforcement learning. (Abstract)
column14: DISAGREES with current_registry_entry, which files RL-Hammer under 'mechanism'. RL-Hammer is an adversarial attack technique (a GRPO-trained attacker model that rewrites injection goals), not a non-adversarial failure mode; contribution is proposes_attack and origin is invents. It builds on GRPO (Shao et al. 2024) as the RL algorithm and on automated red-teaming lineage (AdvPrompter, Perez et al.), but the attack recipe itself is new and trained from scratch with no warm-up data, so invents rather than improves. Useful for the SoK as evidence that named defenses (Instruction Hierarchy, SecAlign/Meta SecAlign) reported as near-0% ASR fall to a stronger automated attacker.

column3: PromptShield: Deployable Detection for Prompt Injection Attacks
column5: Conference on Data and Application Security and Privacy
column11: PromptShield benchmark eval split (Ultrachat, Alpaca, IFEval, LMSYS, databricks-dolly, natural-instructions, SPP benign data; FourAttacks, HackAPrompt, OpenPromptInject injections); compared against PromptGuard (Meta), ProtectAI DeBERTa detectors, InjecGuard, Lakera-style open-source detectors at target FPRs of 1%, 0.5%, 0.1%, 0.05%; appendix measures ASR of GPT-3.5-Turbo/GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini/Llama 3 and two adaptive injection attacks against the detector
column12: To support research in this area, we introduce PromptShield, a benchmark for training and evaluating deployable prompt injection detectors. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: PromptShield (benchmark plus the fine-tuned PromptShield detector). The paper's abstract leads with the benchmark and then the detector fine-tuned on it, so coded benchmark_or_dataset rather than proposes_defense; the registry entry calls it a defense, which is defensible but under-weights the benchmark as the lead contribution. It names no new attack: the attack data it curates (FourAttacks, HackAPrompt, OpenPromptInject) is all prior work, and the appendix's adaptive attacks are only labelled 'Attack A'/'Attack B'. Also contributes a deployment/threshold-calibration scheme for low-FPR operation.

column3: MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval
column11: MetaGPT DataInterpreter agent with GPT-4o, standard BM25 + FAISS union retrieval; 110 curated experience seeds (100 benign, 10 poisoned); measured by Poisoned Retrieval Proportion (PRP) on benign evaluation queries. Positioned relative to MINJA, PoisonedRAG, Phantom, CorruptRAG but no head-to-head baseline run. Two further attacks (Schema-Spoofing / ReAct Trace Injection, JudgeJacking rubric-mimicry) were built but excluded from the main results.
column12: We introduce MemoryGraft, a persistent memory poisoning attack that exploits the semantic imitation heuristic. (Introduction, Our contribution)
column14: Disagree with the current registry entry, which records MemoryGraft as a 'mechanism' with origin None: the paper explicitly frames it as a novel indirect-injection / memory-poisoning ATTACK that it invents. Evaluation is thin: the headline metric is retrieval share (PRP) of poisoned records, not downstream unsafe-action success rate, so persistence and 'behavioral drift' are argued mechanistically rather than measured end to end. Two additional named attack ideas (Schema-Spoofing, JudgeJacking) appear only in an appendix as excluded experiments.

column3: ReSum: Unlocking Long-Horizon Search Intelligence via Context Summarization
column11: GAIA (103-sample text-only validation subset), BrowseComp and BrowseComp-zh, Pass@1/Pass@3 accuracy; WebSailor-3B/7B/30B-A3B agents; baselines ReAct, Recent History (truncation), MEM1; summary tools Qwen3-30B, GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-235B, DeepSeek-R1-671B; LLM-as-a-judge scoring with Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct
column12: To overcome these limitations, we introduce ReSum, a lightweight, plug-and-play paradigm that enables unbounded exploration by periodically invoking an external tool to condense interaction histories into compact summaries. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around context-window exhaustion under ReAct's append-all-history growth, but every reported number is task accuracy (Pass@1/Pass@3) on GAIA, BrowseComp and BrowseComp-zh plus token-consumption curves; nothing measures degradation from long or noisy context itself (no dilution, distraction or lost-in-the-middle measurement). Registry calls it a 'defense'; there is no adversary anywhere in the paper, so proposes_fix is the right slot. ReSum names no failure mode of its own.

column3: Embedding-based classifiers can detect prompt injection attacks
column11: Self-curated dataset of 467,057 benign and malicious prompts assembled from Hugging Face datasets; embeddings from OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, gte-large and all-MiniLM-L6-v2; AUC/accuracy comparison of Logistic Regression vs XGBoost vs Random Forest, plus comparison against open-source encoder-only prompt-injection classifiers (ProtectAI DeBERTa-v3, Meta Prompt Guard); PCA/t-SNE/UMAP visualisation for RQ1
column12: In this paper, we propose a novel approach based on embedding-based Machine Learning (ML) classifiers to protect LLM-based applications against this severe threat. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: (none - the detector is never given a name). Coded applies_existing rather than proposes_defense because every component is off-the-shelf (three public embedding models, three standard sklearn/XGBoost classifiers) and the contribution is the pipeline plus the curated dataset; the registry's 'UNNAMED: embedding-based traditional-ML classifier, needs_read' is confirmed as unnamed. A defender-side paper that names no attack or failure mode. Note AUCs are modest (0.608-0.764 in Table 3) despite the abstract's claim of outperforming state-of-the-art detectors.

column3: Dynamic Parametric Retrieval Augmented Generation for Test-time Knowledge Enhancement
column11: F1 on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, PopQA and ComplexWebQuestions with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, LLaMA-3.2-1B-Instruct, LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct; baselines Vanilla, Standard RAG, PRAG, PRAG-Combine; inference/training/storage cost comparison; RAGTruth benchmark with GPT-4o as judge comparing standard RAG vs DyPRAG-Combine; appendix analysis of contextual-vs-parametric knowledge conflict
column12: To address these challenges, we propose Dynamic Parametric RAG (DyPRAG), a novel framework that leverages a lightweight parameter translator model to efficiently convert documents into parametric knowledge. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The abstract claims DyPRAG resolves knowledge conflicts and mitigates RAG hallucination, but the main evaluation is F1 accuracy on four QA datasets (2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, PopQA, CWQ) plus inference/training/storage cost; the knowledge-conflict and hallucination claims rest on a secondary RAGTruth comparison judged by GPT-4o and on qualitative appendix case studies, with no measured conflict rate or hallucination rate reduction. Explicitly an extension of PRAG, so improves_existing, not the registry's 'proposed'. belongs_in_corpus marked unsure because the paper's core concern is RAG cost/efficiency and parametric knowledge injection rather than context becoming untrustworthy; the knowledge-conflict framing is what keeps it borderline in scope.

column3: ChatInject: Abusing Chat Templates for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
column11: AgentDojo and InjecAgent benchmarks, attack success rate; compared against traditional plain-text indirect prompt injection baselines (default InjecPrompt and hand-crafted/automated injections), reported as 5.18% -> 32.05% on AgentDojo and 15.13% -> 45.90% on InjecAgent, with Multi-turn reaching 52.33% on InjecAgent; transferability across frontier open and closed-source LLMs (Qwen-3, gpt-oss, Llama-4, Grok-2, GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2, GPT-4o, Gemini); robustness against existing prompt-based defenses
column12: To this end, we introduce ChatInject, an attack that formats malicious payloads to mimic native chat templates, thereby exploiting the model's inherent instruction-following tendencies. (Abstract)
column14: Disagree with the current registry entry, which lists ChatInject as a 'mechanism' with origin None: this is squarely a newly invented attack technique, evaluated with attack success rates on two established injection benchmarks. Related work is woven into the introduction rather than given its own section; the parent lineage it positions against is indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., AgentDojo) and chat-template vulnerabilities (ChatBug).

column3: Memory as Action: Autonomous Context Curation for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
column11: Multi-objective HotpotQA-derived QA (up to 8 objectives, 200 samples/level), 2WikiMultihopQA, Bamboogle, HotpotQA, Musique, Frames, BrowseComp-Plus; baselines Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct full context, Sliding Window, Summarization, A-MEM, MEM1, Tongyi-DeepResearch, Search-R1; metrics task accuracy (LLM judge, three-pass consensus), solved sub-objective count, total tokens, tool-call frequency
column12: We propose Memory-as-Action (MemAct), a framework that treats working memory management as learnable policy actions. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself on attention dilution, context saturation with irrelevant information and 'lost-in-the-middle' behaviour, and coins 'Context Curation' for the problem, but the evaluation measures only task accuracy on multi-hop QA / deep-research benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, Bamboogle, Musique, Frames, BrowseComp-Plus) plus efficiency numbers (average context length reduced 51%, token counts, tool-call counts). No measurement of attention dilution, positional degradation or lost-in-the-middle is reported. DEFENSE-NAMES: Memory-as-Action (MemAct); Dynamic Context Policy Optimization (DCPO). Disagree with current_registry_entry labelling MemAct a 'defense': there is no adversary - it addresses a non-adversarial context-management failure, so proposes_fix.

column3: Invisible Injections: Exploiting Vision-Language Models Through Steganographic Prompt Embedding
column7: mechanism: steganographic prompt injection (multi-domain ; defense: Multi-Layer Defense Framework (preprocessing +
column11: 12 datasets and 8 VLMs (GPT-4V 16.2% ASR, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14.8%, Gemini Pro Vision 18.3%, LLaVA); embedding methods adaptive LSB, DCT frequency-domain, neural steganography (overall 24.3% ASR, neural up to 31.8%); imperceptibility via PSNR/SSIM; robustness to JPEG compression, Gaussian noise, scaling, rotation, brightness/contrast, format conversion and platform pipelines; defense evaluation against chi-square, RS, SPA and WS steganalysis, CNN detectors and preprocessing defenses; baseline comparison to direct adversarial examples, patch-based attacks and traditional prompt injection
column12: We present the first comprehensive study of steganographic prompt injection attacks against VLMs, where malicious instructions are invisibly embedded within images using advanced steganographic techniques. (Abstract)
column14: Single-author independent-researcher arXiv preprint; the printed 'evaluation' material is largely protocol description (power analysis, Bonferroni correction, 5-fold CV) with aggregate ASR numbers and no released artifact mentioned - treat the reported numbers with caution. It also proposes countermeasures (multi-layer preprocessing/detection defense), but the contributions list leads with the attack framework, so proposes_attack. Registry entry already lists both the attack mechanism and the Multi-Layer Defense Framework; the attack is the lead contribution.

column3: BadRAG: Identifying Vulnerabilities in Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
column11: Retrieval attack on NQ, MS MARCO and SQuAD corpora with Contriever, DPR and ANCE retrievers; generative attacks (denial-of-service AaaA, sentiment-steer SFaaA) on LLaMA-2, GPT-4 and Claude-3; robustness against passage-embedding-norm defense and perplexity/average-token-log-likelihood fluency detection
column12: In this paper, we propose BadRAG to identify the vulnerabilities and attacks on retrieval parts (RAG database) and their indirect attacks on generative parts (LLMs). (Abstract)
column14: Registry lists BadRAG as 'mechanism'; it is an adversarial corpus-poisoning attack, so proposes_attack is the better label. Evaluation genuinely measures retrieval rate and downstream generation harm, not just task utility. Sub-attack acronyms AaaA/SFaaA appear in the evaluation section; MCOP is the optimization used to craft retrieval triggers.

column3: F2A: An Innovative Approach for Prompt Injection by Utilizing Feign Security Detection Agents
column7: mechanism: F2A (Feign Agent Attack); defense: Defe-Prompt
column11: unsure - the paper reports qualitative injection case studies against commercial LLM services (figures show GLM-4-Plus and DeepSeek-V2.5) using F2A prompts across harmful contexts (e.g. Weapon, Fraud); no quantitative ASR table was located in the retrieved text
column12: Hence, this paper proposed an attack named Feign Agent Attack (F2A). (Abstract)
column14: Short arXiv paper with no related-work section and a thin, largely qualitative evaluation; the extractor's 'evaluation' block is actually the contributions list. The three attack stages are named (Convert Malicious Content; Feign Security Detection Results; Construct Task Instruction). The registry also lists a defense 'Defe-Prompt'; I could not confirm that name in the retrieved text - the paper only recommends that LLMs critically evaluate agent detection results. Registry's current_origin=ambiguous resolved to invents.

column3: Efficient Universal Goal Hijacking with Semantics-guided Prompt Organization
column11: Alpaca-derived normal user prompts (1,000-prompt candidate pool, sampled training/test sets) against Llama-2-7b-chat-hf, Vicuna-7b-v1.5, Guanaco-7B-HF and Mistral-7B-Instruct, with ten types of target responses; ASR and time/convergence compared against M-GCG and random-ordering ablations of the sampling and ranking strategies
column12: To this end, we propose a method called POUGH that incorporates an efficient optimization algorithm and two semantics-guided prompt organization strategies. (Abstract)
column14: Registry has no origin recorded; the paper explicitly positions POUGH as a faster, prompt-aware replacement for SOTA M-GCG, so origin=improves. The attack is direct (fixed adversarial suffix concatenated to user prompts) rather than indirect context poisoning, but it is squarely a prompt-injection/goal-hijacking attack on model context, so it belongs.

column3: TrojanRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Can Be Backdoor Driver in Large Language Models
column11: NQ, WebQuestions, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO (fact-checking), SST-2 and AGNews (classification), BBQ (harmful bias) and AdvBench-V3 (backdoor-style jailbreaking); retrievers DPR, BGE-Large-En-V1.5, UAE-Large-V1; victim LLMs Vicuna, LLaMA-2, ChatGLM, Gemma, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4; baselines clean RAG and a prompt-based in-context-learning backdoor; metrics EMR/KMR and harmful ratio
column12: Specifically, the adversary constructs elaborate target contexts and trigger sets. (Abstract)
column14: Registry labels it 'mechanism'; it is a deliberate joint backdoor/poisoning attack on the retrieval corpus, so proposes_attack with origin=invents. The paper also names three attack scenarios (Deceptive Model Manipulation; Unsurprising Diffusion and Malicious Harm; Inductive Alignment Jailbreaking). No related-work section was found in the extracted text.

column3: MobileSafetyBench: Evaluating Safety of Autonomous Agents in Mobile Device Control
column11: 250-task Android-emulator suite (100 low-risk, 100 high-risk daily-scenario tasks plus 50 high-risk indirect-prompt-injection tasks) run with GPT-5, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama-3.2-90B-Vision, Grok-2, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Pixtral-Large, Phi-4 and OpenAI-o1, plus the SeeAct and M3A agent workflows; metrics goal achievement rate, refusal rate, and number of successful defenses against injection; SCoT prompting compared against basic prompting and QA-format risk detection
column12: We introduce a novel benchmark platform for evaluating the helpfulness and safety of agents controlling mobile devices in realistic interactive environments. (Contributions)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Safety-guided Chain-of-Thought (SCoT). Disagreement with registry: the registry records only the SCoT defense, but the paper's contributions list leads with the benchmark platform and SCoT is a secondary prompting method, so the primary contribution is benchmark_or_dataset. The benchmark names no reusable attack or failure mode - its injection tasks are generic indirect prompt injections embedded in messages - hence names_registry_technique=no. Note the injection results are strikingly weak defensively (3/50, 8/50, 15/50 defenses for GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5 and Claude-3.5).

column3: Poisoning Retrieval Corpora by Injecting Adversarial Passages
column11: BEIR benchmark, focusing on Natural Questions and MS MARCO, with transfer to seven unseen domains (HotpotQA, FiQA, Quora, FEVER, TREC-COVID, ArguAna, SCIDOCS). Dense retrievers attacked: Contriever, Contriever-ms, DPR-nq, DPR-mul, ANCE, and the multi-vector retriever ColBERT. Metric: top-k attack success rate with 1-500 injected adversarial passages.
column12: We present a novel corpus poisoning attack, where a malicious user can inject a small fraction of adversarial passages to a retrieval corpus, with the aim of fooling systems into returning them among the top retrieved results. (Introduction)
column14: DISAGREE WITH REGISTRY: current entry codes this as 'mechanism: UNNAMED: gradient-based corpus poisoning'. It is a deliberate adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial mechanism, and the paper does name it ('corpus poisoning attack'), a name widely cited and tested against by later RAG-poisoning work. The optimization is adapted from HotFlip (Ebrahimi et al., 2018) plus k-means clustering for multiple passages, but the attack itself is the paper's own.

column3: Goal-Guided Generative Prompt Injection Attack on Large Language Models
column11: Seven LLMs (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo, ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2-7b and others) on four datasets including SQuAD2.0, GSM8K and a Math dataset; compared against black-box baselines BertAttack, DeepWordBug, TextFooler, TextBugger, PromptBench, Semantic and CheckList; metrics Clean Acc, Attack Acc, ASR, plus a transfer-success-rate matrix and ablations on insertion position and the epsilon/delta parameters.
column12: Then we designed a simple and effective goal-guided generative prompt injection strategy (G2PIA) to find an injection text that satisfies specific constraints to achieve the optimal attack effect approximately. (Abstract)
column14: DISAGREE WITH REGISTRY: entry codes G2PIA as 'mechanism'; it is a deliberate black-box prompt injection attack, so contribution should be proposes_attack. Note this is a direct (user-channel) injection of noise text into the prompt, not indirect/retrieved context; relevance to context poisoning is partial.

column3: Counterfactual Evaluation for Blind Attack Detection in LLM-based Evaluation Systems
column7: mechanism: Blind attacks; defense: SE+CFE (Standard Evaluation + Counterfactual E
column11: Six English QA datasets (GSM8k train, HotpotQA train, SQuAD 1.1, StrategyQA train, TriviaQA unfiltered v1.0 and one further set) with evaluator models o1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5-turbo; blind attack instances are direct prompt injection and rewording attacks; Standard Evaluation (SE) is the baseline and SE+CFE the proposed framework, measured by attack detection and evaluation accuracy trade-off.
column12: We formalize a class of threats called blind attacks, where a candidate answer is crafted independently of the true answer to deceive the evaluator. (Abstract)
column14: Agrees with registry (mechanism: Blind attacks; defense: SE+CFE), except that blind attacks are adversarial, so 'attack' rather than 'mechanism' is the right label. Contributions list leads with formalizing blind attacks, hence proposes_attack over proposes_defense; the SE+CFE defense is the second contribution. Note the concrete attack actually measured is mostly the rewording attack, since the authors report modern LLMs resist direct prompt injection in this setting.

column3: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Control: Defending Agentic Harness Against Trojan Backdoors
column7: mechanism: ClawTrojan multi-step trojan/backdoor attack p; defense: DASGuard
column11: The authors' own ClawTrojan benchmark in an OpenClaw-style simulated workspace (919-step completeness/validity checks, up to 12 turns) with GPT-5.4, GLM-5.1 and DS-V4-Flash as no-defense baselines; defenses compared are ClawKeeper, StruQ, MELON, PromptShield-1B, PromptShield-8B, CaMeL and the proposed DASGuard; metrics ASR, FC-ASR, Penetration, Doc-False, Side-Eff, Task-Dev, Disclosure, Latency. AgentDojo and InjecAgent are also run and reported as producing near-zero ASR on current models.
column12: To reveal this threat, we introduce ClawTrojan, a benchmark designed to identify multi-step trojan attacks in local agentic harnesses. (Abstract)
column14: Agrees with registry (mechanism: ClawTrojan multi-step trojan/backdoor attack; defense: DASGuard). Contributions list leads with identifying the multi-step trojan threat, then the ClawTrojan benchmark, then the DASGuard defense, so coded proposes_attack rather than benchmark_or_dataset - but it is nearly equally defensible as benchmark_or_dataset since the threat is operationalized entirely through ClawTrojan. Defense name: DASGuard (Detect-Attribute-Sanitize).

column3: Safe to Check, Unsafe to Use: Relinking at the Compression Boundary of LLM Agents
column7: mechanism: Relinking; defense: KBRA (Keyed Binding Reassembly Audit)
column11: 619 samples derived from four long-context agent benchmarks - AgentDojo, ASB, InjecAgent and tau^2-bench - with paired clean-split controls (86.9% Relink Rate and Backend Action Rate vs 17.0% control); mechanism probes on attention gap, typed-slot log-prob gap and helpfulness utility gap; generalization across compression rates, summarization prompts, compressors and backend models (default Gemma-4-31B-it); case studies on OpenClaw and Claude Code; 11 representative defenses evaluated and found insufficient; KBRA reduces residual Backend Action Rate to 0.0% (exact matcher) with adaptive-adversary analysis.
column12: We identify a new compression-boundary vulnerability, relinking, in which the compressor acts as a confused deputy: it summarizes distributed, locally benign fragments into a complete and malicious backend-actionable instruction. (Abstract)
column14: Broadly agrees with registry (mechanism: Relinking; defense: KBRA), but the coding is genuinely two-sided: the paper argues relinking is an ENDOGENOUS, non-adversarial property of summarization-based compressors (which would make it proposes_mechanism), while everything it measures is the attacker-induced form via the Relink tool and ASR-style metrics, so proposes_attack is the better fit for what was evaluated. Defense names: Keyed Binding Reassembly Audit (KBRA). Distinguished by the authors from payload splitting, which reconstructs a complete instruction already present in the source.

column3: Rewriting the Response Path: Silent Tampering and Provider-Signed Defense in BYOK LLM Agents
column7: mechanism: RTA-PostForge (response-path tampering attack); defense: sign-c (server-side signing of execution-beari
column11: SWE-bench Django (SWE-bench Verified) paired with a ControlArena-style security side-task, 12 of 18 issues x 5 models = 60 instances; APPS at scale (100 problems per model); AgentDojo and ASB for general agent tasks; five models gpt-5.4, gemini-3.1-pro, claude-opus-4.6, glm-5.1, MiniMax-M2.5; all run through new-api, a real open-source BYOK relay. Baselines: Honest, Prompt injection, RTA-PreWrite vs RTA-PostForge, measured by utility (public-test pass rate) and security-defeat (hidden-oracle failure). Defense sign-c compared against Direct/Trusted relay/Hop-by-hop TLS/Agent-side detection/Full-path encryption/Whole-response signing, with 0.0167% latency overhead and zero false rejections.
column12: We show that this trust is misplaced under the Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) configuration used by roughly 88% of mainstream real-world agents, where traffic passes through a user-authorized relay. (Abstract)
column14: Agrees with registry (mechanism: RTA-PostForge; defense: sign-c). The contributions list technically leads with the 'Response-Path Integrity Gap' (a vulnerability, not a technique), with 'Attack Construction: We build RTA' second, so proposes_attack is the right code. Scope note: the untrusted content here enters on the model-to-agent response path via an authorized relay rather than through retrieved/tool context, so it extends the corpus boundary; it is still an agent executing content it should not trust. Defense names: sign-c; canonical execution contract kappa(c).

column3: Manipulating Multimodal Agents via Cross-Modal Prompt Injection
column11: Two custom VQA agents (RecipeMaster, PoetryGenius) on Qwen2-VL and Phi-3.5-vision; injected tasks from CoEDIT and SST2; baselines JIP, FB, and a Naive direct-instruction baseline; metrics ASR and PNA; plus a real-world multimodal autonomous driving agent.
column12: Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art attacks, achieving at least a +30.1% increase in attack success rates across diverse tasks. (Abstract)
column14: Registry lists this as 'mechanism: CrossInject' with origin None; disagree on both counts - this is a deliberately adversarial cross-modal prompt injection ATTACK that the authors invent, not a non-adversarial failure mechanism. Two sub-components (Visual Latent Alignment, Textual Guidance Enhancement) are named within the framework.

column3: May I have your Attention? Breaking Fine-Tuning based Prompt Injection Defenses using Architecture-Aware Attacks
column9: ASTRA (short for Adversarial Subversion through Targeted Redirection of Attention)
column11: Fine-tuning-based prompt injection defenses SecAlign, SecAlign++ and StruQ; baseline attacks GCG and an unguided greedy search, and Attn-GCG weighting variants; 50 AlpacaFarm evaluation examples with a 'Print exactly Hacked!' payload; attacker budget scaled in injected tokens.
column12: Specifically, we construct a novel attention-based attack algorithm for textual LLMs and apply it to three recent whitebox defenses SecAlign (CCS 2025), SecAlign++, and StruQ (USENIX Security 2025), showing attacks with success rates of up to 85-95% on unseen prompts with modest increase in attacker budget in terms of tokens. (Abstract)
column14: Registry says 'mechanism: ASTRA (and ASTRA++)' with origin None; disagree - this is an adversarial attack, invented by the authors, not a non-adversarial mechanism. It is architecture-aware (attention-based) rather than a GCG variant, though ASTRA++ uses GCG-style search as a sub-routine; the paper explicitly distinguishes itself from Attn-GCG.

column3: ObliInjection: Order-Oblivious Prompt Injection Attack to LLM Agents with Multi-source Data
column11: Three datasets spanning diverse application domains (incl. Amazon Reviews) and twelve LLMs; existing single-source prompt injection attacks and RAG poisoning attacks as baselines; prevention defenses (incl. SecAlign, and an adaptively fine-tuned Llama-3-8B-SecAlign-Adapt) and detection defenses (perplexity/PPL, DataSentinel) reported with FPR/FNR; leave-one-segment-out and segment deletion ablations; varying 1 contaminated segment out of 6-100.
column12: In this work, we propose ObliInjection, the first prompt injection attack targeting LLM applications and agents with multi-source input data. (Abstract)
column14: Registry says 'mechanism: ObliInjection' with origin None; disagree - it is an invented adversarial attack. Two named sub-contributions, the order-oblivious loss and the orderGCG algorithm; orderGCG is an adaptation of GCG, but the paper's headline contribution is the attack itself, so origin is invents rather than improves.

column3: Supply-Chain Poisoning Attacks Against LLM Coding Agent Skill Ecosystems
column11: 1,070 generated adversarial skills from 81 seeds across 15 MITRE ATT&CK categories, run against four agent frameworks (Claude Code, OpenHands, Codex, Gemini CLI) and five models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GLM-4.7, MiniMax-M2.5); baseline is natural-language explicit instruction injection; metrics Bypass Rate and Direct Execution Rate; static analysis detectors; responsible-disclosure outcomes.
column12: We introduce Document-Driven Implicit Payload Execution (DDIPE), which embeds malicious logic in code examples and configuration templates within skill documentation. (Abstract)
column14: Registry lists 'mechanism: PoisonedSkills / DDIPE' with origin None; disagree on origin - the authors invent DDIPE, and PoisonedSkills is their generation pipeline/framework name used in the evaluation section. Note the baseline is weak by the authors' own admission ('evaluating DDIPE against more sophisticated injection baselines remains future work'), and the headline 11.6%-33.5% bypass rate counts mere code generation, not execution; direct execution is as low as 2.3% under Claude Code.

column3: Synapse: Trajectory-as-Exemplar Prompting with Memory for Computer Control
column11: MiniWoB++ (64 tasks, average success rate, demonstrations from 48 tasks, incl. book-flight) and Mind2Web (average step success rate), compared against prior ICL prompting schemes such as RCI and MindAct.
column12: First, the limited context length of LLMs and complex computer states restrict the number of exemplars, as a single webpage can consume the entire context. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper is framed around context problems - limited context length, raw states cluttered with task-irrelevant information, and it cites Lost in the Middle - and its state-abstraction component is explicitly a filter for task-irrelevant context. But the evaluation measures ONLY capability: average success rate on MiniWoB++ (99.2%) and average step success rate on Mind2Web, with no measurement of context dilution, distraction, token budget effects, or any harm from irrelevant context in isolation. No evaluation or related-work heading was found by the extractor; section locations above come from the abstract and body text. Registry calls SYNAPSE a 'defense'; disagree - there is no adversary anywhere in this paper, so 'fix' for a non-adversarial context problem is the right code. Borderline in-scope: the untrustworthy content here is merely irrelevant, never planted.

column3: PromptSleuth: Detecting Prompt Injection via Semantic Intent Invariance
column11: PROMPTSLEUTH-BENCH (Easy/Medium/Hard tiers, subsuming two prior prompt injection benchmarks plus new manipulation techniques and multi-task scenarios); eight existing defenses evaluated on it - Instructional, Sandwich, Random_Sequence, Delimiter, Known-Answer, SecAlign, DataSentinel, PromptArmor - with FPR/FNR; PromptSleuth itself evaluated on the same benchmarks across GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1 and GPT-5, plus runtime and token overhead.
column12: To address this gap, we construct a new benchmark that systematically extends prior efforts. (Abstract)
column14: Dual contribution: the paper proposes both PROMPTSLEUTH-BENCH and the PromptSleuth defense.
