Coded benchmark_or_dataset because the paper's own contributions list leads with the benchmark bullet ('We construct PROMPTSLEUTH-BENCH...') before the defense bullet; registry records only 'defense: PromptSleuth', which misses the benchmark half. technique_name left blank per the benchmark_or_dataset rule, but the defense is named PromptSleuth. names_registry_technique is yes because the paper introduces a three-way named taxonomy of prompt injection categories (System Prompt Forgery, User Prompt Camouflage, Model Behavior Manipulation) alongside the defense; these are attack categories it introduces rather than previously-established named attacks, so a reviewer may wish to downgrade this to no.

column3: When Bots Take the Bait: Exposing and Mitigating the Emerging Social Engineering Attack in Web Automation Agent
column11: Five web agent frameworks (Browser Use, Skyvern-AI, Agent-E, LiteWebAgent, SeeAct) with GPT-4o; 500 generated web tasks across 20 attack-vector classes (five inducement contexts x four attack objectives) instantiated under five attack patterns; external-validity replication on real-world pages; SUPERVISOR compared against existing lightweight defenses on ASR reduction, 7.7% runtime overhead and usability.
column12: Empirical results show that mainstream frameworks are highly vulnerable to AGENTBAIT, with an average attack success rate of 67.5% and peaks above 80% under specific strategies (e.g., trusted identity forgery). (Abstract)
column14: Dual attack+defense paper; coded proposes_attack because the abstract and contributions lead with the attack side. Registry entry (mechanism: AGENTBAIT; defense: SUPERVISOR, proposed) is substantively right, except AGENTBAIT is an adversarial attack paradigm rather than a non-adversarial mechanism. Named inducement strategies within AGENTBAIT: Trusted Entity, Urgency, Social Proof, Contextual Integration, Reward; named objectives: Permission Abuse, Malicious Download, Personal Disclosure, Sensitive Disclosure. Note the attack pages are purpose-built simplified templates rather than cloned real sites, with a smaller real-world replication for external validity. The defense is named SUPERVISOR.

column3: Demystifying RCE Vulnerabilities in LLM-Integrated Apps
column11: 11 LLM-integrated frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Pandas-ai, Langflow, Pandas-llm, Auto-GPT, Griptape, Lagent, MetaGPT, vanna, langroid) yielding 51 call chains, 18 user-level APIs and 20 vulnerabilities; call-chain extraction compared against the PyCG baseline; 51 collected real-world apps of which 17 were successfully exploited (16 RCE, 1 SQL injection); post-exploitation attacks demonstrated (output hijacking, API-key theft, phishing); RQ1-RQ3 on detection accuracy, app collection and prompt attack effectiveness.
column12: In this study, we propose LLMSmith to detect, validate and exploit the RCE vulnerabilities in LLM-integrated frameworks and apps. (Abstract)
column14: Registry says 'mechanism: LLMSmith: prompt-injection-to-RCE exploitation' with origin None; agree on the substance, disagree on origin (the authors invent LLMSmith) and on 'mechanism' (this is a deliberate exploitation pipeline, not a non-adversarial failure mode). Borderline between proposes_attack and measurement_study: the contributions list leads with a static-analysis detection method for vulnerable call chains and the paper reads as a vulnerability-discovery measurement (20 vulns, 13 CVEs, $1350 bounty), but the named artifact LLMSmith is an end-to-end exploitation framework and the prompt-based exploitation method (hallucination test + LLM escaping) is the part the SoK cares about, so proposes_attack is the better fit. The context-poisoning relevance is that prompt injection is the delivery vector that reaches hazardous code-execution APIs.

column3: Pandora: Jailbreak GPTs by Retrieval Augmented Generation Poisoning
column5: Workshop on AI Systems with Confidential COmputing
column11: Four OpenAI content-policy violation scenarios (Adult, Harmful, Privacy, Illegal), 10 prompts per scenario x 10 iterations (100 tests per scenario), on GPTs backed by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; baseline is direct jailbreak prompting of ChatGPT on the same models (3.0% and 1.0% success); manual inspection for relevance and content quality.
column12: To fill this gap, we investigate indirect jailbreak attacks on LLMs, particularly GPTs, introducing a novel attack vector named Retrieval Augmented Generation Poisoning. (Abstract)
column14: Registry says 'mechanism: PANDORA (RAG Poisoning jailbreak)' with origin None; disagree on both - it is an invented adversarial attack. The paper self-describes the evaluation as preliminary (workshop paper, 32k chars, no related-work heading found, small scale forced by the 40-queries-per-3-hours GPTs limit), and success is judged by manual inspection with no inter-rater procedure. Important for the SoK as an early named instance of poisoned retrieved documents being used to carry a jailbreak, i.e. the attacker's content enters through the RAG knowledge base rather than the user prompt.

column3: Agent Skills Enable a New Class of Realistic and Trivially Simple Prompt Injections
column11: Hand-built malicious Agent Skill (modified Anthropic pptx skill + file_backup.py exfiltration script) run against Claude Code and the Claude Web Interface; demonstration only, no ASR numbers, no baselines.
column12: Although Agent Skills can be a very useful tool, we show that they are fundamentally insecure, since they enable trivially simple prompt injections. (Summary/Abstract)
column14: Short demo report (5 pages). The attack is never given a name - it is prompt injection via Agent Skill files plus carry-over of a 'Don't ask again' approval to a related harmful action. Evaluation is two qualitative case demonstrations (screenshots), no quantitative measurement. Registry calls it 'mechanism: UNNAMED skill-file prompt injection'; I disagree with 'mechanism' - this is deliberately adversarial, so proposes_attack, though the UNNAMED part is right.

column3: Follow My Instruction and Spill the Beans: Scalable Data Extraction from Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
column11: Retrieval-In-Context RAG built on Llama2, Mistral/Mixtral, Vicuna, SOLAR, WizardLM, Qwen1.5 and Platypus2 (extraction/repeat rates, effect of RAG setup and position bias); plus production GPTs: 25 customized GPTs from the GPT store (100% datastore-leak ASR within 2 queries) and reconstruction-rate experiments on a Harry Potter GPT (77k words, 41%) and a Wikipedia-corpus GPT (1.57M words, 3%).
column12: We investigate Prompt-Injected Data Extraction, an attack that extracts data from the datastore of a RAG system. (Conclusion)
column14: Registry labels this 'mechanism'; it is an adversarial, deliberately crafted extraction attack, so proposes_attack is the better code. Also measures a mitigation (position-bias elimination) but that is secondary.

column3: How Not to Detect Prompt Injections with an LLM
column11: DataSentinel (a Strong known-answer-detection defense, fine-tuned Mistral-7B detector) and an instruction-fine-tuned detector baseline; Combined Attack as the attack baseline; 500 detection instructions for key extraction and 7 target/injected tasks (DupDet, GramCor, HateDet, NLI, SentAna, SpamDet, Summary), 100 samples each, with GPT-4.1, Llama 4 Scout, Claude 4 Sonnet and Deepseek-R1 as backend LLMs; metrics are extraction rate, detection rate, FNR/FPR and ASV.
column12: To exploit this fundamental vulnerability, we methodically design an adaptive attack, DataFlip. (Abstract)
column14: Also contributes a formal characterization of known-answer detection (two axioms, Type II failures) - but the contributions list leads with the vulnerability analysis and culminates in DataFlip, a named adaptive attack. Registry labels it 'mechanism: DataFlip'; it is an attack, not a non-adversarial mechanism.

column3: Backdoored Retrievers for Prompt Injection Attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
column7: mechanism: UNNAMED: retriever fine-tuning backdoor attack
column11: Llama-3-8B, Vicuna-7B and Mistral-7B as generators with GTE-large-en-v1.5 as retriever; three attack objectives (link insertion, advertising, denial of service) across six directive-strength levels and all 10 injection positions in the retrieved set; corpus poisoning vs retriever-fine-tuning backdoor compared by attack success rate on standard retrieval corpora.
column12: We build upon existing corpus poisoning techniques and propose a novel backdoor attack aimed at the fine-tuning process of the dense retriever component. (Abstract)
column14: The backdoor attack is never given a name. Novelty is in the threat model (backdoor planted during retriever fine-tuning, and objectives beyond misinformation: malicious links, advertising, DoS) rather than a new mechanism, so origin=improves. Registry's 'UNNAMED retriever fine-tuning backdoor attack' is accurate, though it labels it 'mechanism' where proposes_attack fits.

column3: TopicAttack: An Indirect Prompt Injection Attack via Topic Transition
column11: Inj-SQuAD and Inj-TriviaQA (900 samples each, phishing/advertisement/propaganda injections) for chatbots and InjecAgent 'Direct Harm' (510 samples) for agents; attack baselines Naive, Ignore, Escape-Character, Fake completion and Combined; defenses Sandwich, Spotlight, StruQ and SecAlign; victim models Llama3-8B/70B, Llama3.1-8B/70B/405B, Qwen2-7B/72B, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1; metric is ASR, plus an injected-to-original attention-ratio analysis.
column12: Motivated by the limitations of existing attack methods, we propose TopicAttack, which prompts the LLM to generate a fabricated conversational transition prompt that gradually shifts the topic toward the injected instruction, making the injection smoother and enhancing the plausibility and success of the attack. (Abstract)
column14: Registry labels it 'mechanism: TopicAttack'; it is a deliberate attack, so proposes_attack. Evaluation is thorough and matches the claim (ASR over 90% in most settings, including under StruQ/SecAlign).

column3: Scalable Multi-Robot Collaboration with Large Language Models: Centralized or Decentralized Systems?
column7: defense: HMAS-2 (Hybrid Multi-Agent System with feedbac
column11: Four simulated multi-robot warehouse environments (BoxNet1, BoxNet2, Warehouse, BoxLift) with 4-32 robots, 10 trials each, comparing DMAS, CMAS, HMAS-1 and HMAS-2 on task success rate, steps per plan, tokens per plan and API calls per plan; plus 3D simulation demonstrations.
column12: In this work, we compare the task success rate and token efficiency of four multi-agent communication frameworks (centralized, decentralized, and two hybrid) as applied to four coordination-dependent multi-agent 2D task scenarios for increasing numbers of agents. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper motivates itself partly with context-window pressure and the claim that 'the immediately relevant information in the context can become diluted in longer prompts', but the evaluation measures only multi-robot planning capability and efficiency: task success rate, number of steps per plan, tokens per plan and API calls per plan on BoxNet1/BoxNet2/Warehouse/BoxLift. Nothing measures dilution, distraction or information loss, and no content in this setting is untrusted. This row is borderline out_of_scope (pure robot task-planning, ICRA, 2023) and I flag it as such; kept in the corpus per Ruling 1 since the stated motivation is a context problem. Disagree with the registry's 'defense: HMAS-2' - there is no adversary anywhere in this paper, so HMAS-2 is at most a fix for context/token pressure, not a defense.

column3: Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks in Generative AI Systems: A Hybrid SIEM and One-Class SVM Framework
column7: defense: UNNAMED: Hybrid SIEM + One-Class SVM prompt-in
column11: 1100 prompts: 900 malicious from CySecBench stratified across direct injection, indirect injection, token smuggling, context hijacking and role-based jailbreak (180 each), 200 benign from Stanford Alpaca; three incremental scenarios (keyword-filter baseline, +SIEM rules R1-R4, +OCSVM) on a Phi-3 Mini Instruct gateway; metrics precision 0.971, recall 0.810, F1 0.883, ASR 19.0%, FPR, MTTD 2.3 s, AUC-ROC.
column12: This paper presents a hybrid detection framework that instruments a Phi-3 Mini Instruct gateway to emit structured telemetry, correlates events in Elastic SIEM using four expert-authored detection rules, and augments rule coverage with a One-Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM) trained exclusively on 1200 benign interactions. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: UNNAMED hybrid SIEM + One-Class SVM detection framework (four expert-authored SIEM detection rules R1-R4; OCSVM behavioural-anomaly layer). Coded applies_existing rather than proposes_defense because the pipeline is assembled from off-the-shelf components (Elastic SIEM correlation, OCSVM one-class anomaly detection, keyword gateway filter) and is never given a name; the novelty claimed is the SOC-level integration and session-level visibility. No adaptive attacker is considered, the benign test set is small (200 Alpaca prompts) and the attack corpus is jailbreak-heavy CySecBench rather than agentic IPI. Broadly agrees with the registry entry.

column3: Your Agent is More Brittle Than You Think: Uncovering Indirect Injection Vulnerabilities in Agentic LLMs
column11: AgentDojo Banking suite extended to 576 test scenarios (16 user tasks x 9 injection objectives), four IPI attack vectors (ignore-previous-instructions, AgentDojo direct task modification, InjecAgent-style tool-content injections, Stealth/obfuscated prompt attacks; 144 cases each) against six defenses (Prompt Warning, Sandwich Method, Paraphrasing, Spotlighting, Keyword Filtering, LLM-as-a-Judge) on nine open-source backbones (Qwen-2.5/3, Llama-3-8B, GLM-4-9B, Gemma-3-12B, Mistral-7B); metrics Hijack Rate, Utility, behavioural dynamics, Resistance Rate, Semantic Compliance, log-probability and entropy; then a RepE probe/circuit breaker measured by detection accuracy.
column12: To bridge this gap, we systematically evaluate six defense strategies against four sophisticated IPI attack vectors across nine LLM backbones. (Abstract)
column14: The contributions list leads with the systematic evaluation ('We construct a specialized study...', 'By benchmarking six defense strategies across nine open-source backbones...'), so measurement_study rather than proposes_defense; the RepE-based circuit breaker is contribution (iii) and is never given a name. It names no new attack - its four vectors are borrowed (Perez & Ribeiro ignore attack, AgentDojo, InjecAgent, Stealth attacks). Registry entry calls it 'defense: UNNAMED Representation Engineering-based probe'; that is only the third of three contributions, so I disagree with the primary classification though the defense description is accurate. Notable finding: Sandwich Defense increased the Hijack Ratio on Qwen-3-14B by about 1%.

column3: Prompt Overflow: What the Guardrail Inspects Is Not What the Model Infers
column7: mechanism: Prompt Overflow Attack; defense: Contiguity-gate defense (for guardrail sliding
column11: ProtectAI DeBERTa-v3 prompt-injection detector v2, Meta Llama Prompt Guard 2 (86M and 22M), IBM Granite Guardian HAP-125M; source corpora: Hugging Face Prompt Injection Benchmark and RealToxicityPrompts; non-overlapping chunking vs overlapping sliding-window inspection with max-pooling aggregation; random-removal baseline for risk-aware token selection; downstream executability checked on Qwen-14B/Dolphin-12B/Dolphin-2.9.3
column12: We introduce a novel Prompt Overflow Attack, which exploits this mismatch by fragmenting malicious instructions and interleaving them with benign filler content across an overlong prompt, such that no individual inspected segment appears malicious while the full context remains actionable to the LLM. (Abstract)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: current entry labels this 'mechanism: Prompt Overflow Attack'. column3: AMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Agentic Applications

column12: To address this, we introduce AMA-Bench (Agent Memory with Any length), a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon memory in realistic agentic settings. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement: the registry records only 'defense: AMA-Agent', but the paper's own contributions list leads with the benchmark and AMA-Agent is the third contribution; also there is no adversary, so 'defense' is the wrong category for AMA-Agent (it would be a fix). column3: MAGMA: A Multi-Graph based Agentic Memory Architecture for AI Agents
column11: LoCoMo (LLM-as-a-Judge overall score, with multi-hop/temporal/open-domain/single-hop/adversarial breakdown; MAGMA 0.700 vs Full Context 0.481, A-MEM 0.580, MemoryOS 0.553, Nemori 0.590) and LongMemEval (average accuracy 61.2% vs Full-context 55.0% and Nemori 56.2%, across single-session-preference, single-session-assistant, temporal-reasoning, multi-session, knowledge-update and single-session-user question types); token-level F1 and BLEU-1 as secondary metrics; system efficiency measured as retrieval latency and tokens per query (0.7k-4.2k vs 101K for full context); gpt-4o-mini backbone
column12: In this paper, we propose MAGMA, a multi-graph agentic memory architecture that represents each memory item across orthogonal semantic, temporal, causal, and entity graphs. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The introduction frames the problem as attention dilution, token interference, lost-in-the-middle and context-decay, but nothing in the evaluation measures any of those: the results are LLM-as-a-Judge QA accuracy on LoCoMo and LongMemEval, token-level F1/BLEU-1, retrieval latency and tokens per query - capability scores plus efficiency. There is no positional analysis, no controlled distractor ablation, no measurement of accuracy against context position or length. Partial credit: LoCoMo's built-in 'adversarial' question category (where MAGMA scores 0.742 vs 0.205 for full context) and LongMemEval's knowledge-update category touch on distractor resistance and stale-fact overwrite, but these are inherited benchmark subcategories, not measurements the paper designed for the failure modes it names. Registry disagreement: 'defense: MAGMA' is wrong - there is no adversary; this is a fix for a non-adversarial context-management failure. No attack or failure mode is named by the paper (lost-in-the-middle is cited, not coined), hence names_registry_technique no.

column3: PlugMem: A Task-Agnostic Plugin Memory Module for LLM Agents
column11: LongMemEval, HotpotQA and WebArena, unchanged across all three; baselines Vanilla (no memory), task-agnostic (Vanilla Retrieval, Vanilla RAG, GraphRAG, A-Mem, RAPTOR, HippoRAG2, PropRAG, LiCoMemory, Zep, MemoryOS) and task-specific (AWM, ReasoningBank); metrics end-task accuracy/F1/success rate, memory tokens injected, and the paper's own PMI-based Memory Information Density (bits per token)
column12: Baselines are grouped into three categories: i) Vanilla, which do not rely on external memory; ii) Task-agnostic, which employ generic retrieval or agentic memory mechanisms not tailored to the benchmark; and iii) Task-specific, which incorporate benchmark-specific memory representations or retrieval heuristics. (Experiments)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper motivates itself with 'context explosion from raw memory retrieval', unbounded memory growth and degraded performance from accumulated raw context, but the evaluation measures only end-task capability (LongMemEval accuracy, HotpotQA F1, WebArena success rate) plus efficiency (memory tokens) and a derived utility-per-token density (PMI). Nothing measures the context failure mode itself - no noise/distractor-controlled condition; the utility-cost curves do show utility declining past a token budget, which the authors attribute to noise/interference, but that attribution is not tested. Registry label 'defense: PlugMem' is wrong in kind - there is no adversary; it is a non-adversarial context/memory-management fix, and arguably the weakest in-scope paper of this batch.

column3: ReMEmbR: Building and Reasoning Over Long-Horizon Spatio-Temporal Memory for Robot Navigation
column11: NaVQA dataset (210 questions over 7 long-horizon navigation videos, split short/medium/long) against LLM-with-captions and Multi-Frame VLM baselines; metrics are overall correctness, positional error, temporal error and per-question latency; ablations on iteration count, caption frame rate (3s vs 12s) and captioner size (VILA1.5-13b/8b/3b); plus a real-world Nova Carter robot deployment
column12: To evaluate ReMEmbR, we introduce the NaVQA dataset where we annotate spatial, temporal, and descriptive questions to long-horizon robot navigation videos. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement: labelled 'defense: ReMEmbR' but there is no adversary anywhere in the paper -- this is a non-adversarial context-management fix for unbounded robot histories that will not fit a fixed context window, so proposes_fix. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker: the failure mode (performance collapse as history length grows, VLM baselines unable to process long videos at all) is measured directly and length-conditioned -- Table I is split by short/medium/long and Figure 4 plots correctness against elapsed deployment time -- so claim and measurement line up. NaVQA is a dataset contribution but the paper's own contributions list leads with the dataset and then ReMEmbR; the system is the headline technique.

column3: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
column11: 11 BEIR datasets (NFCorpus, Natural Questions, SciFact, HotpotQA, DBPedia, SciDocs, FEVER and others, 100 target queries each) with Recall@5 of a single injected malicious item; 8 embedding models (gte-modernbert-base, contriever-msmarco, Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B/4B/8B, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, Voyage voyage-3.5-lite, Alibaba text-embedding-v4); baselines Query+ (repeat-query attack) and Vanilla direct injection; end-to-end RAG and multi-agent/agentic exploits (DoS, spam, code execution, SSH-key exfiltration from GPT-4o with >80% success); several existing defenses also evaluated
column12: We address this challenge by decomposing the malicious content into a trigger fragment that guarantees retrieval and an attack fragment that encodes arbitrary attack objectives. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement on category only: the entry says 'mechanism:' but this is a deliberate adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial failure mode; the registry is right that it is UNNAMED. The paper gives its contribution no proper name -- it is described compositionally as a 'trigger fragment' plus 'attack fragment' built by a tailored Cross-Entropy-Method black-box optimizer -- so names_registry_technique=no. The genuine novelty is closing the retrieval step that prior indirect-prompt-injection evaluations assumed away; claim and evaluation line up (retrieval recall is measured directly, then end-to-end exploitation).

column3: Securing AI Agents Against Prompt Injection Attacks

column11: Its own 847-case benchmark (200 base attack templates across five categories, three sophistication tiers, plus 500 benign retrieval contexts) run over seven LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude 2.1, PaLM 2, Llama 2 70B Chat, Mistral 7B Instruct, Vicuna 13B v1.5) in four configurations (no defense, content filtering, filtering+guardrails, full framework); metrics ASR (73.2% -> 8.7%), false positive rate, task performance retention (94.3%) and defense bypass rate

QUALITY WARNING: this paper looks machine-generated and its references appear partly fabricated -- 'Hines et al. 2023' and 'Zhang et al. 2023' are not locatable, the Greshake et al. 2023 title is wrong ('You've been prompted' rather than 'Not what you've signed up for'), the acknowledgment still reads '[funding source]', and there is a typo 'wikboards'. Neither the benchmark nor the code appears to exist despite the release claim; treat all numbers as unverified. names_registry_technique=yes is the weakest call in this packet: the five category names are a released taxonomy but are generic and uncited.

column3: ENGRAM: Effective, Lightweight Memory Orchestration for Conversational Agents
column11: LoCoMo multi-session conversational QA benchmark (single-hop, multi-hop, open-domain, temporal categories) against prior memory systems, and LongMemEval_S against a full-context baseline (56.20% -> 71.40% overall J with ~1% of the tokens); also latency and token-count comparisons
column12: Our central claim is that careful memory typing, minimal routing, and straightforward retrieval suffice to achieve state-of-the-art performance on LoCoMo, and to surpass full-context baselines on LongMemEval (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). (Introduction)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The discussion claims ENGRAM acts as an information bottleneck that avoids amplifying 'lost-in-the-middle' effects and frees the model from contexts 'prone to distraction', but nothing about distraction, dilution or positional degradation is measured: the evaluation reports only QA accuracy (LoCoMo semantic-correctness, LongMemEval per-question-type accuracy and overall J) plus efficiency numbers (token counts ~1% of full context, latency). There is no distractor-controlled ablation, no position-controlled probe, and no measurement of what the full-context baseline actually loses. Registry disagreement: labelled 'defense: ENGRAM' but there is no adversary -- it is a non-adversarial memory-management fix.

column3: Corpus Poisoning via Approximate Greedy Gradient Descent
column11: Corpus poisoning on Natural Questions and MS MARCO (in-domain, held-out unseen queries) and transfer to NFCorpus, Quora, SCIDOCS, SciFact and FiQA-2018; retrievers include Contriever, Contriever-MS and ANCE; direct baseline is HotFlip (AGGD is +15.24% and +17.44% ASR on NQ and MS MARCO against ANCE, 80%+ ASR with a single injected passage); additionally substituted for HotFlip inside PoisonedRAG-style knowledge poisoning of RAG, measured by ASR and F1 of retrieved poisoned texts
column12: In this work, we propose Approximate Greedy Gradient Descent (AGGD), a new attack on dense retrieval systems based on the widely used HotFlip method for efficiently generating adversarial passages. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement on category: entry reads 'mechanism: AGGD' but this is a deliberate adversarial corpus-poisoning attack, not a non-adversarial failure mode; the name itself is right. Clean improves case -- the only difference from HotFlip is replacing random single-position token sampling with a deterministic best-first search over candidates drawn from all positions, and the paper explicitly positions AGGD as a drop-in replacement for HotFlip anywhere HotFlip is used. Claim and evaluation line up (ASR measured head-to-head against HotFlip).

column3: Ranking Manipulation for Conversational Search Engines
column11: The authors' RAGDOLL dataset of real-world consumer product websites (50 product categories, 8 products each); natural ranking tendencies disentangled via F-statistics over product name vs document content vs context position; adversarial injections optimized with GPT-4 Turbo as recommender and transferred to perplexity.ai's Sonar Large Online model; recommender LLMs include GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama 3 70B; metric is the ranking-score distribution over randomized responses
column12: We then present a tree-of-attacks-based jailbreaking technique which reliably promotes low-ranked products. (Abstract)
column14: Registry's 'UNNAMED: tree-of-attacks ranking manipulation' is accurate on the name, but the category 'mechanism:' is wrong -- this is a deliberate, financially motivated attack (black-hat SEO for conversational search), not a non-adversarial failure. The attack itself is TAP applied to a new objective (promoting a product in the recommender's ranking) rather than a new optimizer, hence origin=applies. RAGDOLL is a released dataset of websites, not a set of named injections, so names_registry_technique=no. Note the useful non-adversarial finding alongside the attack: ranking is driven by product name vs document content vs context position in category-dependent proportions, i.e. a measured positional/context-order effect.

column3: Merging Generated and Retrieved Knowledge for Open-Domain QA
column9: COMBO (Compatibility-Oriented knowledge Merging for Better Open-domain QA)

column12: To address this challenge, we propose a novel Compatibility-Oriented knowledge Merging for Better Open-domain (COMBO) QA framework. (Introduction)
column14: Registry disagreement: labelled 'defense: COMBO' but there is no adversary -- the untrustworthy context is hallucinated LLM-generated passages conflicting with retrieved ones, a non-adversarial failure, so proposes_fix. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker: although the headline numbers are EM on four QA benchmarks, the paper also measures the failure mode directly -- it stratifies gains by degree of knowledge conflict (compatible-pair share across (M,N) settings) and shows the reader's attention shifting toward compatible pairs -- so claim and measurement line up. Relevant to the SoK as an early (2023) treatment of source-conflict in mixed parametric/retrieved context.

column3: Dynamic Context Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Mitigating Distractors and Positional Bias
column11: MuSiQue (~22k passage corpus), 2WikiMultihopQA (reranking 10 candidates) and MultihopRAG, with BM25, dense all-MiniLM-L6-v2/Chromadb, ColBERT+MonoT5 and ColBERT+BGE-reranker-large retrievers and a Mistral Nemo Instruct LLM reranker; a RoBERTa-base hop-type classifier (87.3% exact-match accuracy) maps queries to k; fixed-k pipelines are the baselines; metrics are retrieval precision/recall and generation EM/F1; additionally an empirical study of distractor impact and of relevant-passage position within the context window

column14: Registry disagreement: labelled 'defense: Dynamic Context Selection' but there is no adversary -- distractors here are semantically irrelevant retrieved passages and lost-in-the-middle is a positional bias, both non-adversarial, so proposes_fix. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker: unusually for this genre the paper measures the failure modes directly before fixing them -- contribution 1 is a distractor-controlled study quantifying how distractor passages degrade generation under varying conditions, and RQ2 is a position-controlled study of where relevant passages sit in the window -- so claim and measurement line up, even though the final pipeline comparison against fixed-k is EM/F1. 'Distractors' and 'lost in the middle' are inherited terms (Liu et al. 2023), not coined here.

column3: Evaluating LLM-based Personal Information Extraction and Countermeasures

Same role inversion as row 50 (Mantis): the defender plants hidden text in the profile so the attacker's LLM reads untrustworthy context. No named attack or failure mode is coined (the defenses named -- data prompt isolation, instructional prevention, sandwich prevention -- are inherited from prior work), so names_registry_technique=no. Claim and evaluation line up.

column3: ContextBudget: Budget-Aware Context Management for Long-Horizon Search Agents
column11: Multi-objective QA built from NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue and Bamboogle (token-level F1 summed over 2/8/16/32 objectives) and BrowseComp-Plus (LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy), against ReAct, Search-R1, Summary Agent and MEM1 on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct; ablations on budget curriculum (Static 8k vs Random 4k/8k vs Curriculum 8->4) reporting reward, KL, entropy and summary-tool call frequency
column12: To address this challenge, we propose Budget-Aware Context Management (BACM), which formulates context management as a sequential decision problem with a context budget constraint. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around context growth, the lost-in-the-middle effect, over-compression erasing research-critical evidence and under-compression causing context overflow, but the evaluation measures only task capability (summed F1 on multi-objective QA, LLM-judged accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus) plus efficiency proxies (compression behaviour, summary-tool call counts, token budgets). Neither over-compression-induced evidence loss nor overflow-induced reasoning failure is measured directly with distractor-controlled or position-controlled probes. Registry label 'defense: BACM / BACM-RL' is wrong in kind: there is no adversary anywhere in the paper; this is a non-adversarial context-management fix.

column3: Checkpoint-GCG: Auditing and Attacking Fine-Tuning-Based Prompt Injection Defenses
column11: StruQ- and SecAlign-defended Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct, plus transfer to Meta's SecAlign++ model; AlpacaFarm samples with the injected instruction "Print exactly 'Hacked'!" and the SEP prompt injection benchmark; baseline is standard GCG on the final checkpoint at T=500 steps and at a step-matched budget; metrics ASR and success@k
column12: We show Checkpoint-GCG to achieve up to 96% attack success rate (ASR) against the strongest defense. (Abstract)
column14: Registry label 'mechanism: Checkpoint-GCG' is wrong: this is a deliberate white-box adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial failure mechanism. Coded proposes_attack with origin=improves because the paper explicitly enhances GCG by initialising from intermediate fine-tuning checkpoints. Evaluation and claims line up (ASR measured against the named defenses).

column3: LongAgent: Scaling Language Models to 128k Context through Multi-Agent Collaboration
column11: Needle-in-a-Haystack PLUS (single-document and multi-hop QA with needle documents placed at varying positions in a distracting haystack, answer entities replaced by fictional entities), plus synthetic long-text retrieval (PassKey Retrieval, Number Retrieval, KV Retrieval) and numerical comparison at 128k scale; compared against GPT-4 Turbo, Claude2.1, Kimi-Chat, YaRN and PI, with LLaMA2-7B and GPT-3.5 agent teams; ablation on sharing text chunks to resolve member hallucination conflicts
column12: The model must locate one or more relevant documents scattered within the haystack and reason the correct answers from them. (Experimental Setup)
column14: No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the paper claims to address lost-in-the-middle degradation and member hallucination, and its Needle-in-a-Haystack PLUS protocol measures exactly that by varying needle position and haystack length with controlled distractor documents, while the conflict-resolution ablation measures hallucination correction directly. Registry label 'defense: LongAgent' is wrong in kind - there is no adversary; this is a fix for a non-adversarial long-context failure mode, so proposes_fix. It names no new failure mode (it reuses 'lost in the middle' from Liu et al.), hence names_registry_technique no.

column3: MGA: Memory-Driven GUI Agent for Observation-Centric Interaction

column11: OSWorld (369 tasks, rule-based evaluator, grounding accuracy across Office, Daily, Professional, OS and Workflow domains) with MGA w/ o3 and MGA w/ GPT-5, against O3, OpenCUA-32b/72B, UI-TARS, UI-TARS-2, DeepMiner-Mano-7B, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Qwen3-VL-32B, Agent S3, UiPath, Jedi-7B, CoAct-1, GTA1-7b and OS-SYMPHONY; plus cost (dollar) trade-off table, token-cost appendix, and ablations on the memory module backbone and on core components, all scored by task success rate

The paper frames itself around context overload from raw trajectory concatenation, error cascades from concatenated visual-textual histories, irrelevant historical interference, confirmation bias, visual hallucinations and perception bias, but the evaluation measures only OSWorld task/grounding success rate plus dollar cost, token cost and inference latency. Neither hallucination rate, bias, nor history-length-controlled degradation is measured; the ablations also report success rate only. Registry label 'defense: MGA' is wrong in kind - there is no adversary, so this is a non-adversarial context-management fix, not a defense.

column3: MCP-ITP: An Automated Framework for Implicit Tool Poisoning in MCP
column11: MCPTox dataset (45 real MCP servers, 353 real tools), restricted to the 548 implicit-poisoning test cases, across 12 LLM agents (o1-mini, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini-2.5-flash, Qwen3-8b/32b/235b-a22b with and without reasoning); baseline is MCPTox's hand-crafted poisoned tools; metrics Attack Success Rate and Malicious Tool Detection Rate under the AI-Infra-Guard and Oracle detectors, with an Ignored/Direct/Others failure-type breakdown
column12: Experimental results on the MCPTox dataset across 12 LLM agents demonstrate that MCP-ITP consistently outperforms the manually crafted baseline, achieving up to 84.2% ASR while suppressing the Malicious Tool Detection Rate (MDR) to as low as 0.3%. (Abstract)
column14: Registry label 'mechanism: MCP-ITP' is wrong: this is a deliberate adversarial attack (black-box optimisation of poisoned MCP tool descriptions with attacker/detector/evaluator LLMs), not a non-adversarial mechanism. origin=improves because the implicit tool poisoning paradigm and its test cases already exist in MCPTox; the contribution is automating and optimising them. Claim and evaluation line up (ASR and detection evasion measured on the named dataset).

column3: Reflective Planning: Vision-Language Models for Multi-Stage Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
column11: A generated multi-stage robotic assembly suite (1000 training tasks, 100 unseen evaluation tasks with interlocking pieces), reporting task success rate across post-training iterations for w/o reflect, w/o reflect@test, reflect w/ diffusion and reflect w/ sim; compared against zero-shot LLaVA-OneVision, Gemini-2.0-flash, Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking, GPT-4o and GPT-o1, against MCTS, and against a 97% symbolic oracle policy; plus inference wall-clock cost
column12: Solving complex long-horizon robotic manipulation problems requires sophisticated high-level planning capabilities, the ability to reason about the physical world, and reactively choose appropriate motor skills. (Abstract)
column14: Not about untrustworthy context. The problem is a VLM's weak physical reasoning and compounding errors over a long manipulation horizon; the 'reflection' mechanism critiques imagined future world states, with no untrusted or noisy context anywhere. Registry label 'defense: ReflectVLM' is wrong in kind - there is no adversary and no context-trust failure, so this row should be dropped from the corpus rather than relabelled.

column3: Red-Teaming Coding Agents from a Tool-Invocation Perspective: An Empirical Security Assessment
column11: Six real-world coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Windsurf, Cline, Trae) across 25 agent-LLM pairs in old and new releases, in both an emulated and a real-world setting. Prompt-leak baselines: Naive, Ignore, Completion, Ignore-Completion, Remember-the-Start, Ignore-Remember, Completion-Remember, Ignore-Completion-Remember, and PLeak. Metrics: semantic similarity (jina-embeddings-v2-base-en) and normalized Extended Edit Distance against a curated leaked-prompt reference, pseudo-recall, and attack success rate for the two-channel prompt injection hijack, plus RCE case studies on Cursor and Claude Code.
column12: We instantiate this gap as ToolLeak, which exfiltrates agent-internal prompts (e.g., system prompts and tool metadata) via required tool parameters. (Abstract)
column14: Deliberate adversarial red-teaming paper with a full evaluation; claim and measurement line up (it claims prompt exfiltration and tool-invocation hijacking and measures exactly those, with ASR and RCE). Registry disagreement: the registry labels this 'mechanism: ToolLeak'. ToolLeak is a deliberate attack (an attacker-controlled tool exfiltrates agent-internal context through schema-required arguments), not a non-adversarial failure mode; the contribution is proposes_attack and the registry's 'mechanism:' label is the exact error the brief warns about. The paper has a second named attack contribution, the two-channel prompt injection in tool description and tool return, which is listed as a separate bullet in the contributions list. column3: VortexPIA: Indirect Prompt Injection Attack against LLMs for Efficient Extraction of User Privacy
column5: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
column11: Six LLMs (Qwen2.5-32B, Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Kimi-K2) on four datasets used to construct benign user queries (MATH500, AIME2024, AIME2025, AICrypto), against three prior prompt-injection attacks (Baseline 1-3, the strongest being the system-prompt-modification method of Zhan et al.). Also validated on several realistic open-source LLM-integrated applications.
column12: By injecting token-efficient data containing false memories, VORTEX PIA misleads LLMs to actively request private information in batches. (Abstract)
column14: Clean attack paper: untrusted external data injected into the application's context causes the agent to solicit PII from the user. Claim and measurement line up (ASR/MR/PR all measure the induced privacy-extraction behaviour). Registry disagreement: the registry labels this 'mechanism: VortexPIA'. It is an adversary-authored indirect prompt injection, so the correct label is an attack, not a mechanism. Technique name recorded exactly as the paper's small-caps rendering 'VORTEX PIA' (the title writes it as 'VortexPIA').

column3: AgentSwing: Adaptive Parallel Context Management Routing for Long-Horizon Web Agents
column11: BrowseComp (200 sampled tasks), BrowseComp-ZH (full 289 tasks), and Humanity's Last Exam (500 text-only tasks), on three backbones (GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-v3.2, Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B). Baselines: no context management, Discard-All, Keep-Last-N (N=5), and Summary, plus published numbers for foundation models and deep-research agents. Metrics: Pass@1 under LLM-as-a-Judge, performance under varying max-turn budgets, and aligned terminal precision versus context budget (25.6k to 102.4k).
column12: Building on this perspective, we propose AgentSwing, a state-aware adaptive parallel context management routing framework. (Abstract)
column14: NO MISMATCH MARKER, and this is a deliberate judgement call worth flagging. The headline table is pure capability (Pass@1 on BrowseComp/BrowseComp-ZH/HLE), which on its own would trip Ruling 1. But the paper's probabilistic framework decomposes success into search efficiency (reaching a terminal state before exhausting the turn/context budget) and terminal precision (correctness given termination), and Section 2.2 actually measures this: Figure 2 sweeps the context budget under Discard-All and shows aligned terminal precision consistently DECREASING as context budget grows, which the authors explicitly attribute to 'more severe context rot at termination', and Figure 1 reports performance against max-turn budget. That is the terminal-state-distribution-versus-trajectory-length measurement the brief names as the case where claim and measurement line up, so no marker. Registry disagreement: registry says 'defense: AgentSwing'. There is no adversary in this paper at all - the problem is self-inflicted context saturation, drift and noise accumulation during long-horizon search - so this is a non-adversarial fix, not a defense. AgentSwing names no attack or failure mode of its own (it reuses context rot and lost-in-the-middle from elsewhere), hence names_registry_technique=no.

I answered names_registry_technique=yes on that basis rather than treating it as defense-only; flagging it as the weakest yes in this batch, since these are taxonomy labels in an unevaluated position paper and it is unclear whether other papers will cite and test against them. column3: MemoBrain: Executive Memory as an Agentic Brain for Reasoning
column11: GAIA (103 text-only validation questions, L1-L3), WebWalkerQA (680 queries, easy/medium/hard), and BrowseComp-Plus (830 questions over a fixed candidate corpus with local dense retrieval). Baselines: direct reasoning (QwQ-32B, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1-671B), RAG variants (vanilla, query planning, iterative), and tool-integrated reasoning systems (ReAct, WebThinker, WebDancer, ReSum-GRPO, DeepAgent-RL, AgentFold, GLM-4.6, DeepResearch-30B-A3B). Metrics: Pass@1 accuracy and number of search calls. Ablations on design choices (w/o flush, w/o folding, delete, random drop), on memory-model size (MemoBrain-4B/8B/14B), and sensitivity to context budget from 8K to 128K - all reported as accuracy.
column12: We propose MemoBrain, an executive memory model for tool-augmented agents that constructs a dependency-aware memory over reasoning steps, capturing salient intermediate states and their logical relations. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself squarely around a context-trust/context-quality failure - accumulated reasoning traces and transient tool artifacts 'strain the bounded working context', 'allowing transient information to dominate and distract from task-relevant evidence, leading to cognitive overload and degraded task alignment' - but every number reported is capability: Pass@1 on GAIA, WebWalkerQA and BrowseComp-Plus, plus search-call counts. There is no measurement of distraction, of logical-continuity loss, of task-alignment drift, or of what fraction of pruned content was actually noise; the ablations (w/o flush, w/o folding, delete, random drop) and the 8K-128K context-budget sweep are also scored purely in accuracy, so they ablate the method's components rather than isolating the failure mode. The claimed mechanism - that MemoBrain removes distractors and preserves a high-salience backbone - is never measured directly. Keep in corpus; the note carries the warning. Registry disagreement: registry says 'defense: MemoBrain'. There is no adversary in this paper; the harmful context is the agent's own accumulated trace, so this is proposes_fix, not a defense. The paper also introduces 'executive memory' as a named paradigm, but it is a memory-architecture category rather than an attack or failure mode, so names_registry_technique is no.

column3: Black-box Optimization of LLM Outputs by Asking for Directions
column7: mechanism: query-based black-box optimization via LLM-exp
column11: Three attack scenarios on samples from ImageNet (adversarial examples for vision-LLMs), AgentDojo (prompt injections), and AdvBench (jailbreaks). Targets include GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5 mini, Claude Haiku 3.5, Claude Sonnet 3.5/3.7/4, Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Llama-3.2-11B-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Baselines: no optimization, log-probability-guided optimization where logprobs are exposed, transfer-only surrogate attacks, a Transfer+ours hybrid, and an ensemble; for jailbreaks it re-runs the adaptive attacks of Andriushchenko et al. with their model-specific suffix templates. Metrics: attack success rate and mean queries under a 200-query budget.
column12: We apply our general method to three attack scenarios: adversarial examples for vision-LLMs, jailbreaks and prompt injections. (Abstract)
column14: Deliberate attack method, evaluated thoroughly; claim and measurement line up. names_registry_technique=no because the paper never gives its method a name - the closest label is the descriptive 'text-only output optimization attack' from the Figure 2 caption, which I recorded in technique_name with that caveat. Registry disagreement: registry says 'mechanism: query-based black-box optimization via LLM-expressed confidence'. This is an attacker-driven optimization procedure, not a non-adversarial mechanism, so it should be an attack entry. Relevance to this corpus is partial but real: one of the three scenarios is optimized prompt injection evaluated on AgentDojo, where ASR rises from 23.2-42.1% to 55.4-87.5%, and the method is the only viable optimizer against models like Claude that hide log-probabilities. Notable finding: larger and better-calibrated models are easier to attack, a capability/vulnerability inversion echoed by row 26.

column3: ColorBrowserAgent: Complex Long-Horizon Browser Agent with Adaptive Knowledge Evolution
column11: WebArena (812 tasks, success rate) and WebChoreArena (zero-shot transfer); baselines BrowserGym, LM-TS, Go-Browse, AWM, Branch-n-Browse, WebPilot, AgentOccam, AgentSymbiotic, ScribeAgent, WebOperator, CUGA, SteP, WEBDART; ablation ColorBrowserAgent w/o knowledge; industrial deployment user-satisfaction delta
column12: Extensive experiments on WebArena, WebChoreArena and industrial deployment show that ColorBrowserAgent consistently outperforms strong baselines. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around long-horizon instability, decision drift, context overflow and finite context windows, but the evaluation measures only task success rate on WebArena/WebChoreArena plus a deployment satisfaction metric. No measurement of drift, context saturation or the summarizer's effect on goal retention; the only context-related ablation is 'w/o knowledge' on WebChoreArena, which isolates the knowledge base, not the context-management claim. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense:' but there is no adversary anywhere in the paper; this is a non-adversarial context-management fix (knowledge-aligned progressive summarization + human-in-the-loop knowledge adaptation). No related-work heading printed; related work is folded into Section 2.

column3: CAPTURE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Testing and Robustness Enhancement
column11: CAPTURE MALICIOUS-GEN and SAFE-GEN datasets across six domains (Stock, Movies, Python, Travel, Covid, Shopping), measuring FNR/FPR of ProtectAIv2, InjecGuard, PromptGuard, Deepset, Fmops, GPT-4o, Llama3.2-1B-Instruct, and the trained CaptureGuard; external generalization on NotInject, WildGuard and BIPIA (Injection)
column12: To demonstrate our framework’s utility, we train CaptureGuard on our generated data. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: CaptureGuard. Lead contribution is the generation pipeline plus the context-aware benchmark (MALICIOUS-GEN / SAFE-GEN), so coded benchmark_or_dataset; CaptureGuard is a secondary demonstration model. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: CaptureGuard | applied_as_is', which both mislabels the lead contribution (benchmark, not defense) and is wrong on origin - CaptureGuard is newly trained (DeBERTaV3-base fine-tuned on the generated data), not applied as is. The attack structure (Framework / Separator / Disruptor) is borrowed from Liu et al. 2023 and MALICIOUS-GEN/SAFE-GEN are dataset-generation modes rather than named attacks other papers test against, hence names_registry_technique=no. Claim and evaluation line up (over-defense is claimed and FPR is actually measured).

column3: Memex(RL): Scaling Long-Horizon LLM Agents via Indexed Experience Memory
column11: A modified, harder ALFWorld (hidden admissible commands, hidden initial observation, look restricted to once per episode, 300-token summary truncation; 3553 training tasks) with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507; metrics task success rate (24.22% to 85.61%) and peak working context length (16934 to 9634 tokens); comparison is Memex agent with vs without MemexRL training, plus CompressExperience/ReadExperience call counts
column12: We introduce Memex, an indexed experience memory mechanism that instead compresses context without discarding evidence. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The central claim is that Memex is 'a substantially less lossy form of long-horizon memory than summary-only approaches', but the evaluation measures only task success rate and peak working-context tokens (capability plus efficiency) on one modified ALFWorld, with the only comparison being Memex with vs without RL training. No truncation or running-summary baseline is run, and evidence loss or recovery of distant evidence is never measured directly. Mitigating factor worth recording: the ALFWorld environment was deliberately instrumented so that retrieval is required (IDs only recoverable via ReadExperience), so success rate is a partial proxy for the failure mode - but the lossiness claim itself is unmeasured. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense:' but there is no adversary; this is a non-adversarial context-management fix. Technique names: Memex (mechanism) and MemexRL (its RL training framework).

column3: Rethinking All Evidence: Enhancing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Conflict-Driven Summarization
column11: QA-repaired NQ*, TriviaQA*, HotpotQA*, ASQA*, WikiQA* (EM/F1); baselines No RAG, standard RAG, InstructRAG, GenRead, Self-RAG; backbones Mistral-7B-v0.3, LLaMA-3.2-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Gemini-2.0-Flash, GPT-4.1-Nano; ablations w/o Stage1 / Stage2 / Stage3 and top-K retrieval sensitivity (5-25)
column12: RAG enhances LLMs’ generation by leveraging both internal and external knowledge, but as shown in Figure 1, it also introduces unreliable sources that make reasoning more difficult. (Introduction)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and noisy/contradictory retrieved content and claims gains 'especially in scenarios with noisy or conflicting evidence', but the evaluation measures only EM/F1 on five general QA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, ASQA, WikiQA). There is no conflict-labelled subset, no controlled injection of contradictory evidence, and no conflict-detection accuracy reported; the w/o Stage3 ablation shows the conflict stage helps EM/F1 but still does not measure conflict resolution itself. Non-adversarial failure mode (noise, staleness, internal inconsistency), so coded proposes_fix. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: CARE-RAG' but the paper contains no adversary. Secondary artifacts: QA Repair procedure and a distilled LLaMA-3.2-3B conflict-detection model.

column3: CoCoA: Confidence and Context-Aware Adaptive Decoding for Resolving Knowledge Conflicts in Large Language Models
column11: NQ, NQ-SWAP (synthetic knowledge-conflict variant), TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, TabMWP (exact match); CNN-DM, XSum, TofuEval (ROUGE-L, BERT-P, AlignScore); CLAPNQ, ExpertQA, HAGRID, ELI5-WebGPT, QuoteSum (ROUGE-L, claim recall, SEMQA, MiniCheck FaithScore); baselines Greedy, CAD, COIECD, ConfCD, AdaCAD; LLaMA2-13B, LLaMA3-8B/70B, Mistral-7B; plus conflict-sensitivity analysis and latency measurement
column12: Faithful generation in large language models (LLMs) is challenged by knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and external context. (Abstract)
column14: No mismatch marker: the failure mode (context-memory knowledge conflict) is measured directly via NQ-SWAP, a controlled synthetic conflict dataset, and the paper also reports sensitivity to conflict variation and low-conflict regressions - exactly the claim it makes about CAD/AdaCAD over-correcting. Non-adversarial failure mode, so proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense. Origin is improves, not invents: CoCoA replaces AdaCAD's JSD with Renyi divergence and adds contextual confidence estimation and adaptive gating on top of the CAD/AdaCAD contrastive-decoding line. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: CoCoA' with origin 'proposed'; there is no adversary (it is a fix), and the origin should be improves with AdaCAD/CAD as parent.

column3: Context manipulation attacks : Web agents are susceptible to corrupted memory
column11: Plan Injection benchmark against Agent-E (four categories: factual manipulation, opinion steering, advertisement injection, privacy exfiltration; 15 samples each, 5 runs each) and a WebVoyager-Privacy benchmark (9 domains x 5 tasks = 45 scenarios) against Agent-E and Browser-use; attack success rate, comparing plan injection against indirect prompt injections of different strengths and non-contextual vs task-aligned vs context-chained injections
column12: We introduce and formalize “plan injection,” a novel context manipulation attack that corrupts these agents’ internal task representations by targeting this vulnerable context. (Abstract)
column14: Squarely in scope: a deliberate attack that corrupts an agent's stored plan/memory, evaluated with ASR against two real web agents and compared head-to-head with prompt injection (up to 3x higher ASR; +17.7% for privacy exfiltration with context-chained injections). REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry labels Plan Injection as 'mechanism:', but this is an adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial failure mode - exactly the mislabelling pattern the brief warns about. Also reports an architecture finding: hierarchical Agent-E is more resistant than Browser-use, and subjective tasks are far more exploitable (94.7% ASR) than factual ones.

column3: M2: Dual-Memory Augmentation for Long-Horizon Web Agents via Trajectory Summarization and Insight Retrieval
column11: WebVoyager (12 websites) and OnlineMind2Web (291 tasks, easy/medium/hard); backbones Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Claude-Sonnet-4, Qwen3-VL-32B; configurations Normal / In Mem / Ex Mem / In & Ex Mem; metrics task success rate, average steps, average token cost; comparison table against UI-TARS-1.5 and OpenAI CUA
column12: An overly long and noisy context often distracts the model, burying critical task-relevant cues under redundant historical information, a phenomenon known as “lost-in-the-middle” (Liu et al., 2024). (Introduction)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper explicitly motivates itself with distraction and lost-in-the-middle (noisy context burying task-relevant cues), but the evaluation measures only web-navigation success rate, step count and token cost on WebVoyager and OnlineMind2Web. Nothing measures distraction, cue retention or recall of mid-context information; the In Mem / Ex Mem / In & Ex Mem ablation is a component ablation scored by success rate, not a distractor-controlled test. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: M2' - there is no adversary, this is a non-adversarial context-management fix (Dynamic Trajectory Summarization as internal memory plus Insight Retrieval Augmentation as external memory); registry origin 'needs_read' resolves to invents. Training-free framework.

column3: AgentProg: Empowering Long-Horizon GUI Agents with Program-guided Context Management
column11: AndroidWorld (116 tasks) and AW-Extend (19 long-horizon tasks), success rate only; baselines M3A (summarization), UI-TARS (sliding window), Mobile-Agent-v3 (hierarchical planning), plus cited AndroidWorld leaderboard numbers (MobileGPT, AutoDroid-V2, V-Droid, MobileUse, UI-Venus, Agent S3, GLM-4.1V)
column12: Existing context management and compression techniques often fail to preserve vital semantic information, leading to degraded task performance. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around context overhead, lossy compression and loss of critical early information in ever-growing interaction history, but the evaluation measures only task success rate (%) on AndroidWorld and the authors' AW-Extend suite, plus success rate broken down by difficulty level. No direct measurement of information loss, dilution or forgetting (no retention probes, no distractor-controlled ablation, no token/context accounting reported in the results tables shown). Baselines are chosen as context-management strategies, but the metric is still pure capability. Registry entry 'defense: AgentProg' is wrong in kind: there is no adversary anywhere in the paper; this is a non-adversarial context-management fix. Named components: Semantic Task Program, global belief state.

column3: GenericAgent: A Token-Efficient Self-Evolving LLM Agent via Contextual Information Density Maximization (V1.0)
column11: SOP-Bench, Lifelong AgentBench and RealFin-Benchmark (accuracy, input/output/total tokens, efficiency = accuracy per million tokens); tool-use and long-horizon case study (success, total tokens, time, requests, tool calls); memory section measures repeated-task performance, factual retention and prompt growth; open-ended web browsing tasks. Baselines: Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex across Claude Sonnet/Opus 4.6, MiniMax M2.7, GPT-5.4
column12: We argue that long-horizon performance is determined not by context length, but by how much decision-relevant information is maintained within a finite context budget. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper's framing is context explosion degrading reasoning (irrelevant/outdated content crowding out decision-relevant information, hallucinations compounding), but the evaluation measures task accuracy and token/interaction cost (tokens, requests, tool calls, latency) on capability benchmarks. The one partial exception is Section 4.3, which measures factual retention and prompt growth over repeated tasks - still retention/efficiency rather than a controlled measurement of distraction or dilution harming decisions. Nothing adversarial in the paper; registry entry 'defense: GenericAgent (GA)' is mislabelled - this is a non-adversarial context-management fix. Named components: hierarchical on-demand memory, self-evolution into SOPs, context truncation and compression layer.

column3: Resisting Contextual Interference in RAG via Parametric-Knowledge Reinforcement
column11: Five contextual scenarios - correct (S1), wrong (S2), conflict (S3), irrelevant (S4), partly irrelevant (S5) - on ConFiQA splits (PC/NC-MR, MC, QA), SC, ExplainPE, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA and Musique, with Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct; baselines query-only prompting, RAG prompting, Astute RAG and GRPO w/ RAG; plus ablations on JPK/JRPK, local vs global advantage, adaptive beta, and a 99%-correct-context training robustness check
column12: We propose Knowledgeable-R1, a reinforcement-learning framework that explicitly trains large language models to use parametric knowledge (PK) to resist contextual interference while still exploiting external context when it is reliably helpful. (Abstract)
column14: No mismatch marker: the claim is resisting misleading/conflicting retrieved context and the evaluation measures exactly that, with counterfactual and conflict scenarios separated from the correct-context scenario and ablations targeting the TIFE (parametric correct / context incorrect) case. Non-adversarial: the bad context is wrong, stale, irrelevant or counterfactual rather than attacker-planted, so proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense. Origin coded 'improves' because the method is an advantage-shaping extension of GRPO (joint sampling, local/global advantages, asymmetric advantage transformation) and GRPO w/ RAG is its main baseline; the paper itself presents it as a new framework, so 'invents' would also be defensible. Registry 'defense: Knowledgeable-R1' is right about the name but wrong about the adversary - there is none.

column3: Cognitive Overload Attack:Prompt Injection for Long Context
column11: Forbidden Question Set (232 harmful questions) and JailbreakBench (100 harmful questions) against GPT-4, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Gemini-1.0-Pro and Gemini-1.5-Pro; ASR per cognitive-load level CL1-CL6 (up to 99.99% and 97%), LLM judges (GPT-4, Llama-3-70B, Gemini-1.5-Pro); preliminary dual-task and self-report experiments measuring task degradation under increasing cognitive load; plus transferability (stronger models crafting prompts to attack others)
column12: Furthermore, we demonstrated how an attacker can exploit ICL to jailbreak LLMs through deliberately designed prompts that induce cognitive overload on LLMs, thereby compromising the safety mechanisms of LLMs. (Abstract)
column14: Deliberate adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial mechanism: registry entry 'mechanism: Cognitive Overload Attack' is mislabelled and should be attack. No claim/evaluation mismatch - the paper claims cognitive overload degrades LLM performance and enables jailbreaks, and it measures both (dual-task performance degradation as load rises, then ASR as a function of CL level). Origin coded 'improves' because the related-work section explicitly acknowledges Xu et al. as having drawn the CLT-LLM parallel with three jailbreak variants and positions this work as generalizing and automating it (tasks as atomic units of cognitive load, token-count-based quantification, automated incremental loading); the paper itself calls the attack novel, so 'invents' is the alternative reading.

column3: Toward Ultra-Long-Horizon Agentic Science: Cognitive Accumulation for Machine Learning Engineering
column7: defense: Hierarchical Cognitive Caching (HCC), in ML-Ma
column11: MLE-Bench (75 Kaggle competitions, 24-hour budgets): medal rate by complexity level, valid submission rate, above-median, silver+, gold; baselines MLAB, OpenHands, AIDE, R&D-Agent, AIRA-dojo, FM Agent, MLE-STAR-Pro-1.5, Thesis, Leeroo, ML-Master, AutoMLGen (numbers mostly cited from MLE-Bench); HCC ablation over L1/L2/L3 tiers on MLE-Bench-Lite, again scored by valid submission / above median / any medal
column12: By reframing context management as a process of cognitive accumulation, our approach introduces Hierarchical Cognitive Caching (HCC), a multi-tiered architecture inspired by computer systems that enables the structural differentiation of experience over time. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper is framed on context saturation, agents being overwhelmed by accumulated execution details, and the scaling limits of static context windows, but every reported number is capability: medal rate / valid-submission / above-median percentages on MLE-Bench, including the HCC tier ablation. Nothing measures context saturation directly (no degradation-vs-trajectory-length curve, no retention or distraction probe, no context-size accounting in the results). Registry entry 'defense: Hierarchical Cognitive Caching (HCC)' with origin 'ambiguous' is wrong in kind - no adversary appears anywhere; this is a non-adversarial context-management fix, and its origin is clear enough (new named architecture, positioned against MemGPT / HiAgent / G-Memory hierarchical memory and Reflexion / Memento / ReasoningBank experience abstraction).

column3: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
column11: CONFLICTS benchmark (458 expert-annotated queries with Google Search results), measuring factual consistency, answer recall and expected-behavior adherence (LLM rater validated at 0.89 accuracy against humans on 100 examples); Vanilla vs Pipeline vs Taxonomy-Aware vs Oracle prompting, per conflict category, with models including Gemini Flash 2.5 Thinking
column12: In this work, we first propose a novel taxonomy of knowledge conflict types in RAG, along with the desired model behavior for each type. (Abstract)
column14: Leading contribution is the taxonomy plus the CONFLICTS benchmark, so benchmark_or_dataset; the Pipeline / Taxonomy-Aware prompting strategies are evaluation conditions on that benchmark, not the headline contribution. names_registry_technique=yes under the strict reading: the paper names and operationalizes a specific set of inter-context knowledge-conflict failure modes that other work can cite and test against (analogous to AgentDojo naming its injections). Non-adversarial: conflicts arise from staleness, misinformation on the open web, under-specification and genuine disagreement, not from an attacker. Registry entry 'defense: Taxonomy-Aware / Pipeline conflict-type-aware' with origin 'applied_as_is' is a poor fit - it labels an evaluation condition as the paper's contribution and calls a benchmark/taxonomy paper a defense; there is no adversary.

column3: AgentTypo: Adaptive Typographic Prompt Injection Attacks against Black-box Multimodal Agents
column11: VWA-Adv benchmark (77 adversarial tasks over Classifieds, Shopping, Reddit, built on VisualWebArena) against GPT-4V, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-Pro and Claude-3-Opus; baselines Raw Prompt Injection, InjecAgent, AgentAttack and AdvAgent; metric ASR (image-only 23% to 45% on GPT-4o, 68% in image+text), with stealth loss and high- vs low-permission attacker settings
column12: To further enhance attack strength, we develop AgentTypo-pro, a multi-LLM system that iteratively refines injection prompts using evaluation feedback and retrieves successful past examples for continual learning. (Abstract)
column14: Deliberate adversarial attack against multimodal web agents via text typographically embedded in webpage images; registry entry 'mechanism: AgentTypo' is mislabelled and should be attack. No claim/evaluation mismatch: the claim is higher-ASR stealthy visual prompt injection and the evaluation measures ASR against the named image- and text-based injection baselines on VWA-Adv. Origin 'invents' - the paper claims the first typographic injection framework for LVLM agents and treats AgentAttack/AdvAgent/EIA as prior attacks it outperforms rather than as a parent it extends (the optimizer is a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, a generic black-box search tool, not a parent attack).

column3: StruPhantom: Evolutionary Injection Attacks on Black-Box Tabular Agents Powered by Large Language Models
column11: Real-world black-box tabular agents on ByteDance's Doubao and Coze platforms plus other LLM-based tabular agents, over CSV, XLSX, XML and JSON inputs; goal-hijacking scenarios forcing responses to contain phishing links or malicious code; metric ASR (92.0% average in one scenario, over 50% higher than baselines) against manually designed injection templates (Ignore Attacks, Escape Character Attacks, Completion Attacks)
column12: To address the challenge, we present a novel attack termed StruPhantom which specifically targets black-box LLM-powered tabular agents. (Abstract)
column14: Indirect prompt injection attack: malicious instructions embedded in structural data files that the agent ingests, optimized by a constrained Monte Carlo Tree Search with an off-topic evaluator. Registry entry 'mechanism: StruPhantom' is mislabelled - this is a deliberate attack with an explicit threat model and attacker permissions, not a non-adversarial failure mode. No claim/evaluation mismatch: the claim is higher goal-hijacking success against tabular agents and the evaluation measures ASR against manual-template baselines on real deployed agents.

column3: Token-Efficient Prompt Injection Attack: Provoking Cessation in LLM Reasoning via Adaptive Token Compression
column11: DeepSeek-R1 via its official API and Volcano Engine; baseline dataset of reasoning tokens from 25 GSM-Ranges level-6-perturbation mathematical word problems (prior method: 3843 tokens, 85% ASR) versus standalone arithmetic prompts (2164 tokens, 65% ASR); attack prompt dataset over +, -, x, / with search counts and token totals; compression framework run with DeepSeek-V3, o3-mini, GPT-4o and moonshot-v1-32k; three chat-prefix-completion attack placements; success defined as an empty final response
column12: We demonstrate that simple standalone arithmetic tasks can effectively trigger this vulnerability, and the prompts based on such tasks exhibit simpler logical structures than mathematical word problems. (Abstract)
column14: Deliberate prompt injection attack (injected via external data into an LLM-integrated application) that weaponizes an existing non-adversarial vulnerability; registry entry 'mechanism: Reasoning Interruption Attack' is half right - the underlying thinking-stopped behaviour is a failure mode, but the named contribution is an attack and should be coded as such. Origin 'improves': the vulnerability and its original trigger method are from Cui et al. (2025); the contribution here is cheaper triggering (standalone arithmetic seeds) plus an adaptive token compression framework. No claim/evaluation mismatch - the claim is cheaper triggering at comparable ASR and both token cost and ASR are measured head to head against the prior method.

column3: Hidden in Memory: Sleeper Memory Poisoning in LLM Agents
column11: Full three-stage pipeline (memory write / retrieval / downstream influence) across stateful LLM assistants including GPT-5.5 and Kimi-K2.6, under both model-issued memory tools and an external memory manager (Mem0); payload variants including an actor-critic optimized payload (AC) and its defense-adaptive variant (AC+), plus goal-rewrite retrieval optimization; measured as memory-injection rate (up to 99.8%), retrieval rate, and attacker-intended behavioral/agentic action rates (41.0-89%). Also evaluated against defenses: hardened system prompt, spotlighting / untrusted-content markers, and an LLM document scanner.
column12: We propose and study sleeper memory poisoning, a delayed attack in which an adversary manipulates external context, such as a document, webpage, or repository, to cause the assistant to store a fabricated memory about the user. (Abstract)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'mechanism: Sleeper Memory Poisoning'. This is a deliberate adversarial attack with an explicit black-box external-content threat model, not a non-adversarial mechanism - it should be 'attack'. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the paper measures the failure mode end to end (write rate, retrieval rate, downstream attacker-intended action rate) rather than capability scores. Defenses tested but not proposed; the paper notes defenses 'can mitigate injection but remain brittle across models and adaptive attacks'.

column3: MUZZLE: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Web Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
column11: 4 sandboxed web applications (Gitea, Postmill, Classifieds, plus cross-app targets Northwind/Postmill), 10 adversarial objectives spanning confidentiality/integrity/availability, k=5 runs per spec; target web agents powered by GPT-4.1, GPT-4o and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct under the BrowserUse and Agent-E scaffolds; metrics are Partial Attacks and End-to-End Attacks, plus framework runtime/cost breakdown. Result: 44 distinct IPI attacks discovered, including 3 cross-application attacks and an agent-tailored phishing scenario.
column12: To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to address fully automated red-teaming of web agents against indirect prompt injection attacks, operating end-to-end in a sandboxed web environment without human intervention. (Contributions)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'mechanism: MUZZLE'. MUZZLE is an adversarial red-teaming/attack-generation framework with a live adversary, not a non-adversarial mechanism - should be 'attack'. Borderline between proposes_attack and benchmark_or_dataset: it is an automated attack-discovery system rather than a fixed benchmark, and the contributions list leads with the attack framework, so proposes_attack. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: it measures attack success (partial and end-to-end) directly. Evidence quote taken verbatim from the contributions list; note the PDF renders the system name in small caps as 'M UZZLE' elsewhere in the text.

column3: Bypassing AI Control Protocols via Agent-as-a-Proxy Attacks
column11: AgentDojo v1.2.1 (Slack suite, 20 user tasks x 5 injection tasks, 'important instructions' attack template, 89 usable samples); monitoring protocols AlignmentCheck, Extract-and-Evaluate and LlamaFirewall (PromptGuard 2 + AlignmentCheck); monitor LLMs of varying scale including Qwen2.5-72B; agents including GPT-4o mini and Llama-3.1-70B; metric attack success rate against the monitor (over 90% against AlignmentCheck).
column12: We propose the Agent-as-a-Proxy attack framework, which utilizes the victim agent to deliver adversarial attack strings to the monitoring system. (Contributions)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'mechanism: Agent-as-a-Proxy attack'. This is a deliberate adaptive attack against monitoring defenses, not a non-adversarial mechanism - should be 'attack'. Origin coded invents for the Agent-as-a-Proxy framing; note that its optimizer, Parallel-GCG, is an extension of GCG (Zou et al. 2023) and of multi-objective GCG (Zhan et al. 2025), so the optimization component is an improvement rather than an invention. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: it claims monitoring-based defenses can be bypassed and measures ASR against those monitors directly. Limitation acknowledged in the paper: the gradient computation assumes a fixed trajectory and perfect verbatim echoing of the attack string.

column3: When Compression Becomes an Attack Surface: Black-Box Attacks on Prompt-Compressed LLM Agents
column11: Three tasks (agent tool selection, question answering, system prompt corruption) across six widely used prompt compressors (extractive and abstractive, incl. LLMLingua2); average attack success rate 0.71 versus 0.21 for the strongest non-compression-based attack baseline; generalization across compression budgets, backend LLMs and surrogate compressors; two real-world agent case studies; an LLM-judge reliability check; and a mitigation study showing trusted/untrusted input isolation improves robustness.
column12: We present COMA, a transfer-based black-box attack that exploits prompt compression to induce the misbehavior in LLM agents. (Contributions)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'mechanism: COMA'. COMA is a deliberate black-box adversarial attack (the paper's own framing: 'our attack target is the compressor rather than the backend LLM') - should be 'attack'. Highly relevant to the SoK because the attack surface is the context-management layer itself: adversarially steering a lossy compressor to discard task-critical evidence or safety guardrails. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: 'adversarial information loss' is measured through downstream behavioral distortion and ASR, with explicit non-compression attack baselines, not through token counts or latency.

column3: Self-interpreting Adversarial Images
column7: mechanism: self-interpreting images via adversarial meta-

column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'mechanism: self-interpreting images via adversarial meta-instructions'. This is a deliberate indirect cross-modal injection attack by a third-party content producer against VLM users - should be 'attack'. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the paper claims adversary-chosen steering of interpretation and measures exactly that with automatic classifiers across 12 meta-objectives and 3 VLMs. Relevant to the SoK as the non-text channel of untrusted context: the perturbation carries no readable instruction and survives perplexity/naturalness screening.

column3: From Shield to Target: Denial-of-Service Attacks on LLM-Based Agent Guardrails
column11: Eight guardrail model backbones (surrogate TS-Guard-8B plus Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen families) with varied safety templates and agent benchmarks; six prior DoS baselines (ENGORGIO, OverThink, CRABS, ReasoningBomb, RECUR, ThinkTrap) and a length-matched benign control; think-length/token amplification (13-63x, 27.7x vs 1.1-1.2x for baselines) and latency amplification up to 148x; four end-to-end deployments (web, desktop, OpenHands coding agent on 20 SWE-bench instances, LangGraph multi-agent); mechanism measurements (attention-to-schema-header weights, entropy collapse); ablation of the optimization framework and several mitigations.
