column14: Registry says 'mechanism: Reasoning-Extension Denial-of-Service (DoS)' - this is a deliberate adversarial attack (poisoned documents/web content crafted by beam search), not a non-adversarial mechanism; it should be an attack entry. Note the printout's 'EVALUATION' extract showed appendix payload examples rather than the evaluation section; the fields above come from grep of Section 6 setup, Table 3 and Section 7. The payload text printed inside the excerpt is attacker data quoted by the paper, not instructions, and was ignored. No mismatch: the paper measures the availability failure (think length, latency, cascading starvation) it claims.

column3: When Benchmarks Lie: Evaluating Malicious Prompt Classifiers Under True Distribution Shift
column11: A benchmark pool of 18 datasets / 105K samples (BIPIA, deepset, jayavibhav, qualifire, safeguard, wildjailbreak, advbench, harmbench, injecagent, llmail, mosscap, yanismiraoui, 10k prompts, dolly 15k, enron, openorca, softAge); 5-fold CV vs held-out test vs Leave-One-Dataset-Out on four backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-27B, Qwen-3.5-4B/2B, partial Llama-3.3-70B); raw-activation probe vs SAE probe vs MLP; a dataset-identity classifier; and domain-generalization fixes (adversarial training, subspace projection, reweighting, class balancing).
column12: We train activation-based classifiers (linear probes on LLM hidden states) on a benchmark of 18 datasets (prompt attacks plus benign sources) and propose Leave-One-Dataset-Out (LODO) evaluation, where the held-out dataset is never seen during training. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement: entry reads 'defense: Activation-based (linear probe) prompt-injection ... needs_read'. The paper does not propose that probe as its contribution - it uses the existing activation-probe recipe (Abdelnabi et al.) as the object of study and contributes an evaluation protocol (LODO), a coefficient-retention/shortcut metric, and the finding that standard CV overstates generalization by 8-16pp. Coded measurement_study accordingly, with technique_name/origin blank per the field rules. Names no attack or failure mode of its own (the attack datasets it cites are other papers'), so names_registry_technique=no. No mismatch marker: the claimed problem (benchmark-driven overestimation) is exactly what is measured.

column3: Cache What Lasts: Token Retention for Memory-Bounded KV Cache in LLMs
column11: GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME24 (math reasoning), LongProc (procedural generation), LongMemEval (long-memory chat), LongBenchV2 and SCBench (long-context understanding), against full-cache and eviction/retrieval baselines (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, and a SOTA learnable KV-retrieval baseline), at matched and 4x KV budgets; plus qualitative retention-score analyses and layer/head sparsity.
column12: We propose TRIM-KV, a novel approach that learns each token's intrinsic importance at creation time via a lightweight retention gate. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper claims selective retention acts as a regularizer 'suppressing noise from uninformative tokens' and motivates itself partly by distracting context causing premature eviction, but the evaluation measures only task accuracy/pass@1 on GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME24, LongProc, LongMemEval, LongBenchV2 and SCBench plus KV-budget/memory efficiency - no distractor-controlled ablation, no measurement of noise or interference as such. Registry disagreement: entry reads 'defense: TRIM-KV'; there is no adversary anywhere in this paper, so it is a non-adversarial context-management fix, not a defense. Borderline on scope: primary framing is memory/compute efficiency, and only the noise-suppression claim ties it to the corpus; kept in per Ruling 1 and Ruling 3.

column11: 480 runs on a fully local testbed with a qwen2.5:7b agent and attacker-controlled page server/collection endpoint; injection carriers varied (title, meta description, Open Graph tags, body, comments, anchor text, redirect chains up to 3 hops), single-shot vs sharded (4-fragment) exfiltration; metrics P(tool), P(egress) ~0.89, Leak@k (sharding cuts Leak@1 by 73%), output-based safety-check detection rate (95% missed); ablation of prompt-layer vs system/network-layer defenses (domain allowlisting, redirect-chain analysis).
column12: We show that this workflow gives rise to implicit prompt injection: adversarial instructions embedded in automatically generated URL previews, including titles, metadata, and snippets, can introduce a system-level risk that we refer to as silent egress. (Abstract)
column14: Registry says 'mechanism: Silent Egress (implicit prompt injection via U...)' - this is a deliberate attack with an explicit adversary and attacker-controlled endpoint, so it belongs under attacks, not mechanisms. Origin coded invents: the paper defines implicit prompt injection as a new named subclass of Greshake-style indirect injection (could defensibly be 'improves' on indirect prompt injection). No mismatch: it measures network egress and leakage directly, which is precisely the failure it claims prior output-only evaluation misses. Single model (qwen2.5:7b) and deliberately unobfuscated payloads, so authors frame rates as a lower bound.

column3: Zombie Agents: Persistent Control of Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Self-Reinforcing Injections
column11: Four indirect prompt injection baselines (Naive, Context Ignoring, Escape Characters, Fake Completion) on two memory architectures (sliding-window and RAG memory) and three evolution strategies (Raw History, Verbal Reflection, Refined Experience); metrics cumulative ASR for data exfiltration and command execution, payload retention over 20+ rounds, payload count in the memory store, Recall@k at top-10/50/100; also tested against Sandwich, Instructional and Spotlight prompt defenses.
column12: Our results show that memory evolution can convert one-time indirect injection into persistent compromise, which suggests that defenses focused only on per-session prompt filtering are not sufficient for self-evolving agents. (Abstract)
column14: No registry entry; should be added as an attack (persistent memory poisoning of self-evolving agents). No mismatch: persistence itself is measured (retention rate across rounds, payload proliferation in the RAG store, retrieval density), not just end-task success. Note the printout found no evaluation heading; the fields come from the mid-document RQ1/RQ2 sections.

column3: Hippocampus: An Efficient and Scalable Memory Module for Agentic AI
column11: LoCoMo (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain; F1, BLEU-1, LLM-as-a-Judge) and LongMemEval (accuracy) against memory-module baselines ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT, A-mem, MemoryOS and MemOS; plus efficiency metrics - average end-to-end retrieval latency (up to 31x lower) and average token consumption per query (up to 14x lower).
column12: Existing memory systems use dense vector databases or knowledge-graph traversal (or hybrid), incurring high retrieval latency and poor storage scalability. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The introduction motivates the system with the bounded context window and the 'Lost-in-Middle' effect - agents that 'lose track of prior actions, repeat failed strategies, or misinterpret context' - but the evaluation measures only QA accuracy on LoCoMo and LongMemEval plus latency and per-query token footprint. Nothing measures positional degradation, distraction or any context failure mode; there is no distractor-controlled ablation. Registry disagreement: entry reads 'defense: Hippocampus (Dynamic Wavelet Matrix memory)' - there is no adversary in this paper; it is a non-adversarial memory/efficiency fix. Core technical novelty is the Dynamic Wavelet Matrix (DWM) append-friendly index.

column3: Prometheus: Towards Long-Horizon Codebase Navigation for Repository-Level Problem Solving
column11: SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks; 74.4% resolve rate with GPT-5) and SWE-PolyBench Verified (382 tasks; 33.8%), against leaderboard/reported baselines SWE-agent, OpenHands, Agentless, live-SWE-agent, mini-SWE-agent, SWE-Exp, Lingxi, Amazon Q Developer Agent and Aider; plus RQ2, a trajectory analysis on 100 SWE-bench Verified instances comparing agent-retrieved context against a human-constructed gold context for Prometheus, Agentless, OpenHands and SWE-agent.
column12: To address these limitations, we present Prometheus, a memory-centric coding agent framework for long-horizon codebase navigation. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around the 'Needle-in-a-Haystack' problem - relevant evidence 'overwhelmed by large volumes of irrelevant code and documentation' and stateless agents repeating traversals - but the headline evaluation measures only issue-resolution rates on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-PolyBench Verified. Partial mitigation worth noting: RQ2 compares retrieved context against a gold context, which does measure context precision/recall rather than task score, but nothing measures distraction or dilution as a failure mode (no distractor-controlled ablation, no terminal-state analysis vs trajectory length). Registry disagreement: entry reads 'defense: Prometheus (memory-centric context engine...)' - there is no adversary in this paper; it is a non-adversarial context-management fix.

column11: Mind2Web (Cross-Task / Cross-Website / Cross-Domain splits) with EA, AF1, StepSR, TaskSR, and WebArena success rate; baselines MindAct and flat-memory AWM (offline and online). Offline and online memory-induction settings.
column12: We propose HMT, a hierarchical memory architecture for web agents, which mitigates intention-execution entanglement by organizing stored interaction trajectories into a hierarchy of intent, stage, and action levels. (Contributions)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around a context-integrity failure ('intention-execution entanglement', 'workflow mismatch and context pollution' when retrieved flat-memory trajectories are conflated with the current page), but the evaluation measures only capability: element accuracy, action F1, step success rate and task success rate on Mind2Web splits plus WebArena success rate. There is no distractor-controlled or pollution-specific measurement of the named failure mode itself; the mitigation claim is inferred from higher success rates in cross-website settings. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: HMT', but there is no adversary anywhere in the paper - this is a non-adversarial fix, so proposes_fix. Named failure mode 'intention-execution entanglement' is newly coined here (and 'context pollution' used descriptively).

column3: Mind Mapping Prompt Injection: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks in Modern Large Language Models
column11: ASR and Helpful Rate against four baseline attack families - pure text-based prompt injection, visual prompt injection, encoding-based injection (Base64, Leetspeak) and masked/ASCII-art injection (ArtPrompt) - on the harmful_behaviors_custom and harmfulqa datasets, against gemini-1.5-flash-latest, gpt-4o-11-20 and grok-3-beta, with human evaluation of harmfulness (90% ASR vs 30.5% best baseline).
column12: This study introduces a novel method for bypassing LLM security policies by embedding malicious instructions within a mind map image. (Abstract)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry labels this 'mechanism: Mind Mapping Prompt Injection'; it is a deliberate adversarial attack (proposes_attack), not a non-adversarial mechanism. Scope caveat: this is a multimodal jailbreak that elicits harmful content from a chat LLM via an attacker-supplied image, not an agent ingesting untrusted pipeline content - it belongs to the prompt-injection family but is direct, not indirect. Evaluation is well matched to the claim (ASR against named baseline attacks on two harmful-behavior datasets).

No defense baseline and no ASR against prior attacks.
column12: In this research, we explore converting a nonsensical suffix attack into a sensible prompt via a situation-driven contextual re-writing. (Abstract)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'mechanism: situation-driven contextual adversarial prompt'; it is a deliberate attack, so proposes_attack. origin is improves, not invents: the explicit framing is doing gradient-free what Wang et al. (2024) did with gradients. Scope caveat: this is a direct jailbreak authored by the user (movie synopsis as 'situational context'), not untrusted content arriving through a pipeline; keep in corpus as prompt-injection family but flag as marginal. The attack name is descriptive rather than a brand, so names_registry_technique=yes is a soft yes. Evaluation is thin (Table 1, 5 models, one judge score each).

No end-to-end agent or adaptive-attack evaluation.

Registry entry ('defense: UNNAMED: Embedding-based semantic context analysis', needs_read) is correct; coded improves_existing rather than proposes_defense because the method is unnamed and is an extension of prior embedding + tree-classifier detection from direct to indirect injection. Claim/evaluation line up, but note the limitation: evaluated only as offline binary classification on BIPIA-derived samples with LLM-generated benign counterparts, and the paper itself cites adaptive attacks (Zhan et al.) that break deployed defenses without testing against any.

Evaluation section is short and the comparison numbers are presented only in a small table; baselines are the three named prior injection families.

No mismatch marker: the context failure mode is measured directly (position-sensitivity experiments over early/middle/late evidence sessions, i.e. lost-in-the-middle, and context-scalability variants of LONGMEMEVAL), not only end-task accuracy. column3: Seeing through the Conflict: Transparent Knowledge Conflict Handling in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
column11: Wikidata-Conflict-5K (own conflict-detection set); ConflictTQA (TriviaQA-based) and ConflictPQA (PopQA-based) with golden/irrelevant/conflicting contexts; KILT (NQ, HotpotQA, FEVER); ConflictBank 2024; single-document top-1 NQ. Baselines: Prompt, KAFT, IRCAN, RAAT, PARENTING, Astute RAG plus decoding baselines. Metrics: conflict-detection F1/AUROC, EM drop under 30% noise, cross-domain F1 (Bio/Fin), knowledge-gap recovery, misleading-context override rate.
column12: We propose a novel framework to resolve knowledge conflicts in RAG. (Proposed Method)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: TCR (Transparent Conflict Resolution). Non-adversarial context-memory conflict in RAG (temporal mismatch, misinformation in retrieved documents, misleading prompts), so proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense; there is no adversary. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the evaluation measures the failure mode directly with purpose-built conflicting-context datasets and reports misleading-context override reduction and EM drop under injected noise, which lines up with the claim. Registry says 'defense: TCR' - disagreement only on defense vs fix (no deliberate attacker in the paper); the name and 'proposed' origin are correct. Paper names no attack or failure mode that others cite and test against (it uses the generic term 'context-memory conflict'), hence names_registry_technique=no.

column3: StackPlanner: A Centralized Hierarchical Multi-Agent System with Task-Experience Memory Management
column11: 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, GAIA, FRAMES (F1/accuracy); DeepResearch Bench report generation (RACE quality and FACT citation metrics); 100 multi-turn follow-up instances; GSM8K, MATH, TriviaQA, PopQA, GPQA for the RL/experience ablation. Baselines: Base, FS-RAG, ReAct, IRCoT, OWL, MacNet, AFlow, ReSearch, ARPO, STORM, WebWeaver, EDR. Ablations: w/o Task Memory, w/o Experience, w/o Both, w/o RL.
column12: However, central agents often suffer from unstable long-horizon collaboration due to the lack of memory management, leading to context bloat, error accumulation, and poor cross-task generalization. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. DEFENSE-NAMES: StackPlanner. The paper frames itself around context bloat, contextual noise, error accumulation and the central agent becoming 'lost in the middle', but every number reported is capability or task performance: F1/accuracy on 2Wiki, MuSiQue, GAIA, FRAMES, RACE/FACT report-quality scores on DeepResearch Bench, follow-up refinement scores, and GSM8K/MATH/TriviaQA/PopQA/GPQA. Nothing measures context bloat, noise propagation or positional degradation directly; the 'w/o Task Memory' ablation is a component ablation on the same task scores, not a distractor-controlled or saturation-controlled measurement of the failure mode. Registry says 'defense: StackPlanner' - disagreement: there is no adversary anywhere in the paper, this is a non-adversarial context-management fix (LIFO task memory stack with RL-trained REVISE actions plus structured experience memory).

Metrics: AlignScore and T5-NLI faithfulness, EM Recall and hit-rate correctness. Baselines: in-context prompting with gpt-4o and Llama-3.1-8b, CAD contrastive decoding, extractive sentence selection (stella-1.5b, instructor-large), standard SFT (greedy and beam3), and the GenDiE answer-level and gold-answer variants.
column12: Experiments on ASQA (in-domain LFQA) and ConFiQA (out-of-domain counterfactual QA) datasets demonstrate that GenDiE surpasses various baselines in both faithfulness and correctness, and exhibits robust performance for domain adaptation. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: GenDiE (Generate, Discriminate, Evolve). Non-adversarial failure (unfaithfulness to provided context under knowledge conflict), so proposes_fix, not proposes_defense. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: ConFiQA supplies counterfactual passages that instantiate the knowledge conflict, and faithfulness is measured directly with AlignScore and an NLI-trained T5-11B, so the measurement matches the claim. Registry says 'defense: GenDiE' - same defense-vs-fix disagreement as rows 47/48; name and 'proposed' origin are correct.

column3: Separator Injection Attack: Uncovering Dialogue Biases in Large Language Models Caused by Role Separators
column11: Attack success rate on Llama2-7B, Vicuna-7B, Llama3-8B and Qwen2-7B over MRPC, RTE, SST2, SMS, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA, MMLU and ARC; manual injection baselines (naive, escape/ignore-style handcrafted prompts, a combined strategy, and a repeated-character fuzzing method) and automatic attacks TAP and MGCG; plus positional-bias (PBI) and task-bias (TBI) metrics and an attention analysis. column12: We further develop the Separators Injection Attack (SIA), a new orthometric attack based on role separators. (Abstract)
column14: Deliberate prompt-injection attack exploiting role separators, preceded by an empirical study of positional and task bias in multi-task instruction following. Evaluation measures the failure mode directly (bias metrics plus ASR), no mismatch. Registry says 'mechanism: Separator Injection Attack' - two disagreements: (a) this is an adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial mechanism, exactly the mislabelling pattern the brief warns about; (b) the paper writes the name as 'Separators Injection Attack' (plural Separators), and origin should be 'proposed'/invents rather than None. The paper also analyses weaknesses of existing defenses but proposes none.

column3: Beyond Compaction: Structured Context Eviction for Long-Horizon Agents
column11: Terminal Bench 2.0 (89 agentic tasks, n=5), SWE Bench Lite (50-task sample, n=3), Recovery Bench (n=3) and LongCLI Bench (n=3), all with GPT-5.4, comparing single-session CWL under an 80,000-token budget against the standard per-task isolated-session baseline on mean task accuracy, plus total token consumption and inference cost. Results: 68.25 vs 68.40, 43.00 vs 40.00, 66.80 vs 69.75, 20.00 vs 20.00.
column12: Across all four benchmarks, the CWL and baseline conditions differ by at most 3 percentage points in either direction. (Empirical Evaluation)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. DEFENSE-NAMES: Context Window Lifecycle (CWL). The paper claims CWL keeps context below 'the regime where attention degrades and hallucination rates rise' and that it avoids compaction's unpredictable lossiness, destroyed causal structure and compression-induced hallucination, but the evaluation measures only task accuracy on Terminal Bench 2.0, SWE Bench Lite, Recovery Bench and LongCLI Bench plus token consumption and cost. No measurement of attention degradation, hallucination rate, information loss or causal-structure preservation, and no comparison against summarization compaction or recency truncation - the only baseline is per-task isolated sessions that 'never face context pressure'. The headline result is a non-result (differences within run-to-run variance), and the authors concede that harness-level token optimisations made it hard to even reach the budget on the shorter benchmarks. Registry says 'defense: CWL' - disagreement: no adversary at all, this is a non-adversarial context-management fix.

column3: TruthfulRAG: Resolving Factual-level Conflicts in Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Knowledge Graphs

column12: To address this limitation, we propose TruthfulRAG, the first framework that leverages Knowledge Graphs (KGs) to resolve factual-level knowledge conflicts in RAG systems. (Abstract)

Non-adversarial (temporal staleness, counterfactual and multi-hop fact-level conflicts), so proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the datasets are conflict datasets (FaithEval unanswerable/inconsistent/counterfactual contexts, KRE fact-level conflicts, RealtimeQA temporal conflicts) and the paper additionally checks behaviour in non-conflicting contexts, so the measurement matches the claim. Registry says 'defense: TruthfulRAG (knowledge-graph-based factual con...)' - same defense-vs-fix disagreement; name and 'proposed' origin are correct.

column3: Document-Authored Control-Signal Impersonation: A Low-Cost Indirect Prompt Attack on RAG Safety Boundaries
column11: Six model settings (DeepSeek V4 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Flash, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Low, Qwen3.5-397B, GLM-4.7) in seven experiments: prompt pressure (E1), DACSI vs. conventional imperative-injection baselines (E2), control-signal taxonomy (E3), RAG mediation with toy insertion, BM25, hybrid-embedding retrieval and a LangChain-style public-corpus reproduction (E4), system-control probes for source separation and redaction (E5), source-authority placement probe (M1), and canary formats including bearer tokens, AWS-like keys, GitHub PAT-like strings, Slack bot tokens, database URLs and JWTs (E6). Outcome is unsafe disclosure rate of synthetic credential canaries, measured as lift over a defended baseline B1, n=200 per condition, with Wilson intervals, exact paired McNemar/sign tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
column12: We call this pattern Document-Authored Control-Signal Impersonation (DACSI). (Introduction)
column14: Registry disagreement: entry reads 'mechanism: DACSI'. This is a deliberate adversarial attack - an attacker authors retrievable text that impersonates metadata, provenance, authority or disclosure-policy signals - so it should be classified as an attack, not a non-adversarial mechanism. This is exactly the mislabelling pattern the brief warns about. No claim/evaluation mismatch: the paper claims a command-free control-signal impersonation surface and measures unsafe canary disclosure lift against matched imperative-injection and defended baselines, including a RAG-mediated pipeline. The paper is unusually careful about scope (regime-based interpretation, saturation and ceiling effects, 'behavioral attribution evidence, not proof of an internal mechanism'). It also reports a mitigation (system/document source separation and redaction probes) but does not name it as a defense.

column3: PI-Hunter: Automated Red-Teaming for Exposing and Localizing Prompt Injections
column11: AgentDojo and AgentDyn, with ReAct and Planner-Executor agent architectures and backbones Gemini-3.1-pro, GPT-5.4-mini, Claude-4.6-sonnet (plus Gemini-2.5-pro and DeepSeek in the appendix). Injections include the benchmarks' own direct, ignore_previous, system_msg and important_inst attacks plus the stronger AgentVigil attack. Defenses tested: None, Spotlighting, MELON, PIGuard. Four injection scenarios (single_single, single_multi, multi_single, multi_multi). Metrics: source- and instruction-level localization precision/recall, entropy-based diversity, and query/token cost, all against an unconstrained agentic red-teaming baseline.
column12: We propose PI-Hunter, an automated agentic auditing framework for proactive vulnerability exposure in LLM agents. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement: entry reads 'mechanism: PI-Hunter'. PI-Hunter is not a non-adversarial failure mode; it is an automated red-teaming / attack-generation framework that evolves source-aware test cases to surface latent injections, so it is coded proposes_attack even though it is framed defensively as pre-deployment auditing. Borderline between proposes_attack and benchmark_or_dataset: it is a technique rather than a fixed artifact, and the contributions list leads with the framework, so proposes_attack. No claim/evaluation mismatch - the claim is improved exposure and localization of latent injections, and that is exactly what is measured (source/instruction precision, recall and diversity), including under four published defenses. Useful registry leads cited here but not contributed: AgentVigil, AgentDyn, Spotlighting, MELON, PIGuard.

column3: AgentRedBench: Dynamic Redteaming and Integration-Aware Defense for LLM Agents over SaaS Integrations

column12: We introduce AGENTREDBENCH, a dynamic LLM-driven redteaming benchmark of 215 subtle underspecified-authorization scenarios across 24 enterprise integrations and five attack types. (Abstract)

The paper's own contributions list leads with the benchmark, not the guard, so contribution is benchmark_or_dataset (technique_name left blank per the field rule) and AGENTREDGUARD is the secondary artifact. names_registry_technique is yes on the AgentDojo precedent: the benchmark defines and names three active attack types that others can cite and test against (output_channel_url_relay, content_hijack, destination_hijack), plus two universally-bound delegation patterns whose names are in Appendix A and were not retrievable from the printed text. column3: MemMachine: A Ground-Truth-Preserving Memory System for Personalized AI Agents

Partial credit: the WikiMultiHop condition pools all question contexts into one episodic store with fully randomized ordering, which is a distractor-controlled setting, but it is reported as an accuracy number and is never tied back to the factual-drift claim; no ablation compares extraction-based against ground-truth-preserving storage for error accumulation. Registry disagreement: 'defense: MemMachine' is wrong - no adversary anywhere; this is a non-adversarial memory/context-management fix.

The contributions lead with the benchmark (MisBench), with RtD presented afterwards as a derived countermeasure, so coded benchmark_or_dataset rather than proposes_defense; registry entry 'defense: Reconstruct to Discriminate (RtD)' captures the secondary contribution only and misses that the paper's headline artifact is MisBench. Claim and measurement line up: the paper measures susceptibility to the misinformation types and styles it defines (Success Rate, Memorization Ratio, Evidence Tendency), with ablation across conflict type, style, hop count and presence/absence of parametric knowledge -- no CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. Note the benchmark's misinformation is LLM-generated and deliberately planted, so this straddles adversarial and non-adversarial context poisoning. Note also that the paper renders its benchmark name in small caps; it appears in the extracted text as 'M IS B ENCH'.

column3: Improving Coherence and Persistence in Agentic AI for System Optimization
column11: Nine systems problems (eight from the ADRS benchmark plus the Glia LLM request router): multi-cloud multicast (Cloudcast 71-node topology), LLM inference request routing, KV cache reuse / LLM-SQL, Telemetry, EPLB, Prism, TXN, CBL, CBL-Multi, Vidur. Baselines: human SOTA, OpenEvolve, Glia, FunSearch, EoH, and single-turn LLM prompting (o3, gpt-4o, gpt-5.2, gpt-5.2-xhigh). Metrics: best cost ($622 vs human SOTA $626), mean response time (23.9 s vs Glia 25.7 s), task scores, and median normalized AUC of the best-so-far curve. Ablations: Struggle protocol removal, GGR-seeded prompt sensitivity.
column12: Conversely, existing agentic frameworks suffer from context degradation over long horizons or fail to accumulate knowledge across independent runs. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper names two failure modes and explicitly invokes 'context rot' and uneven attention over a long-running context as the motivation for Engram, but the evaluation measures ONLY capability and efficiency: dollar cost, mean response time, task scores on ADRS problems, and median normalized AUC of the best-so-far improvement curve. Context degradation itself is never measured -- there is no experiment varying context length, trajectory length, or amount of accumulated history, and no terminal-state-vs-length analysis. The closest thing is a narrative remark in the Fig. 6 discussion that Glia 'eventually exhausts its context/budget'. Both failure-mode names ('evolutionary neighborhood bias', 'the coherence ceiling') are new coinages by this paper, so names_registry_technique=yes is on the paper's own naming, not on established third-party uptake. Registry entry 'defense: Engram (Archive + Research Digest)' mislabels it: there is no adversary; this is non-adversarial context management, i.e. proposes_fix. Defense-side component names: Archive; Research Digest; structured handoff; Struggle protocol.

column3: MetaMem: Evolving Meta-Memory for Knowledge Utilization through Self-Reflective Symbolic Optimization
column11: LongMemEval benchmark, accuracy across Single User, Single Assistant, Single Preference, Multi-Session, Temporal Reasoning and Knowledge Update dimensions; baselines Full Text, RAG, MapReduce, Mem0, A-Mem, MemoryOS and LightMem (primary baseline); backbones Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct and Llama3.1-70B-Instruct with Qwen3-235B-A22B as judge; plus an out-of-domain generalization check on ShareGPT and component ablations.
column12: However, while recent approaches have succeeded in constructing effective memories, they often disrupt the inherent logical and temporal relationships within interaction sessions, resulting in fragmented memory units and degraded reasoning performance. (Abstract)
column14: No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker. The paper's claimed failure mode is fragmented, contradictory memory units and distracting evidence pulled from scattered sessions, and the evaluation does probe this fairly directly rather than capability alone: the LongMemEval Knowledge Update dimension measures adaptation to newly introduced conflicting information (the pivot-after-contradictory-update case named in Ruling 1's carve-out), and the Multi-Session and Temporal Reasoning dimensions target cross-session fragmentation and temporal-order disruption. Caveat: all measurements are still accuracy on a single benchmark; there is no controlled distractor-density ablation. Figure 1 explicitly contrasts correct vs 'distracting evidence'. Registry entry 'defense: MetaMem (self-evolving meta-memory)' mislabels the genre: there is no adversary anywhere; this is a non-adversarial context/memory fix. Note that MetaMem builds its factual memory layer on LightMem, so it is a layer added on top of existing memory systems rather than a from-scratch system, but the contribution is framed and named as new, hence origin=invents.

column3: RAG-Modulo: Solving Sequential Tasks using Experience, Critics, and Language Models
column11: BabyAI-Synth, BabyAI-BossLevel, AlfWorld-Seen (140 instances) and AlfWorld-Unseen (132 instances); baselines Expert, ProgPrompt and LLM-Planner; metrics success rate (SR), infeasible executions (InExec) and plan length (Len), with GPT-4o as the planner and text-embedding-3-large as retriever; ablations over number of retrieved interactions K and over retrieval granularity (interaction-level vs skill-level).
column12: We propose RAG-Modulo, a framework that enhances LLM-based agents with a memory of past interactions and incorporates critics to evaluate the agents’ decisions. (Abstract)
column14: Borderline scope, kept in the corpus but flagged. The paper's stated problem is a capability gap (LLM agents cannot learn from past interactions in long-horizon robotic tasks), not untrustworthy context, and the headline metrics are task success rate, infeasible-execution count and plan length on BabyAI and AlfWorld. What keeps it arguably relevant is one ablation: varying the number K of retrieved past interactions produces a rise-then-fall curve, which the authors attribute to the model's sensitivity to irrelevant or noisy retrieved context (citing Shi et al. on distraction by irrelevant context and Liu et al. 'Lost in the Middle'), concluding that K between 5 and 10 is best. That is a distractor-density ablation measuring retrieval-noise degradation directly, so no CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker -- the paper never claims to solve a context problem in the first place. Registry entry 'defense: RAG-Modulo' is wrong on genre: there is no adversary; it is an extension of LLM-Modulo with episodic memory and critics, hence improves_existing.

column3: FlashMem: Distilling Intrinsic Latent Memory via Computation Reuse
column11: GSM8K, MATH, GPQA (reasoning), KodCode (coding), BookSum and GovReport (summarization); baselines Vanilla, CoT-SC, SnapKV (KV compression) and MemGen (generative latent memory), plus SoftCoT, LatentSeek, MemOS and matched SFT controls in the appendix; backbones Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen3-4B, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.2-3B and (appendix) Qwen3-14B/32B; metrics Accuracy, ROUGE-1, inference latency (5x reduction) and VRAM overhead; appendix also reports LongBench v2 (41.5) and RULER-64k NIAH / multi-hop tracing (88.5 / 97.2).
column12: Experiments demonstrate that FlashMem matches the performance of heavy baselines while reducing inference latency by 5 times, effectively bridging the gap between efficiency and persistent cognition. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper is framed around context saturation -- token-level memory 'crowding out the finite context window with raw text' and 'exhausting finite attention budgets' -- plus statelessness and redundant reprocessing of history. What is actually measured is capability and efficiency only: task accuracy on GSM8K/MATH/GPQA/KodCode, ROUGE-1 on BookSum/GovReport, inference latency and VRAM. No experiment varies history length, distractor density or noise to show that context crowding is reduced. Partial mitigation worth recording: appendix RULER-64k NIAH / multi-hop tracing and LongBench v2 numbers do probe long-context retrieval, but they are reported as additional capability scores, not as a measurement of the saturation mechanism, and they sit outside the main results. Component names: Shared-KV Consolidator; Cognitive Monitor (attention-entropy trigger). Registry entry 'defense: FlashMem' is wrong on genre: no adversary anywhere, this is a non-adversarial context/memory efficiency fix.

column3: MEMO: Memory-Augmented Model Context Optimization for Robust Multi-Turn Multi-Agent LLM Games
column11: Five TextArena-style games (SimpleNegotiation, TwoDollar, KuhnPoker, Briscola, SimpleTak) spanning negotiation, imperfect-information and perfect-information classes; baselines: static prompting (default TextArena prompt, CoT, ToT), prompt optimization (TextGrad, MIPRO, GEPA) and self-play RL (UnstableBaselines, SPIRAL); base models GPT-4o-mini and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, evaluated against held-out opponents Grok-4-Fast-Non-Reasoning, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507; metrics mean win rate, relative standard error (RSE) across runs, output token cost and number of games to reach a win rate.
column12: In long-horizon interactions, small early deviations compound across turns and are amplified by multi-agent coupling. (Abstract)
column14: No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker, but the judgement is mixed and worth recording. The claimed failure is run-to-run instability caused by each model output becoming part of the subsequent input, so early deviations compound into divergent trajectories; the evaluation measures that directly via relative standard error across repeated runs (RSE drops from 44.9% baseline to 6.4% for GPT-4o-mini), alongside capability win rates. Scope is borderline: the untrusted content is the agents' own accumulated turn history rather than external or attacker-planted context, and there is no adversary. Component names: Retention (persistent memory bank); Exploration (TrueSkill-based tournament prompt evolution); prioritized replay. Registry entry 'defense: MEMO' mislabels the genre: no deliberate attack is involved, so proposes_fix, not a defense.

column3: Prompt Injection Vulnerability of Consensus Generating Applications in Digital Democracy
column11: Attack-free vs adversarial variants of consensus-generation prompts built from UK public policy questions and 2024 party manifesto positions; six injection rhetorical strategies (Emotional Appeals, False Authority, Imperative Order, Impossibility of Agreement, Misleading Statistics, Negative Consequences) crossed with three attack goals (amplify a viewpoint, erase opinions, divert consensus); models LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct, GPT-4.1 Nano and Apertus 8B; measurement via a fine-tuned BERT valence classifier and LLM-human majority agreement rates. Mitigation pipeline (GPT-OSS-SafeGuard injection detection + structured opinion representations + GSPO reinforcement learning, plus a DPO alignment variant) evaluated on the same adversarial prompts, with an overrefusal analysis.
column12: Here, we examine the vulnerability and robustness of off-the-shelf consensus-generating LLMs to prompt-injection attacks, in which texts are injected to amplify particular viewpoints, erase certain opinions, or divert consensus toward unrelated or irrelevant topics. (Abstract)
column14: Genuinely adversarial paper: deliberate prompt injection by participants in digital-democracy consensus generation. Coded measurement_study because the abstract and the stated three-step structure lead with examining vulnerability and robustness; the paper's own novelty on the attack side is a taxonomy of injection rhetorical strategies rather than one new named attack, and the defense pipeline is assembled from existing parts (GPT-OSS-SafeGuard, structured representations, GSPO/DPO) rather than invented. Claim and measurement line up (attack success measured as consensus-valence shift and LLM-human agreement change); no CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. Registry entry 'defense: GPT-OSSafeGuard + structured-representations + ...' records only the secondary mitigation pipeline and misses that the paper's lead contribution is the attack taxonomy and vulnerability measurement; per the brief, attack/failure-mode names go in named_techniques, with the defense names kept here: GPT-OSS-SafeGuard injection detection; structured opinion representations; GSPO-based reinforcement learning; DPO ethical-guideline alignment.

column3: A Modular Generative Honeypot Shell
column11: 11 LLMs (Gemma, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, Llama2, Llama3, Mistral, Mixtral, OpenChat, Qwen, Tinyllama) scored for prompt-alignment under a rudimentary shell prompt; prompt-injection input-guard classifiers (random forest vs SVM vs naive Bayes, n-gram sweep) on the deepset Hugging Face prompt-injections dataset (662 prompts, 263 adversarial), best accuracy 0.88 under 5-fold CV; single-blind within-subjects study of 4 cybersecurity professionals interacting with LIMBOSH vs a control bash shell (commands issued, time, Likert realism ratings)
column12: For this purpose, we deploy an input guard (see Figure 2) employing a random forest text classification model trained on n-grams of size 1-3. (Section IV-C, Prompt Injection Mitigation)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: LIMBOSH; input guard; input transformer; output guard; output transformer. Generative honeypot shell: the LLM is deliberately exposed to attacker-controlled input, and the paper's defensive layers are aimed squarely at prompt injection (three named exploitation scenarios: revealing the honeypot, obtaining unfettered LLM access, escaping the sandbox). Claim and evaluation line up only partially: the injection mitigation is evaluated as a standalone text-classifier accuracy number on an external dataset, NOT end-to-end against attackers in the user study, where participants were not told it was a honeypot and the measured outcome was perceived realism. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker (the eval is adversarial-relevant, not capability-only), but note the mitigation claim rests on offline classifier accuracy. No registry entry existed; a defense/honeypot label is appropriate. Related-work heading not extracted (Section II exists in the text).

column3: GUI-PRA: Process Reward Agent for GUI Tasks
column9: GUI-PRA (Process Reward Agent for GUI Tasks)
column11: Two online GUI benchmarks, AndroidWorld and Mobile-MiniWoB++ (92 tasks), with base agents Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3-8B-Instruct supervised by Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct / InternVL3-78B-Instruct; baselines are Base Agent (no guidance) and Standard PRM guidance, plus a cross-family generalization setting; metrics are Success Rate and Difficulty-Stratified Success Rate (easy/medium/hard), with an ablation removing the dynamic memory and adaptive UI perception components
column12: When processing dense artificial inputs with long history data, PRMs suffer from a "lost in the middle" phenomenon, where the overwhelming historical context compromises the evaluation of the current step. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper is framed on the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon caused by overwhelming historical context in long GUI trajectories, but the evaluation measures ONLY task capability: Success Rate and Difficulty-Stratified Success Rate on AndroidWorld and Mobile-MiniWoB++ (headline +14.53% average SR vs +8.56% for the standard PRM baseline). Nothing measures positional degradation, history length, distractor density or retrieval quality; the component ablation attributes SR gains to the dynamic memory and UI perception modules but still reports only SR. Method names: GUI-PRA; Relevance-based Retrieval Module; Progressive Summarization Module; Adaptive UI Perception / UI Tool Routing. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: current entry is 'defense: GUI-PRA', but there is no adversary anywhere in this paper - the failure is ordinary context dilution from a long interaction history, so proposes_fix (non-adversarial) is correct, not a defense. origin=improves because GUI-PRA is explicitly built as a GUI-domain upgrade of the standard PRM it is benchmarked against. names_registry_technique=no: 'lost in the middle' is borrowed from Liu et al., and the paper coins only method names.

column3: QwenLong-CPRS: Towards $\infty$-LLMs with Dynamic Context Optimization
column11: Five long-context benchmarks with inputs from 4K to 2M words, including Ruler-128K and InfiniteBench; baselines are direct prompting, RAG and sparse attention (other context management methods); cascaded with GPT-4o, Gemini2.0-pro, Claude3.7-sonnet, DeepSeek-v3, Qwen2.5-max and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct; metrics are benchmark accuracy/score, input-token compression ratio (21.59x) and prefill inference efficiency
column12: We introduce dynamic context optimization, a novel paradigm for long-context management through dynamic, instruction-guided token-level compression. (Contributions)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The abstract and Section 2.1 motivate the work on the 'lost in the middle' degradation (plus prefill cost), but the evaluation measures only capability and efficiency: accuracy/score on Ruler-128K, InfiniteBench and three further long-context benchmarks, compression ratio (21.59x), and prefill complexity. There is no positional analysis, no needle-position sweep, and no direct measurement of mid-context information loss - the lost-in-the-middle claim is inferred from aggregate score gains (19.15-point average). Purely non-adversarial: no attacker, no planted content; the 'bad context' is simply irrelevant bulk. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: current entry is 'defense: QwenLong-CPRS', but the paper contains no adversary, so this is proposes_fix, not a defense. origin=invents (it also coins the 'dynamic context optimization' paradigm); it is compared against RAG and sparse attention but is not derived from either, so no parent_technique. names_registry_technique=no: 'lost in the middle' is borrowed from Liu et al. [25].

column3: A hierarchical memory architecture overcomes context limits in long-horizon multi-agent computational modeling
column11: Domain benchmarks in quantitative systems pharmacology: autonomous PK/PD model selection without human intervention; PK parameter recovery compared against single-agent baselines; stability of model selection across linguistically diverse prompts of the same task; consistency across lower-cost vs frontier LLMs; a feature-level ablation of PI-agent oversight across PBPK models of varying complexity (debugging efficiency and final accuracy); a literature pipeline benchmark (retrieval 7/10 first pass and 10/10 second pass, extraction 5/5, multi-paper synthesis 2/2, wall-clock times); and a GLP-1RA body-weight modeling case study. Context itself is reported only as injected mid-term state token counts (median 301, IQR 215-478, max 4,050 across 104 runs)
column12: Here we present Ensemble QSP, a multi-agent framework featuring a three-layer hierarchical memory architecture that keeps injected context bounded and constant in project duration (mid-term project state: median 301 tokens, max 4,050, across 104 runs) by capping each state category and evicting completed work, enabling continuous autonomous operation without context degradation. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper claims to enable 'continuous autonomous operation without context degradation' and is motivated by the 'context window bottleneck' and O(N x T) history growth, but the evaluation measures only (a) token counts of the injected state and (b) downstream domain capability - PK/PD model selection correctness, parameter recovery vs single-agent baselines, literature retrieval/extraction/synthesis hit rates, wall-clock time. No experiment varies session count or history length and measures accuracy degradation, so 'without context degradation' is asserted from the boundedness of the token budget rather than measured. Entirely non-adversarial: the problematic context is accumulated project history, not planted content. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: current entry 'defense: Ensemble QSP (hierarchical memory architecture)' - there is no adversary in this paper, so proposes_fix is correct, not a defense. Method names: Ensemble QSP; three-layer hierarchical memory architecture (short-term / mid-term / long-term); physics-based checklists; PI (principal investigator) agents. names_registry_technique=no: names no attack or reusable failure mode.

column3: ARC: Active and Reflection-driven Context Management for Long-Horizon Information Seeking Agents
column7: defense: ARC (Active and Reflection-driven Context mana
column11: Five information-seeking benchmarks scored by Pass@1 / Pass@3 accuracy: HotpotQA (512 sampled questions, search-and-browse rather than oracle retrieval), GAIA (text-only subset), xBench-DeepSearch, BrowseComp (BrowseComp-LongContext subsets) and BrowseComp-ZH; baselines are ReAct (raw history accumulation) and ReSum (passive summarization); actors are Qwen2.5-7B/32B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B/32B and DeepSeek-v3.2 with a GPT-OSS-120B Context Manager; headline is up to +11 absolute accuracy on BrowseComp-ZH with Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, plus an ablation over Summary / Summary+Checklist / Reflection+Checklist / ARC (Full) reported in the same accuracy numbers
column12: Motivated by this perspective, we propose ARC, which is the first framework to systematically formulate context management as an active, reflection-driven process that treats context as a dynamic internal reasoning state during execution. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The abstract and introduction are built on 'context rot' (Hong et al., 2025) and attention dilution over growing interaction histories, but every reported number is capability-only: Pass@1/Pass@3 task accuracy on HotpotQA, GAIA, xBench-DeepSearch, BrowseComp and BrowseComp-ZH, including the component ablation (Table 2). Nothing measures accuracy against turn count or context length, no distractor-controlled condition, no measurement of whether early errors or outdated assumptions actually persist and get corrected - the central claimed mechanism (reflection-driven revision rescues a degraded context) is inferred from aggregate benchmark gains over ReSum and ReAct. Non-adversarial throughout: no attacker, the harmful context is the agent's own accumulated history and its own earlier mistaken summaries. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: current entry 'defense: ARC' - there is no adversary, so proposes_fix is correct, not a defense. Method names: ARC; Context Manager (CM); checklist; interaction memory. names_registry_technique=no: 'context rot' is borrowed from Hong et al.

column3: Memanto: Typed Semantic Memory with Information-Theoretic Retrieval for Long-Horizon Agents
column7: defense: Memanto (typed semantic memory + automated con
column11: LongMemEval (full 500-question suite, S setting) and LoCoMo standard split; compared against hybrid graph/vector memory systems (Mem0, Zep, Letta/MemGPT, A-MEM, Supermemory, Hindsight-style pipelines); five-stage progressive ablation over retrieval limit, ITS similarity threshold, prompt design and inference model; plus latency/ingestion-cost measurements.
column12: The study evaluates the effects of retrieval limit tuning, similarity threshold calibration, prompt design, and inference model selection. (Contributions)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Memanto (typed semantic memory + automated conflict resolution + temporal versioning on Moorcheh ITS). CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around non-adversarial context failures -- passive context injection of a static blob, stale/outdated memory, and 'constraint drift' from accumulated unresolved contradictions -- but the evaluation measures only QA accuracy on LongMemEval/LoCoMo plus retrieval latency, ingestion cost and operational complexity ('Memory Tax'). The five-stage ablation varies retrieval budget, similarity threshold, prompt wording and inference model (Claude Sonnet 4 -> Gemini 3); it never isolates the conflict-resolution or typed-schema components, so the contradiction/constraint-drift claim is not measured. No adversary anywhere in the paper. Registry disagreement: labelled 'defense: Memanto', but there is no attacker -- this is a non-adversarial context-management fix, exactly the mislabelling pattern the brief warns about. Also note memory-type assignment is manual at write time, so the typed-schema contribution is partly unautomated.

column3: Prompt Injection as Role Confusion
column11: StrongREJECT attack-success-rate measurements for CoT Forgery across six frontier models with near-zero no-attack baselines; role-probe classification experiments on identical text under correct tags, no tags and all-user tags; and ~1,000 agent exfiltration attempts where probe-measured role confusion is correlated with attack success (2% lowest quantile to 70% highest).
column12: We introduce CoT Forgery, achieving 60% attack success across six frontier models by injecting fabricated reasoning that the model mistakes for its own. (Contributions)
column14: Squarely in scope: untrusted tool/web text inheriting trusted-role authority. The contributions list actually leads with a mechanistic theory (role confusion) and the role-probe measurement method, with CoT Forgery as the demonstrating attack; coded proposes_attack because CoT Forgery is the new named technique with an ASR evaluation, but it could defensibly be read as a measurement study of role perception. Two citable names: 'role confusion' (the representational failure mode -- adversarially exploited, not a benign mechanism) and 'CoT Forgery' (the attack). No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the paper measures the mechanism it claims (probe-measured confusion predicts ASR pre-generation, and correlates across 1,000 agent exfiltration trials). Registry disagreement: entry reads 'mechanism: CoT Forgery' with origin None -- CoT Forgery is a deliberate zero-shot injection attack invented by this paper, so it should be attack/invents; the mechanism label belongs on role confusion, not on CoT Forgery.

column3: Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories
column11: Class-incremental learning on CLINC150, Banking77 and DBpedia; long-context QA/retrieval on LongHealth, QASPER and MK-NIAH (RULER); BABILong up to 10M tokens against GPT-4, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-8B+RAG, RMT, ARMT and Titans; few-shot ARC against ICL, TTT+synthetic updates and SEAL; AIME-24/25 and HMMT-25 against GRPO and SFT.
column12: Our experiments on long-horizon, continual learning, knowledge incorporation, and few-shot generalization tasks support the importance of the sleep stage. (Abstract)
column14: Out of scope: there is no untrustworthy context anywhere in this paper, deliberate or accidental. The problems it targets are knowledge staleness past the training cutoff and catastrophic forgetting under continual parameter updates, i.e. a continual-learning/capability problem, and 'long-horizon' is used in the continual-learning sense (wake/sleep lifecycle), not in the sense of a polluted or untrusted context window. The contribution is a training paradigm (Sleep = Memory Consolidation via Knowledge Seeding/Generalized Distillation + Dreaming via RL-generated synthetic curriculum) that moves short-term in-context knowledge into parameters, and every evaluation is a capability score (class-incremental accuracy, BABILong, ARC, AIME) plus wall-clock efficiency. Not coded as a CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH because the paper never claims to address a context-trust or context-degradation failure mode; claim and measurement agree, they are simply about something else. Registry disagreement: entry reads 'defense: Sleep paradigm (Memory Consolidation + Dreaming)', but there is no adversary and no context threat -- it should not be a defense, and on my reading the paper does not belong in the corpus at all.

column3: Fine-Mem: Fine-Grained Feedback Alignment for Long-Horizon Memory Management
column11: Memalpha (trained on the Memalpha corpus) and MemoryAgentBench, with sub-task splits including SQuAD, HotpotQA, PerLTQA and TREC-C under accurate-retrieval, test-time-learning and long-range-understanding settings; baselines Long-Context, RAG-Top2, A-Mem, LightMem, MemAgent, MEM1 and Mem-alpha; metrics are task success/accuracy plus memory length, with generalization ablations across backbones.
column12: Experiments on Memalpha and MemoryAgentBench demonstrate that Fine-Mem consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving superior success rates across various sub-tasks. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Fine-Mem; Chunk-level Step Reward (CSR); Evidence-Anchored Reward Attribution (EARA). CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper motivates itself with a context problem -- streaming information far exceeding fixed context windows, information decay, loss of long-term coherence -- but the evaluation measures only downstream capability: QA success rates and averaged sub-task accuracy on Memalpha and MemoryAgentBench (SQuAD, HotpotQA, PerLTQA, TREC-C) plus memory length as an efficiency proxy. Nothing measures information decay, dilution or degradation of memory fidelity directly; there is no distractor-controlled or saturation-controlled ablation. In practice the real technical problem solved is an RL one (reward sparsity and credit assignment for a memory-manager policy), which is a further step away from context trustworthiness. Wholly non-adversarial: no attacker, no injected content. Registry disagreement: labelled 'defense: Fine-Mem', but there is no adversary -- this is a non-adversarial context-management fix, the mislabelling pattern the brief flags.

column3: AtlasVA: Self-Evolving Visual Skill Memory for Teacher-Free VLM Agents
column11: Four spatial agentic benchmarks -- Sokoban, FrozenLake, 3D embodied navigation, and 3D robotic manipulation (Place, Stack, Drawer, Align) -- with Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct trained by PPO/GAE, compared against text-centric memory baselines (SkillRL/XSkill-style text skill banks) and larger proprietary VLM agents, plus ablations over the three memory layers and the teacher-free atlas evolution.
column12: We propose AtlasVA, a memory framework for VLM agents that replaces lossy text-only storage with a Visual Skill Memory hierarchy. (Contributions)
column14: Out of scope: no untrustworthy context, deliberate or accidental. The three problems the paper names are modality mismatch (lossy text encoding of spatial layouts), teacher dependency on a proprietary LLM, and sparse textual reward causing RL credit-assignment difficulty. These are capability and training-efficiency problems; 'memory' here is a learned skill library, not a context window at risk of pollution, and 'long-horizon' is used in the RL episode sense. Evaluation is purely task success on spatial benchmarks plus convergence speed. Not a CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the paper does not claim to address a context-trust or context-degradation failure mode, so claim and measurement line up -- they are simply about agent capability. Registry disagreement: entry reads 'defense: AtlasVA (self-evolving visual skill memory)', but there is no adversary and no untrusted content; on my reading this row does not belong in the corpus at all.

column3: Exploring Knowledge Conflicts for Faithful LLM Reasoning: Benchmark and Method
column11: ConflictQA itself, run zero-shot over 12 LLMs (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct, Open-Mistral-7B, Mistral-Large-2512, Deepseek-V3.2, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking, Deepseek-V3.2-Thinking, o3-mini) across the TripleConf and TextConf conflict types under Non-COMP and COMP settings, with macro-F1 and Exact Match, evidence-order swaps, and a clean no-conflict reference; XoT is then compared against direct answering with a conflict-aware QA prompt and against chain-of-thought prompting on the same benchmark.
column12: To address this gap, we introduce ConflictQA, a novel benchmark that systematically instantiates conflicts between textual evidence and KG evidence. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: XoT (two-stage explanation-based thinking framework). Squarely in scope: retrieved external evidence that is outdated, noisy or intentionally manipulated, with corrupted KG triples and corrupted passages as the conflict instruments. Coded benchmark_or_dataset because both the title and the abstract's contribution order lead with ConflictQA and XoT is explicitly derived afterwards ('Based on these findings, we further propose XoT'); technique_name left blank per the field rule even though XoT is the paper's named method. names_registry_technique=yes under the strict reading: the benchmark names reusable conflict conditions (TripleConf, TextConf, Non-COMP/COMP) that other work can test against. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the evaluation measures the failure mode directly as EM/F1 degradation under controlled conflict injection (EM drops near or above 60% under TripleConf, 78-79% relative for Qwen3-8B and Open-Mistral-7B) and isolates which source the model over-trusts. Registry disagreement: entry reads 'defense: XoT', which captures only the secondary half of the paper and misses the primary ConflictQA benchmark contribution.

column3: Towards Large Language Model (LLM) Forensics Using LLM-based Invocation Log Analysis
column11: Six handcrafted prompt-to-SQL (P2SQL) attack samples taken from the categories of Pedro et al. column3: MemWeaver: Weaving Hybrid Memories for Traceable Long-Horizon Agentic Reasoning

column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper is framed on non-adversarial context-integrity failures - temporal conflicts, noisy extractions and accumulated conflicts from missing session-level verification, weakly grounded abstractions, limited traceability - but the evaluation measures only QA capability and efficiency: F1/BLEU-1/ROUGE-2 on LoCoMo plus average input tokens (the headline '95% context reduction'), memory footprint and retrieval latency. Conflict reconciliation is never measured (no conflict-injection or contradictory-update test), and the contribution's claim of 'strong evidence traceability' has no corresponding metric. Partial mitigation: LoCoMo's Temporal question category is reported separately and is a reasonable proxy for the temporal-consistency claim, but it is still standard benchmark accuracy, not a controlled measurement of the failure mode. Notably, LoCoMo's own Adversarial question category was excluded from the main experiments. DISAGREEMENT WITH REGISTRY: current_registry_entry labels this 'defense: MemWeaver', but the paper contains no adversary and no deliberate attack; it is a non-adversarial context-management method and should be proposes_fix, not a defense.

column3: Oracle Poisoning: Corrupting Knowledge Graphs to Weaponise AI Agent Reasoning
column11: Six attack scenarios against a production 42-million-node code knowledge graph (Neo4j/Cypher via MCP), including a zero-node property-modification variant; primary cross-model evaluation via real SDK tool-use, nine models from three providers (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash), N=30 per model, 95% Clopper-Pearson CIs, trust rate 269/269 at L2 sophistication; end-to-end replication against a live poisoned Neo4j instance; an attacker-sophistication gradient; a controlled inline-vs-tool-use delivery-mode comparison and directed-vs-open-ended prompt framing; poisoning-budget quantification; five/six candidate defences; and a structural generalisation analysis of four additional code intelligence platforms. Positioned against ROAR, PoisonedRAG, GragPoison, KEPo, BadRAG, ConfusedPilot, AgentPoison and MaSS as related but distinct attacks.
column12: We define Oracle Poisoning, an attack class in which an adversary corrupts a structured knowledge graph that AI agents query at runtime via tool-use protocols, causing incorrect conclusions through correct reasoning. (Abstract)
column14: Central in-scope paper: the agent reads tool-returned facts it should not trust, with a deliberate adversary. Strong, well-powered evaluation that measures the failure mode directly (per-model trust rates with exact CIs, a live-database replication, a sophistication gradient with discrete break points, and an explicit delivery-mode confound analysis showing GPT-5.1 at 0% trust inline but 100% under real tool-use). No claim/evaluation mismatch. Defense names evaluated (not the paper's lead contribution): read-only access control; multi-tool cross-verification; system prompt hardening; blind devil's advocate; organised under a Visibility-Understanding-Traceability (VUT) framework. DISAGREEMENT WITH REGISTRY: current_registry_entry labels it 'mechanism: Oracle Poisoning', but the paper defines a deliberate adversarial attack class requiring authenticated write access; it should be proposes_attack / attack, not a non-adversarial mechanism. Note the paper's own careful scoping: it is explicitly distinguished from prompt injection, RAG poisoning, training-time poisoning and tool poisoning - the agent receives false facts, not false instructions.

Registry disagreement: current entry labels it a 'defense', but there is no adversary anywhere in the paper; it is a fix for a non-adversarial memory failure. technique_name is Memory-R2 (framework); its core algorithm is named LoGo-GRPO, and it is positioned as going beyond, not reusing, Memory-R1 and Mem-alpha.

Closest prior work (SUPO, ReSum, Context-Folding) also trains summarization with RL, so 'improves' over that line is arguable, but the named joint-optimization method (token-level loss normalization plus cross-trajectory GAE) is new.

column3: BordaRAG: Resolving Knowledge Conflict in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Borda Voting Process
column5: International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management
column11: NQ, PopQA and TriviaQA (1000 sampled queries each, top-10 Google Search snippets as corpus) with Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2-7B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct; baselines No-RAG LLM, GenRead, InstructRAG, DAA, RobustRAG, AstuteRAG and USC; metric answer accuracy with significance testing, plus a theoretical expected-distortion analysis of Majority Voting vs Borda Voting and an analysis confirming retrieved documents carry multiple candidate answers.
column12: Inspired by such an insight, we propose BordaRAG, a model designed to better select the most appropriate documents from conflicting documents. (Abstract)
column14: NO MISMATCH: the failure mode (inter-context knowledge conflict among retrieved documents) is what the evaluation actually exercises - the corpora are shown to contain multiple conflicting candidate answers, the baselines are all conflict-resolution methods, and the distortion analysis targets the selection mechanism directly. Technique is a new named framework that applies Borda Voting from social-choice theory to document selection; coded invents because BordaRAG is newly named, but it is an application of an existing voting rule and a reframing of prior majority-voting methods. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: BordaRAG'; the conflicting documents are not planted by an adversary, so this is a fix for a non-adversarial failure (the paper does mention misinformation-prevalent domains but never models an attacker). Names no citable attack or failure mode of its own.

column3: Micro-Act: Mitigating Knowledge Conflict in LLM-based RAG via Actionable Self-Reasoning
column11: Five datasets across two collections: ConflictBank (misinformation, temporal and semantic conflict subsets, 3000 sampled) and KRE (MuSiQue_KRE and SQuAD_KRE, 2000 sampled), with GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-3.1-70B and LLaMA-3.1-8B; baselines end-to-end QA, few-shot QA, Chain-of-Thought, Self-Ask, Comparative and GKP; metric multiple-choice QA accuracy broken down by conflict type, plus non-conflict questions to check for regression and an analysis of the over-rationalization behaviour.
column12: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems commonly suffer from Knowledge Conflicts, where retrieved external knowledge contradicts the inherent, parametric knowledge of large language models (LLMs). (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE/FIX NAMES: MICRO-ACT (written as M ICRO -ACT in the small-caps PDF rendering). names_registry_technique=yes because, besides the method, the paper coins and characterizes a specific non-adversarial failure mode - 'over-rationalization', the tendency of an LLM facing contradictory evidence to construct justifications that make all of it appear compatible, reported as more frequent in stronger models (GPT-4o more than GPT-4o-mini) and as the cause of GKP's degradation. NO MISMATCH: accuracy is broken out by conflict type (misinformation/temporal/semantic) and tested on non-conflict controls, so the measurement targets the claimed failure mode rather than generic capability. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: Micro-Act'; the conflicting knowledge is noisy/outdated retrieval, not an adversary, so proposes_fix is the right label.

column3: Navigating Unreliable Parametric and Contextual Knowledge: Explicit Knowledge Conflict Resolution for LLM Inference
column11: ConflictBank (misinformation, temporal and semantic conflicts), ConFiQA (counterfactual contexts) and MQuAKE (multi-hop knowledge-editing conflicts), 1,000 sampled instances split 1:2:7 into demonstration/validation/test, two contradicting contexts per query; baselines Direct Answer, In-Context Learning, InstructRAG (ICL version), TruthfulRAG and CK-PLUG; metrics Exact Match and ROUGE-L, with rule Coverage and Support statistics for the induced resolution rules.
column12: To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework MACR for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond the conventional binary choice paradigm and incorporates an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism based on a multi-agent reasoning approach. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE/FIX NAME: MACR (adaptive knowledge assessment via modified semantic entropy, plus a three-agent inductive reasoning module that induces rules, analyzes conflicts and resolves inconsistencies). NO MISMATCH: all three benchmarks are conflict-specific and each query is constructed with two contradicting contexts, so EM/ROUGE-L here measure resolution of the claimed failure mode rather than generic capability; the rule Coverage/Support metrics additionally inspect the resolution mechanism. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: MACR (multi-agent conflict resolution)'; the unreliable context is counterfactual/outdated/misinformed rather than attacker-planted, so this is a fix for a non-adversarial failure. Unlike prior work it assumes BOTH the parametric and the contextual source may be wrong, which is the paper's main conceptual novelty.

column3: Extended to Reality: Prompt Injection in 3D Environments
column11: Three Unity virtual 3D environments (office, home interior, outdoor suburban neighborhood) and three matching real-world environments, under robot-route and human-route camera trajectories; critic/evaluator MLLM pairs Gemini-2.0-Flash + GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o-mini + Gemini-2.0-Flash, GPT-5 + Gemini-2.5-Flash; planner baselines Single-Placement (adapted from 2D typographic injection) and Iterative-Plausibility; defenses evaluated include instructional prevention and known-answer detection; metrics attack success rate, physical plausibility, MLLM calls and tokens
column12: Experiments demonstrate that PI3D is an effective attack against multiple MLLMs under diverse camera trajectories. (Abstract)
column14: DISAGREES with current_registry_entry, which labels PI3D as 'mechanism:'. This is an unambiguously deliberate adversarial attack - an attacker physically places text-bearing objects in a 3D scene to override the MLLM's task - so it should be an attack, not a non-adversarial failure mode. The secondary contribution is an 'experience-guided planner' for finding effective 6-DoF object poses; the injected text itself reuses the known context-ignoring prompt injection. Claim and evaluation line up: ASR of the named attack is measured directly, plus defenses are shown insufficient (instructional prevention still leaves 50.5-56.7% ASR). No mismatch marker.

column3: Clouding the Mirror: Stealthy Prompt Injection Attacks Targeting LLM-based Phishing Detection
column11: A controlled dataset of 2000 phishing-login templates for the 10 most targeted brands of Q2 2025, with 25 injection messages crossed against 8 HTML insertion locations; detection modes Standard, Advanced (prior LLM phishing-detection pipeline), and InjectDefuser; models GPT-5, Grok 4 Fast, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemma 3 27B; separate experiments on URL-based PI and on existing LLM phishing-detection pipelines; metric attack success rate
column12: This paper presents the first comprehensive evaluation of PI against multimodal LLM-based phishing detection. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: InjectDefuser (prompt hardening + allowlist-based retrieval augmentation + output validation). PARTIALLY DISAGREES with current_registry_entry 'defense: InjectDefuser': the defense is real and named, but the paper's own contributions list leads with the two-axis taxonomy (Attack Techniques x Attack Surfaces) and the quantitative vulnerability assessment, so the primary contribution is a measurement study of prompt injection against LLM phishing detectors, with InjectDefuser as a follow-on. The named attack-technique categories are the thing other papers would cite and test against, hence names_registry_technique=yes. Claim and evaluation line up - ASR under injection is measured directly - so no mismatch marker. Note the Advanced detection mode is sometimes WORSE than Standard (76.2% vs 65.1% ASR on Grok 4 Fast).

column3: EquiMem: Calibrating Shared Memory in Multi-Agent Debate via Game-Theoretic Equilibrium
column11: HotpotQA (accuracy), LoCoMo (F1), ALFWorld (success rate) and WebShop (reward); memory architectures Voyager, MemoryBank (embedding) and AriGraph, G-Memory (graph), plus a stateless no-memory lower bound; MAD backbones AutoGen, MacNet, DyLAN on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct; baselines Vanilla, LLM-Audit, PPL-Filter, A-MemGuard; RQ2 adds adaptive attacks with up to 50 percent adversarial agents (Memory Poisoning and Audit Collusion); RQ3 measures token overhead and latency
column12: Multi-agent debate (MAD) systems increasingly rely on shared memory to support long-horizon reasoning, but this convenience opens a critical vulnerability: a single corrupted entry can contaminate the downstream memory-augmented reasoning, and debate alone fails to filter such errors. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: EquiMem; zero-trust memory game. DISAGREES with current_registry_entry 'defense: EquiMem' in emphasis: the failure the paper leads with is NON-adversarial - hallucination, sycophantic agreement, over-confident assertion and hedging corrupting a shared memory under multi-agent debate - so proposes_fix fits the lead contribution better than proposes_defense. Adversarial agents appear only in RQ2 as a robustness check. NO MISMATCH MARKER, but a caveat: RQ1, the main effectiveness result, is capability-only (task accuracy/F1/success/reward on HotpotQA, LoCoMo, ALFWorld, WebShop) and never measures memory integrity directly; the failure mode is measured directly only in RQ2, where the fraction of adversarial agents is controlled. column3: TSUBASA: Improving Long-Horizon Personalization via Evolving Memory and Self-Learning with Context Distillation
column11: LoCoMo (1,294 QA items over the last eight participant pairs) and LongMemEval (500 QA items); Qwen3 models from 4B to 32B with Qwen3-Embedding-8B retrieval; baselines are vanilla RAG over raw utterances, vanilla RAG over extracted observations, standard fine-tuning on raw conversations, a RAG-free TSUBASA variant, static accumulation vs evolving memory, and the prior systems LoCoMo, A-Mem, Mem0 and Memory-R1 (PPO and GRPO); metrics are token-level precision, recall, F1, BLEU-1, ROUGE-L, GPT-5-nano LLM-as-a-judge, and input token length as an efficiency measure
column12: We propose TSUBASA, a novel framework for long-horizon tasks featuring two synergistic wings: dynamic memory writing and internalized memory reading. (Contributions)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper motivates itself with noisy retrieval, the lost-in-the-middle problem, linear-growing vector memories that fail reflective temporal reasoning, and destructive DELETE operations that erase historical context - but the evaluation measures only QA answer quality (F1, BLEU-1, ROUGE-L, LLM-as-a-judge on LoCoMo and LongMemEval) and input token length. No distractor-controlled ablation, no measurement of retrieval noise or of memory staleness itself; the Pareto claim is a quality-versus-token-budget curve. DISAGREES with current_registry_entry 'defense: TSUBASA': there is no adversary anywhere in the paper, so this is a non-adversarial context-management fix, not a defense. DEFENSE-NAMES: none. Names no attack or failure mode.

column3: Oblivion: Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation

NO CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH MARKER, but a close call worth noting: the outcome metrics are capability (QA accuracy, solved scenarios) and efficiency (tokens per query), never a direct measure of interference. column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. There is no contradictory-update probe, no controlled test of pivot accuracy after a state change, and no distractor-controlled ablation; higher Temporal-subset F1 is a task score, not a measurement of conflict resolution, and the lost-in-the-middle claim is never tested against context position. DISAGREES with current_registry_entry 'defense: AriadneMem': no adversary appears anywhere in the paper, so this is a non-adversarial memory-management fix. DEFENSE-NAMES: none. column3: Textual Equilibrium Propagation for Deep Compound AI Systems

column12: In particular, long-horizon agentic workflows exhibit two depth-scaling failure modes: (1) exploding textual gradient, where textual feedback grows exponentially with depth, leading to prohibitively long message and amplifies evaluation biases; and (2) vanishing textual gradient, where limited long-context ability causes models overemphasize partial feedback and compression of lengthy feedback causes downstream messages to lose specificity gradually as they propagate many hops upstream. (Abstract)
column14: DISAGREE WITH REGISTRY: current entry 'defense: TEP' is wrong in kind - there is no adversary anywhere in this paper.
