The contributions list leads with the gap identification (formalizing the two failure modes) and the method is the second bullet; the title/abstract lead with TEP, so coded as the fix with the failure-mode names recorded. NO claim/evaluation mismatch: besides task accuracy, the paper measures the failure mode directly - feedback token count as a function of nesting depth (exponential growth B(d) ~ 3000 x 2.1^d) and accuracy as a function of depth, i.e. depth-controlled ablations - so claim and measurement line up. Relevance to the corpus is as a non-adversarial context-degradation mechanism (feedback messages that bloat or lose specificity before an agent reads them), not as a security paper.

column3: Tagging-Augmented Generation: Assisting Language Models in Finding Intricate Knowledge In Long Contexts
column11: NoLiMa+ and NovelQA+ (the authors' tagged augmentations of the NoLiMa needle-in-a-haystack benchmark and the NovelQA narrative benchmark, 1,035 questions), with Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet; baseline is vanilla RAG with no tagged context and no tag definitions, compared against Tag Definitions only (TD) and Tag Definitions + Tagged Context (TD+TC), with spaCy and privileged taggers; metrics are accuracy at context lengths 250 / 500 / 16K / 32K tokens plus the extremum drop rate from 250 to 32K.
column12: To address these limitations, we propose Tagging-Augmented Generation (TAG), a lightweight prompting and input augmentation technique that explicitly highlights salient elements in the input context. (Introduction)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Tagging-Augmented Generation (TAG); Tag Definitions only (TD); Tag Definitions with Tagged Context (TD+TC). Registry says 'defense: TAG' - the name is right but there is no adversary: TAG addresses a non-adversarial long-context failure, so proposes_fix rather than proposes_defense. names_registry_technique=no because the failure modes it cites (lost-in-the-middle, attention degradation, literal match dependence) are other papers' names used in a background section, not named by this paper. NO claim/evaluation mismatch: the paper claims degradation of retrieval over long contexts and measures that failure mode directly, reporting accuracy as a function of context length (250 to 32K) and an explicit extremum drop rate rather than only an aggregate task score; NoLiMa is designed to strip literal cues so lexical shortcuts cannot carry the result. Gains are modest and not uniform (7 of 8 configurations improve; some tagged settings fall below baseline, e.g. Claude 3.5 at 16K).

column3: Prompt Attack Detection with LLM-as-a-Judge and Mixture-of-Models
column11: Private curated 929-prompt set (770 benign production prompts from Singapore public-service chatbots incl. 'false positive traps' + 159 adversarial prompts generated by Automated Red Teaming using PAIR with GPT-4o); precision/recall/F1 and latency against baselines aws_prompt_attack guardrail, PromptGuard (Meta Prompt Guard 2), ProtectAI encoder, Qwen3Guard-0.6B, gpt_oss_safeguard, and a family of LLM judges (gemini-2.0-flash-lite-001, gemini-2.5-flash-lite, gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-3-flash-preview, gpt-5.1, gpt-5-mini, claude-haiku-4-5); plus thinking vs non-thinking ablation and pairwise/triple Mixture-of-Models combinations.

column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: LLM-as-a-Judge with context-aware taxonomy-guided reasoning (framing stripping, intent decomposition, safety-signal verification, harm assessment, self-reflection); Mixture-of-Models (MoM). Deliberate adversarial setting (jailbreaks and prompt injection), so 'defense' in the registry is the right kind, but DISAGREE with current_origin=proposed: the paper invents no new named defense - it applies the existing LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm plus standard weighted-ensemble aggregation, and its novelty is prompt design, a private production dataset, and a latency/accuracy deployment study. No claim/evaluation mismatch: it measures detection F1 and latency on adversarial prompts, exactly what it claims. Attack types it lists (social engineering, creative framing, code-mixed payload encapsulation, roleplay/privilege escalation) are generic descriptors, not named techniques other papers test against; the only named attack method used is PAIR, which it applies rather than introduces - hence names_registry_technique=no. Scope caveat for the SoK: the deployed guardrail screens USER prompts, so it is mostly jailbreak detection; indirect/tool-output injection is motivation only and is not in the 929-sample evaluation set. Authors themselves flag the dataset's small size as a limitation.

column3: KVEraser: Learning to Steer KV Cache for Efficient Localized Context Erasing
column11: A self-proposed controlled 'erasing needle in a haystack' benchmark (two same-key needles, erase the earlier one) at 1K-32K context sizes, and long-document QA with inserted misleading factual distractors built from Natural Questions, TriviaQA and HotpotQA (filtered so the distractor actually flips the answer), plus three unseen QA datasets for generalization; baselines are Full recompute (quality reference), Delete-and-shift, instruction-only forgetting, and limited suffix cache repair; metrics are post-erasure answer correctness and latency, on Qwen3-8B.
column12: We introduce KVEraser, a learned KV-cache editing method for efficient localized context erasing. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: KVEraser. DISAGREE with registry label 'defense: KVEraser': there is no adversary anywhere in the evaluation. Prompt injection in an imported skill file is named once in the introduction as motivation, but what is actually measured is removal of a stale/incorrect/misleading span (retracted user preference, stale tool observation, out-of-date retrieved fact, inserted factual distractor). It is therefore a non-adversarial context fix (proposes_fix), not a defense. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker: the evaluation measures the failure mode directly - post-erasure accuracy under a controlled, distractor-filtered setup where the inserted chunk is verified to have flipped the model's answer - alongside latency, so claim and measurement line up. The only gap worth flagging for the SoK is that the adversarial motivation (harmful prompt injection in skill files) is never evaluated. The paper also contributes an erasing-NIAH synthetic benchmark as a secondary artifact.

column3: CLIOPATRA: Extracting Private Information from LLM Insights
column11: Anthropic's Clio insights pipeline reimplemented and configured with four model families (Qwen 3 4B/30B, Gemma 3 4B/27B, LLaMA 3 8B/70B, Claude Haiku 3 / Sonnet 4.5); 1K-100K WildChat conversations seeded with 100 synthetic medical target chats built from NLICE personas; attack success rate and precision against a prior-knowledge baseline adversary (Claude Sonnet 4.5 guessing the disease from age, gender and known symptoms, plus in-context-example and randomized-disease baseline variants); stealthy vs non-stealthy variants; and two deployed mitigations including Clio's LLM-based privacy auditing.
column12: Cliopatra involves an external adversary carefully designing and inserting malicious chats into the system that simultaneously (1) bypass PII redaction, (2) cluster with the target chat, (3) trigger the exposure of sensitive information in the aggregated insights, and (4) obfuscate the insights to evade human and automated auditors. (Introduction)
column14: DISAGREE with registry label 'mechanism: Cliopatra'. This is a deliberate adversarial attack, not a non-adversarial failure mode: an external adversary injects crafted poison chats into a privacy-preserving insights pipeline to bypass PII redaction, steer clustering, and exfiltrate a target user's medical history through aggregated cluster summaries. current_origin is empty in the registry; the paper explicitly claims to be the first attack of its kind, so origin=invents. No claim/evaluation mismatch: the evaluation measures exactly the claimed leakage (up to 65% of target chats with near-100% precision) and also tests the stealthy variant and the LLM-auditing mitigation. Combines data poisoning, prompt injection and attribute inference; Regex Attack, LLM Attack and Fast Clio Attack are named sub-variants of Cliopatra rather than independent attacks. Targets are synthetic medical chats mixed into WildChat, so the real-world leakage rate on genuine Clio traffic is untested.

column11: Their own constructed CVE knowledge-conflict dataset (1,260 pairwise conflict CVE items published and modified over the past decade, built from the CVE official GitHub list and the NVD API), scored with their own multidimensional criteria; headline numbers are answer correctness 0.49 -> 0.76 (+27%) and faithfulness 0.36 -> 0.88 (+52%) against an un-finetuned baseline pipeline (GPT-4o-mini with plain retrieval), plus a claim of higher retrieval accuracy for the latest CVEs than external knowledge bases. The detailed experiments section did not print and greps did not recover a baseline table, so the precise baseline set and backbone models are uncertain
column12: In this paper, we focus on the problem of knowledge discrepancy and conflict within CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) detection and analysis. (Abstract)
column14: No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the paper claims to resolve knowledge conflict between stale parametric knowledge and updated retrieved CVE records, and the evaluation is run on a purpose-built dataset of 1,260 paired old/new conflicting CVE entries with correctness and faithfulness metrics - the conflict is the controlled variable, not a generic capability benchmark. Contribution coding is genuinely borderline: the contributions list's FIRST bullet is the conflict dataset (which would be benchmark_or_dataset), but the title, abstract and second bullet centre the CRVA-TGRAG framework, so coded proposes_fix with the dataset noted as a co-contribution. Non-adversarial throughout: the conflicting context comes from ordinary pipeline staleness (CVE records revised after model training), with no attacker, so the registry label 'defense:' is wrong in kind - record as a fix. Origin 'improves' because the two stages are explicit refinements of RAG retrieval and of DPO-style preference fine-tuning.

column3: Conflict-Aware RAG: Multi-Stage Learning with Conflict Signals for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
column11: Six QA datasets - Natural Questions, SQuAD, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA - with Exact Match and F1; baselines LLM w/o RAG, Vanilla RAG, Self-RAG, DTA, RAG-DDR-8B and SFT-on-chosen, all with identical retrievers, knowledge sources and document counts; plus component ablations (SFT / DPO / reranker, each with and without ConScore-based selection), a knowledge-conflict-scenario comparison against Vanilla RAG, ConScore hyperparameter sweeps, and a controlled external-knowledge study on WebQuestion and HotpotQA splitting cases into 'have' (retrieved documents contain the gold answer) and 'miss' (documents are distracting and lack the gold answer)
column12: At the core of this framework lies ConScore, a conflict signal that quantifies the model’s awareness of potential knowledge conflicts by comparing generative probabilities across distinct knowledge sources. (Abstract)
column14: No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker: besides the EM/F1 benchmark scores, the paper runs a distractor-controlled measurement - the 'have' vs 'miss' study in Table 5, where 'miss' means the retrieved documents do not contain the gold answer and actively distract (Vanilla RAG 22.47 vs Conflict-Aware RAG 69.40 EM on WebQuestion) - so the claimed failure (misleading or conflicting retrieved context) is measured directly rather than only through task scores. Uses the standard three-way knowledge-conflict taxonomy (inter-parametric, inter-retrieval, parametric-retrieval) from Xu et al.'s survey rather than coining new failure-mode names, hence names_registry_technique=no. Registry disagreement in kind: labelled 'defense:' but the conflicting and distracting documents arrive through ordinary web retrieval, not from an attacker, so this is a non-adversarial fix; the method would, however, plausibly transfer to planted-content settings. Defense/fix names, for the record: Conflict-Aware RAG; ConScore.

column3: ConflictRAG: Detecting and Resolving Knowledge Conflicts in Retrieval Augmented Generation
column11: Three benchmarks - ConflictQA, AmbigQA and a constructed NQ-Conflict (injected contradictions) - against six baselines including Standard RAG, RAG+Reranking and Self-RAG, all on GPT-4o-mini with hybrid BM25+Contriever retrieval (K=5), 3 seeds, paired bootstrap tests; metrics are Answer Correctness via GPT-4o as judge, token-level F1, Conflict Detection F1 (88.7% vs 58.6% for the best baseline), LLM-rated Resolution and Transparency, and their own CARS; plus four-class conflict-type classification accuracy, cross-dataset detector generalization (ConflictQA-trained detector on AmbigQA, compared to an oracle detector), component ablations, a format-bias control, Entropy-TOPSIS source-selection accuracy against human ground truth (82.7% vs LLM direct selection 78.3%, fixed 75.6%, equal 71.2%, random 53.4%), and a backbone swap to DeepSeek-V3
column12: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems implicitly assume mutual consistency among retrieved documents—an assumption that frequently fails in practice. (Abstract)
column14: No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: conflict detection F1, per-conflict-type correctness (factual 73.8%, temporal 72.1%, opinion 60.4%, no-conflict 76.6%) and the oracle-detector comparison measure the claimed failure mode directly, on data where the contradiction is the controlled variable. Also contributes the NQ-Conflict construction and the CARS diagnostic metric, but the contributions list leads with the detection module, so coded proposes_fix. Conflict taxonomy (inter-document factual/temporal/opinion, parametric-contextual) is taken from Xu et al.'s survey and ConflictQA, not newly named here. Non-adversarial: contradictions come from stale or divergent sources (e.g. 2010 vs 2020 Vitamin D guidelines), not an attacker - so the registry's 'defense:' label is wrong in kind, though the paper does mention misinformation. Defense/fix names for the record: ConflictRAG; two-stage conflict detection; Entropy-TOPSIS; CARS.

column3: Eliminating Retrieval Knowledge Conflicts: Cross-Validation Re-ranking with Large Language Models
column5: IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Network
column11: ContraPRT, their own passage-ranking benchmark built from the ContraDoc dataset (200 documents chunked into passages with generated queries, formatted after the TREC 2019 deep-learning track), scored with nDCG@k for relevance plus conflict-filtering/passage-selection accuracy; run with GPT-4 and LLaMA3-70B against listwise and pairwise LLM re-ranking baselines
column12: We also develop a new dataset, ContraPRT, to evaluate the ability of models to rank passages containing conflicting knowledge. (Abstract)
column14: No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: ContraPRT is constructed so that each query's candidate set contains a marked contradictory passage pair, and the evaluation scores whether the method removes the false passage and ranks the correct one - the failure mode is the controlled variable, not a downstream capability proxy. RQ2 is itself a small measurement result: current LLM re-rankers fail to filter conflicting passages and produce unstable rankings. Borderline between proposes_fix and benchmark_or_dataset since ContraPRT is a co-equal contribution, but the title and abstract lead with the re-ranking technique. Origin 'improves' because the method is a detect-select-rank modification layered on existing listwise and pairwise LLM re-ranking rather than a new mechanism. Mixed adversariality: the motivating examples include fake news and AI-generated misinformation that an adversary could plant, but no attacker model is defined and nothing is attacked, so this is a fix rather than a defense - the registry's 'defense:' label overstates it. Defense/fix name for the record: cross-validation re-ranking.

column3: Beware of Agentic Botnets: Scalable Untargeted Promptware Attacks via Universal and Transferable Adversarial HalluSquatting
column11: Hallucination-rate measurement over 16 GitHub repositories (10 recent/trending, 5 legacy, plus librepods case study) across six foundational LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, Sonnet-4.5, Opus-4.5), ~14,000 runs; cross-application attacks on production agentic apps (Cursor, Cursor CLI, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Cline, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw/ZeroClaw/NanoClaw) measuring resource fetched, payload execution, tool invocation and end-to-end RCE; prompt-framing ablations and ClawHub skill.md content ablations (Modified Var A) measuring squat rate.
column12: We introduce adversarial hallucination squatting, a technique in which attackers identify trending resources (e.g., popular repositories, popular skills, etc.), compute the LLM distribution of hallucinations on the trending resource names, and preemptively register them to host adversarial prompts (e.g., instructing an LLM to install a bot or running a script that installs a bot). (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement: current entry labels this 'mechanism: Adversarial HalluSquatting', but this is a deliberate adversarial attack with an attacker who pre-registers squatted identifiers to host adversarial prompts -- should be attack, not a non-adversarial mechanism. Claim and measurement line up: the paper measures hallucination rates, transferability across models/application layers, and end-to-end exploitation, which is exactly what it claims. No mismatch marker. Mitigations are discussed only qualitatively (search-before-fetch planner bias) and are not evaluated.

It names no new attack or failure mode of its own; the threat categories it uses are imported from prior work.

The threat motivation (prompt injection, supply-chain poisoning, poisoned tool outputs compromising the agent runtime) is squarely untrustworthy context, so it belongs in the corpus.

column3: PARSE: Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization for Professional Domain LLM Agents
column11: A purpose-built real-document benchmark of 122 tasks across five professional domains (24 financial SEC EDGAR 10-K MD&A, 25 legal Federal Register rules, 23 medical PubMed RCT abstracts, 25 scientific arXiv abstracts, 25 DevOps GitHub postmortems from danluu/post-mortems), each paired with a domain-camouflaged injection payload. Eight defense conditions compared, including no-defense baseline, paraphrasing (Jain et al. 2023), spotlighting (Hines et al. 2024), sandwich prompting, Llama Guard 3 and PARSE. Metrics: attack success rate (25.4% baseline vs 15.6% PARSE), utility (91.8% baseline, 82.8% paraphrasing, 86.9% PARSE), statistical significance and power (p=0.014, n=122 > nmin=103; paraphrasing p=0.500, h=-0.019), and directiveness-gate routing share (59% lightweight path). Ground truth by programmatic malicious_output_signal detection plus LLM-as-judge.
column12: We construct a benchmark of 122 tasks spanning five professional domains. (Section 4.1 Real-Document Benchmark)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: PARSE (Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization); directiveness gate; Tagger-Extractor; structure-aware paraphraser; consistency checker. CODING TENSION: the title and abstract lead with the PARSE defense, but the paper's own contributions list leads with 'Real-document benchmark', followed by 'Synthetic-to-real generalization failure', with 'PARSE architecture' third; per the standing tiebreak rule I coded benchmark_or_dataset and left technique_name blank. If the lead prefers the technique framing this row should become proposes_defense / PARSE / invents. Registry disagreement: current entry is 'defense: PARSE', origin 'proposed'; PARSE is in fact fully implemented and evaluated, not merely proposed. The attack it defends against, domain-camouflaged injection with the camouflage degree gap (CDG) metric, is inherited from Pai 2026a, not introduced here, so names_registry_technique is no. Claim and evaluation line up: the paper claims synthetic benchmarks do not transfer to real enterprise documents and measures exactly that, with power analysis -- no mismatch marker. Note the single-author self-citation chain (Pai 2026a, 2026b) supplying both the attack and the prior defense evaluation.

column3: MIRAGE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection against Mobile GUI Agents via User-Generated Content
column9: MIRAGE (Mobile Injection of Realistic Adversarial GUI Examples)
column11: A self-constructed 1,111-sample injected-screenshot benchmark built from 96 base screenshots across ten mobile applications (Facebook, WhatsApp, Amazon, Instagram, ShopMart, Spotify, Telegram, Temu, TikTok, X) and eleven attack intents, run against five VLM GUI action-prediction agents (gpt-4o-mini, GLM-4.5V, Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B/32B). Primary metric attack success rate (23.0%-30.2% overall, >19% in all settings); secondary metrics Realism (LLM-judge Likert, 3.02 vs 2.52 for the baseline) and Coverage. Baseline: AgentHazard (Liu et al. 2025), with its released adv_str payloads re-rendered in MIRAGE style and scored on the three-application overlap (Spotify, Temu, X), where AgentHazard reaches 5-21pp higher ASR. Also CLIP screenshot dispersion and goal-text cluster entropy vs hand-authored baselines, a realism/ASR correlation analysis (rho = -0.03), and a fixed-seed 100-sample stage ablation of Localizer, Generator and Curator.
column12: In this paper, we design MIRAGE, a screenshot injection attack against mobile GUI agents. (Introduction)
column14: Registry disagreement: current entry says 'mechanism: MIRAGE', but MIRAGE is a deliberate adversarial attack pipeline (attacker posts crafted text into user-generated content regions so the rendered screenshot hijacks the agent), not a non-adversarial failure mode. Should be attack, origin invents. Claim and evaluation line up: the paper claims a visual-channel prompt injection and measures ASR, realism and coverage on exactly that -- no mismatch marker. Noteworthy honesty: MIRAGE is NOT the strongest attack by ASR (AgentHazard is 5-21pp higher on the overlap apps); its claimed advantage is realism plus coverage, and the authors state limitations (single-step actions only, no paired benign-success baseline, low embedding diversity, dependence on proprietary generative models). The RQ2 finding that per-sample realism and attack success are uncorrelated is a defense-relevant negative result: visual-quality filtering cannot catch this class.

column3: Poisoning the Watchtower: Prompt Injection Attacks Against LLM-Augmented Security Operations Through Adversarial Log Content
column11: 48 conditions (4 injection strategies x 4 defense modes x 3 SOC tasks) on 200 synthetic logs per condition (120 malicious, 80 benign) with gpt-4o-mini as the analyst. Strategies: direct override (S1), persona hijack (S2), context manipulation (S3), obfuscated payloads (S4). Defenses: naive prompting, structured prompting, field sanitization, constrained output. Tasks: classification, summarization, remediation. Metrics: suppression rate and injection success rate (S1 0% everywhere; S2 68% on naive classification, 15-33% under defenses; S3 96% ISR on naive summarization, 38% under constrained output; average ISR 26.6% naive falling to 17.3% structured, 13.2% sanitized, 11.8% constrained). Also a comparison against a deterministic mock analyst simulator, which is shown to mispredict live model behavior. Log field schemas and attack categories drawn from CIC-IDS2017 and UNSW-NB15 as references, not real traffic.
column12: We call this setting log-substrate prompt injection. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement: current entry says 'mechanism: Log-Substrate Prompt Injection', but this is a deliberate adversarial attack -- a remote attacker writes instructions into fields (user agents, URIs, usernames, DNS queries) that the defender's SOC copilot later ingests. Should be attack. Origin coded applies rather than invents because the paper explicitly defines log-substrate prompt injection as a subclass of indirect prompt injection and borrows its S1-S4 strategies from existing prompt-injection and jailbreak literature (S3's structural mimicry is credited to the jailbreak line); the novelty is the substrate and the empirical characterization, not a new mechanism. Claim and evaluation line up: the taxonomy is measured directly across all 48 conditions -- no mismatch marker. Also effectively a measurement study with notable negative results (direct overrides are now fully mitigated in gpt-4o-mini; simulation-based studies mispredict model behavior; SR and ISR diverge sharply on summarization, so label-only monitoring misses 96% of successful injections). Single model only (gpt-4o-mini) and synthetic logs, so generality is limited.

column3: ADEMA: A Knowledge-State Orchestration Architecture for Long-Horizon Knowledge Synthesis with LLMAgents
column11: Self-constructed materials only, no external benchmark and no baseline system: a four-scenario showcase package; a fixed 60-run mechanism matrix in which individual mechanisms (checkpoint/resume, dual evaluation, segment synthesis, dynamic governance) are removed and runs are scored for validity/completion; targeted micro-ablations and artifact-chain supplements; and a repaired protocol-level benchmark whose code-oriented evaluation is described as the clearest quality-sensitive block. Headline result: removing checkpoint/resume produced the only invalid run, in the interruption-sensitive resume condition; the other mechanisms are reported as shaping trajectory discipline, artifact progression and cost-quality behavior rather than being completion-critical.
column12: This paper presents ADEMA as a knowledge-state orchestration architecture for long-horizon knowledge synthesis rather than as a generic multi-agent runtime. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper opens on a context failure mode -- 'knowledge states drift across rounds, intermediate commitments remain implicit' -- but drift is never measured. What the evaluation measures instead is run validity/completion in a 60-run mechanism-removal matrix, artifact progression and evidence-chain presence (checklists of which files were emitted), and code-oriented quality plus cost on a self-built protocol benchmark; there is no drift metric, no distractor-controlled ablation, and no comparison against any other orchestration framework. Partial exception worth recording: the second claimed failure, interruption fracturing the evidence chain, IS measured directly via the interruption-sensitive resume condition, which is the only place a removed mechanism produced an invalid run. Registry disagreement: current entry labels ADEMA 'defense:', but there is no adversary anywhere in this paper -- it is a non-adversarial context/state-management method, so proposes_fix, not proposes_defense. Mechanism names (not defenses): explicit epistemic bookkeeping; heterogeneous dual-evaluator governance; adaptive task-mode switching; reputation-shaped resource allocation; checkpoint-resumable persistence; segment-level memory condensation; artifact-first assembly; final-validity checking with safe fallback. Borderline for the corpus: it is about governing non-adversarial knowledge-state degradation over long horizons, which is in scope as a mechanism-adjacent fix, but it never considers untrusted content.

column3: Owner-Harm: A Missing Threat Model for AI Agent Safety

column11: AgentDojo (27 injection tasks, 97 user tasks, Banking/Travel/Workspace/Slack suites, ground-truth mode, no adversarial attack LLM) across three defense configurations: L1 only 3.7% (1/27) safety, L1+L4 3.7%, L1+L3+L4 14.8% (4/27), utility 97.9% and FPR 2.1% throughout; AgentHarm (176 harmful + 176 benign, 11 categories) as comparative baseline at 100% TPR / 0% FPR; a self-built post-hoc Owner-Harm diagnostic benchmark (300 harmful + 150 benign, 8 categories) where the gate alone reaches 75.3% TPR / 3.3% FPR and adding the deterministic post-audit verifier raises TPR to 85.3% and Hijacking detection from 43.3% to 93.3%; a controlled zero-shot generic LLM classifier (62.7% vs 59.3%, gap 3.4 pp) to attribute the gap; and two controlled SSDG experiments on context deprivation (gap ratio R = 3.60 vs R = 1.06 with full context) and context injection.
column12: We propose Owner-Harm, a formal threat model defining eight categories of agent behavior that damage the deploying owner’s interests. (Abstract)
column14: Defense names appearing in the paper (its own layers are largely unnamed): L1 deterministic Datalog gate; L3 semantic reasoning layer; L4 deterministic post-audit verifier (rules V1-V6); Symbolic-Semantic Defense Generalization (SSDG) conceptual framework. Registry disagreement: current entry is 'defense: UNNAMED: deterministic post-audit verifier layer', but the paper's leading contribution is the Owner-Harm threat model plus the measured defense gap, not the verifier; the verifier is only one of three layers and contributes zero on AgentDojo. Coded measurement_study because the empirical core is quantifying and attributing the 100% vs 14.8% gap; the threat model itself maps to no clean contribution category and the 300-scenario Owner-Harm benchmark is a secondary artifact. Claim and evaluation line up and the authors are unusually honest: they state explicitly that the Owner-Harm benchmark is post-hoc, built by the same author after optimization loops, NOT a held-out test set, and report it separately from the authoritative benchmarks -- so no mismatch marker. Also records an informative negative result: the gap is not intrinsic to the owner-harm category but comes from environment-bound symbolic rules that do not generalize across tool vocabularies, and three structural blind spots (text-only manipulation, malicious parameters indistinguishable from legitimate ones, multi-step read-then-exfiltrate chains).

column3: DeepSeek Robustness Against Semantic-Character Dual-Space Mutated Prompt Injection
column11: Black-box robustness evaluation of DeepSeek through its API across diverse parameter configurations, using a unified metric system of MSR (mutation/attack success rate), AQS (average queries to success) and Stealth (stealthiness score). Internal comparison of mutation strategies: dual-space cooperation vs semantic-only and character-only mutation, with mean MSR improvements of 12.5% and 5.6% respectively and a peak MSR of 0.375; grid search and parameter tuning over the hybrid epsilon-greedy plus hill-climbing searcher; operator library covering rewriting, emoji, in-context learning, zero-width joiner insertion, Base64 and leetspeak. No external prompt-injection benchmark, no competing attack framework and no defense baselines are run.
column12: To address these gaps, we propose PromptFuzz-SC, a semantic–character dual-space mutation framework for evaluating LLM robustness against prompt injection. (Abstract)
column14: Registry disagreement: current entry says 'mechanism: PromptFuzz-SC', but this is a deliberate adversarial attack-generation framework, so proposes_attack. Origin coded improves, not invents: the paper's own related work credits Cheng et al. with introducing spatial/dual-space mutation and Nasr et al. with alternating semantic/character optimization; PromptFuzz-SC's additions are a unified pluggable operator library, a hybrid epsilon-greedy plus hill-climbing search, and a consistent metric suite. Claim and evaluation line up -- it claims dual-space mutation beats single-space and measures MSR/AQS/Stealth for exactly those conditions -- so no mismatch marker. Two caveats for the corpus: the only target model is DeepSeek (the paper doubles as a single-model robustness measurement study with no cross-model transfer test and no comparison to a prior attack framework), and absolute effectiveness is modest, peak MSR 0.375. The threat setting is closer to direct jailbreak-style injection through the user channel than to third-party poisoned context.

column3: Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs
column11: A controlled holdout benchmark of 480 synthetic queries (369 injection, 111 benign) in English and Brazilian Portuguese, under a unified instrumentation protocol with stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, paired McNemar significance tests, multi-seed sensitivity sweeps and language-stratified analysis. Systems compared head to head: the paper's own four-layer educational guardrail pipeline (46.34% bypass, 0.00% false positive rate, 2.50 ms average latency), NeMo Guardrails (0% bypass, 16.22% FPR, ~1.5 s latency), Prompt Guard 2 (38.48% bypass, 3.60% FPR), and a regex-only filtering baseline. Metrics are bypass rate, false positive rate and latency; Layer 4 behavioral heuristics register zero blocks because the benchmark is single-turn.
column12: The central outcome is practical: guardrail choices in educational AI should be made as explicit trade-offs among bypass resistance, false-positive behavior, and latency, rather than from isolated metrics. (Section 1, Problem Context and Contributions)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: unnamed domain-specific four-layer defense-in-depth pipeline -- Layer 1 deterministic lexical filtering (30 regex patterns, English and PT-BR), Layer 2 structural integrity (JSON schema plus XSS pattern checks on model output), Layer 3 contextual sandboxing (delimiter isolation, boundary-escape and control-character detection), Layer 4 session-level behavioral heuristics. Registry disagreement: current entry codes it as that defense; I lead with benchmark_or_dataset because the paper's own contributions sentence leads with 'a reproducible evaluation methodology and implementation blueprint' and the title is an evaluation, while the pipeline itself is unnamed and performs poorly in absolute terms (46.34% of attacks still bypass). Claim and evaluation line up -- the three claimed trade-off axes are each measured directly -- so no mismatch marker. Important scope caveat for the corpus: the adversary here is the USER (a student trying to extract solutions), i.e. direct injection, and the paper explicitly EXCLUDES indirect injection through retrieved documents, uploads or LMS content from its study, naming it future work. So it touches untrustworthy context only at the margin. Benchmark is synthetic and self-constructed; no external injection benchmark is used.

column3: PINA: Prompt Injection Attack against Navigation Agents
column11: Two victim navigation agents: indoor NavGPT (fine-tuned on the R2R dataset) and an outdoor agent (Balci et al.), prompt-tuned. Four prompt injection baselines following Liu et al.: Naive Attack, Escape Characters, Context Ignoring, Combined Attack. Metrics: attack success rate (ASR 75% indoor, 100% outdoor, 87.5% average, >20% over baselines) plus navigation metrics (Navigation Error, trajectory length, success rate, SPL). Also ablation study and adaptive-attack/defense setting.
column12: In this paper, we propose PINA, an adaptive prompt optimization framework tailored to navigation agents under black-box, long-context, and action-executable constraints. (Abstract)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry labels PINA 'mechanism:' but it is unambiguously a deliberate adversarial attack (black-box prompt injection optimized against LLM navigation agents) - should be attack, origin invents. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the paper claims high ASR against navigation agents and measures exactly that, against four named baseline injection attacks. Notable for this SoK: the paper explicitly frames long context as a defensive dilution effect the attacker must overcome ('their inputs contain long contextual histories that can dilute or override injected prompts'), i.e. context length as an attack-robustness variable; however that dilution claim is motivational and is not itself isolated in an ablation. Sub-components named: Attack Evaluator, Distribution Analyzer, Adaptive Prompt Refinement.

column3: Agent Skill Security: Threat Models, Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation
column11: Controlled repository of 327 real-world benign skills from the SkillMCP repository across 15 capability clusters, plus generated attacks at each lifecycle boundary (6 repository-admission attack classes; retrieval attacks via keyword stuffing, semantic camouflage, trigger poisoning, Sybil-style cloning; planner attacks via fake recommendations, misleading descriptions, permission deception, planner deception, prompt injection; execution attacks on unauthorized tool invocation, unsafe composition, privilege abuse, information-flow violation; evolution attacks via malicious updates, dependency compromise, version rollback, trust decay, abandoned maintainers). 440 benchmark retrieval queries with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 + FAISS FlatL2; Gemini 3.1 pro as planner. Metrics: Malicious Admission Rate, admission latency, Attack Success Rate, nDCG. Defenses compared against undefended and rule-based baselines across five research questions.
column12: In this paper, we present SkillSec-Eval, a lifecycle-aware framework for systematically evaluating the security of reusable agent skills. (Abstract)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry records this as 'defense: SkillSec-Eval defenses (hybrid admission valid...)'. The paper's own abstract and contributions lead with SkillSec-Eval as a lifecycle-aware EVALUATION framework plus threat taxonomy; the defenses are instantiated inside it, so benchmark_or_dataset is the better primary code and names_registry_technique is yes (it names a taxonomy of attacks spanning repository admission, semantic retrieval, planner selection, execution and skill evolution), not a defense-only no. Defense names for the record: hybrid admission defense (static analysis + LLM-based semantic validation); retrieval validation; metadata validation; LifecycleGuard runtime monitor (dynamic taint tracking and policy enforcement); least-privilege enforcement. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: each claimed lifecycle threat is measured at its own boundary with attack-specific metrics (MAR, ASR, nDCG) rather than generic task scores. Minor quality flag: unedited template text left in the paper ('Keywords: Yes, you must specify some keywords.').

column3: Decomposition, Think and Action: Alleviating Hallucinations of Large Language Models with Reasoning–Evidence Interactive Augmented Graph
column11: Four multi-hop QA benchmarks measured by Exact Match and F1: Adversarial HotpotQA (308-sample balanced subset), 2WikiMultihopQA (1,000 samples), MuSiQue (full dev, 2,417), Bamboogle (test, 125). Base LLMs LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B; BM25 retriever over Wikipedia. Baselines: CoT with Self-Consistency, ReAct, adaptive RAG (FLARE, RAT), MCTS-based RAG, RL-based RAG, DeepRAG (paired t-test reference). Efficiency also measured as reasoning time and number of retrievals.
column12: Extensive experiments on four multi-hop QA benchmarks show that RE-IAG outperforms adaptive RAG baselines, achieves competitive or superior performance to RL-based approaches, and demonstrates strong robustness and generalization across model scales and architectures. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper frames itself around untrustworthy/noisy retrieved context - 'indiscriminate incorporation of external knowledge may interfere with reasoning', 'severe interference from noise or irrelevant information in external knowledge during reasoning', knowledge conflicts between internal parametric and external retrieved knowledge, hallucination - but the evaluation measures ONLY capability and efficiency: Exact Match and F1 on Adversarial HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue and Bamboogle, plus reasoning time and number of retrievals. There is no measurement of hallucination rate, no conflict-detection accuracy, no distractor-controlled ablation isolating the noise/conflict mechanism; the conflict-arbitration and denoising claims are supported only by end-task score deltas over RAG baselines. column3: AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning

column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry says 'defense: AttriMem'. There is no adversary anywhere in the paper - the problem is a non-adversarial one of deciding what to keep, compress or discard from long interaction histories where relevant facts are 'scattered across sessions and mixed with irrelevant details' - so proposes_fix, not defense. column3: Compile, Then Page: Executable SOP Programs and a Capability-Gated Runtime for Procedural LLM Agents

But flag a scope gap: the framing is 'long-horizon agents' and 'silent error accumulation over time', while HaluEval / TruthfulQA / SelfAware are static single-turn hallucination benchmarks - no multi-session or long-running experiment is reported, and the corruption-spread model is never empirically validated.

column3: STAR-PólyaMath: Multi-Agent Reasoning under Persistent Meta-Strategic Supervision
column11: Eight competition mathematics benchmarks - AIME 2025, AIME 2026, MathArena Apex Shortlist, MathArena Apex 2025, Putnam 2025, IMO 2025, HMMT February 2026, USAMO 2026 - scored by answer correctness or human proof rubric, against GPT-5.5/5.4/5.2, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7/4.6, DeepSeek-v4-Pro, DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale, Kimi K2.6/K2.5 and GLM 5.1; plus ablations substituting backbones and removing components, also scored on the same benchmarks.
column12: Our key innovation is a persistent Meta-Strategist that maintains cross-attempt memory and exercises meta-level control by issuing high-level strategic guidance or mandatory directives, so the system can escape unproductive loops rather than stagnate or over-rely on tools. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The paper explicitly names three failure modes it claims to address - hallucination accumulation (errors propagating across long trajectories), memory fragmentation (agents either retaining excessive context or losing salient prior-attempt information), and imbalanced reasoning-tool trade-offs - but every number reported is a competition-math task score: pass/correctness on AIME, Apex, Putnam, IMO, HMMT and USAMO, plus the same scores under ablation. None of the three failure modes is measured directly: no hallucination-propagation rate, no context-length or memory-retention analysis, no distractor or contradictory-update probe. The ablations only show that removing a component lowers benchmark accuracy, which is still capability-only evidence. DEFENSE-NAMES (mitigation names, non-adversarial): STAR-PolyaMath; persistent Meta-Strategist; challenge-step-replan loop; trace-back; Reasoner-Verifier logic/goal gates. REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: current entry 'defense: STAR-PolyaMath' is wrong on two counts - there is no adversary anywhere in the paper, and the artifact is a reasoning-orchestration framework, so proposes_fix. Borderline for the corpus: without the stated framing around hallucination accumulation and memory fragmentation this would read as a pure capability paper, and Ruling 1 keeps it in with the marker rather than out_of_scope.

column3: Can LLM Agents Sustain Long-Horizon Organizational Dynamics?
column11: Year-long simulated SaaS company (Company A, 15 agents, 3 tiers, 3 departments) across 6 LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Deepseek-v3, Moonshot-v1-8K, LLaMA3.1-70B, GLM-4-Flash); metrics are organizational coherence (KL divergence of role-assignment distribution vs an expert role prior), plan propagation (timely/finalized completion across monthly and weekly layers), grounded execution traces, downstream enterprise NLP utility, and responsiveness/transferability; compared with representative multi-agent frameworks.
column12: We evaluate TaskWeave in a year-long IT company simulation and compare it with other multi-agent frameworks on organizational coherence, execution grounding, and downstream enterprise NLP utility. (Abstract)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry has 'defense: TaskWeave (Formulate-Partition-Diagnose-Align)'. There is no adversary and no untrustworthy context anywhere in the paper. TaskWeave is a hierarchical multi-agent simulation framework whose concern is sustaining organizational state (role consistency, intent propagation, dependency satisfaction) over a long simulated horizon - i.e. agent planning/coordination capability, with 'long-horizon' used in the organizational-simulation sense, which the brief lists explicitly under out_of_scope. Note this is a borderline call: an alternative reading is proposes_fix for long-horizon state degradation, and in that reading there would be NO claim/evaluation mismatch marker, because the evaluation measures the coherence failure directly (role-allocation KL divergence against a reference prior, plan-propagation completion across temporal layers) rather than only capability. I judged it out_of_scope because no content the agent should distrust is ever involved.

column3: A Scalable Benchmark for Repository-Oriented Long-Horizon Conversational Context Management
column11: LoCoEval itself (128 samples, single-hop and multi-hop subsets, avg 2.5 requirements and 50 turns, 64K-256K token contexts, containing deliberately mutated 'distracting information items' plus noisy input and retrospective questions); 7 baselines including 4 representative context management / memory methods (e.g. Mem0, plus RAG-adapted standalone LLMs and an Oracle) over 3 backbone LLMs, on three tasks: topic awareness, information item extraction, and function generation; plus the authors' Mem0^R variant and token-consumption cost.
column12: To this end, we propose LoCoEval, the first long-horizon conversational context management benchmark for repository-oriented scenarios, aiming to evaluate to what extent context management methods can accurately retain and recall critical contextual information while compressing the context in repository-oriented long-horizon conversations, thereby improving answer correctness. (Introduction)
column14: REGISTRY DISAGREEMENT: registry has 'defense: Mem0^R (unified conversational + repository memory)'. Mem0^R is real but is the paper's LAST contribution ('a simple yet effective extension of Mem0'); the contributions list leads with the LoCoEval benchmark, so per the tie-break rule this is benchmark_or_dataset, not a defense. If one instead coded the method, it would be improves_existing with parent_technique Mem0. No claim/evaluation mismatch: the benchmark deliberately injects mutated, semantically conflicting 'distracting information items' into the conversation and measures whether the agent retains ground truth over them, so the untrustworthy-context claim is measured directly. The distractors are non-adversarial pipeline noise (mutated cues), not an attacker. names_registry_technique=no: the paper defines generic constructs ('distracting information item', 'ground-truth information item', 'prerequisite relation') and interaction patterns (iterative requirements, noisy input, retrospective questions) rather than named attacks or named failure modes that other papers would cite and test against; the only proper noun for a technique is its own method Mem0^R (a defense/fix name, which per the brief does not count).

column3: Adaptive Focus Memory for Language Models
column11: Two custom scripted multi-turn benchmarks (peanut-allergy Thailand travel scenario; US tax-compliance / illegal-evasion scenario), 30 seeds each, against three baselines: Default (stateless) chat, naive truncated replay, and recency-based compression; metrics are strict binary pass rate (constraint recall AND appropriately conditioned generation), token usage on the graded turn, and latency. Backbone gpt-4o-mini.
column12: We present Adaptive Focus Memory (AFM), a lightweight context management system that dynamically assigns each past message one of three fidelity levels—Full, Compressed, or Placeholder—based on semantic relevance, temporal decay, and importance classification. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Adaptive Focus Memory (AFM). Registry says 'defense: AFM' - partially agreed, but there is no adversary: the failure is non-adversarial constraint drift when early high-importance user constraints fall out of effective context under truncation or summarization, so proposes_fix is the right code rather than proposes_defense. NO claim/evaluation mismatch marker: the claim is constraint drift under bounded context and the evaluation measures exactly that (does the model still recall and act on a constraint stated once, 50 turns earlier, under mixed benign distractors), not generic capability; token and latency numbers are reported alongside, not instead. Caveats worth noting for the SoK: the evaluation is only two hand-scripted scenarios on a single backbone, and the tax benchmark is saturated (100% for every method including stateless), so only the allergy benchmark discriminates. names_registry_technique=no - the paper names only its own method; the failure it targets ('constraint drift') is described generically and is not a named mode other papers test against.

column3: PRIMA: Operational Patterns for Resilient Multi-Agent Research with Verifiable Identity and Convergent Feedback
column11: no evaluation
column12: Quantitative evaluation of the meta-optimization loop, baseline comparisons against existing multi-agent frameworks, and broader empirical validation across additional problem domains are left to future work. (Conclusion)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: PRIMA; resilience and recovery protocol (typed rate-limit detection, on-disk pause records, model-preserving resume, strengthened completed-step loader that rejects poisoned outputs); sub-agent operating discipline (structural prompt layer with task-fidelity, tool-use, revision and inter-step context-boundary norms); multi-phase application pattern with cross-document harmonization. names_registry_technique=yes because the contributions list explicitly enumerates the failure modes it targets, including agents that 'treat upstream context as executable directives' - i.e. indirect prompt injection across sub-agent boundaries - alongside task drift, machinery narration and apology loops; the paper did not coin indirect prompt injection or task drift, it reuses them. NO EVALUATION: this is the Ruling 1 second-bullet case, not the mismatch case. The only empirical content is a single qualitative Graph Isomorphism case study producing one artifact; there are no baselines, no attack success rates, no measurement of whether the context-boundary discipline actually blocks injection, and the paper itself defers quantitative evaluation to future work. Implementation details (prompt text, resilience signal patterns) are withheld for IP reasons, so the patterns are not reproducible. REGISTRY: registry has 'defense: PRIMA (context-boundary discipline + reference...)' - the defense label is defensible, but the row should be marked as having zero empirical support.

column3: Portable Agent Memory: A Protocol for Cryptographically-Verified Memory Transfer Across Heterogeneous AI Agents
column11: Transfer Continuity Score on 50 coding/Q&A/planning tasks across three model pairs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet -> GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4-Turbo -> Gemini-1.5-Pro, Gemini-1.5-Pro -> Claude-3.5-Sonnet) vs a no-memory baseline; Re-Hydration Fidelity under four token budgets (8192/6144/4096/2048); 1,500 tamper-mutation trials for hash/provenance detection; 200 prompt-injection attack patterns in four families (role elevation, instruction override, delimiter breakout, encoded/obfuscated injection); 350 capability-token validation trials; artifact size vs raw conversation JSON
column12: Zero injections reached the target model’s instruction-following pathway. (Evaluation)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Portable Agent Memory; injection-resistant re-hydration pipeline; Merkle-DAG provenance structure (BLAKE3 content-addressing + Ed25519 root signing); capability-scoped access tokens. Judgement call on contribution: the paper's contributions list LEADS with a five-component memory model (M = (E,S,P,W,I)) for cross-vendor portability, i.e. an interoperability protocol whose stated motivations (vendor lock-in, session amnesia) are not untrustworthy-context problems; the in-scope piece is contribution #4, the injection-resistant re-hydration pipeline against memory-mediated prompt injection, plus tamper-evident provenance. Coded proposes_defense because that is the only contribution bearing on context poisoning and it IS directly evaluated (200 attack patterns, 0 successful injections; 100% tamper detection). No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH: the security claims are measured directly, not proxied by capability scores. Caveat for the corpus: the security evaluation is an author-run in-house battery of self-generated attack patterns with no external benchmark (no AgentDojo/InjecAgent/BIPIA), and the transfer study is explicitly a pilot (N=50) the authors call directional rather than definitive. Registry entry is empty.

column3: CoMAI: A Collaborative Multi-Agent Framework for Robust and Equitable Interview Evaluation
column11: Defense success rate on 500+ self-constructed adversarial samples (explicit and implicit prompt injection, e.g. "ignore previous instructions" and covert logic manipulation) against a single-agent GPT-5-mini ablation, LLM-Interviewer and AI-Interviewer-Bot v3; plus admission-decision accuracy/recall vs a ten-professor expert gold standard and human interviewers over 55 candidates, score-distribution statistics, dimensional coverage, satisfaction/fluency, and a verbosity-bias correlation
column12: As reported in Table 3, CoMAI achieved a 100% defense success rate on more than 500 adversarial samples, successfully detecting and neutralizing all malicious inputs such as “ignore previous instructions” and covert logic manipulation attempts. (Evaluation, 4.3.4)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: CoMAI; Security agent (layered security strategy of rule-based plus semantic checks as an intermediary layer between user input and the Scoring agent). Applied multi-agent interview-assessment system whose contributions list leads with the architecture but whose first claimed benefit is 'multi-layered security defenses (achieving full protection against prompt injection attacks)'; coded proposes_defense because the named artifact is a defended system and the security claim is the one actually measured in an adversarial test. Caveats for the corpus: the threat model is DIRECT prompt injection by the interviewee in their own answers, not indirect/third-party context poisoning; the 500+ adversarial samples are author-generated with no external benchmark (no BIPIA/InjecAgent/AgentDojo) and no adaptive attacker, so the reported 100% defense success rate is a ceiling result on a self-selected attack set and should not be read as evidence of robustness. origin=invents is for the named system; the underlying mechanism (a dedicated guard/filter agent in front of the scoring LLM) is a well-known pattern the paper does not credit to any parent work. Registry entry is empty.

column3: Agentic Cloud Decoys: A Deception-Driven Framework for Autonomous Intrusion Investigation
column11: Ten controlled AWS S3 decoy scenarios (enumeration only, enumeration+retrieval, multi-object retrieval, denied access, destructive deletion, delayed access, and scripted/SDK variants), scored manually by the authors against driver-script ground truth on complete event coverage, correct ordering, correct attribution of IAM principal/access key/role chain, complete object naming, and unsupported assertions; plus end-to-end latency (four to five minutes). Suite score 9.5/10, nine of ten scenarios reconstructed completely, zero untraceable assertions. The authors state there is no baseline, no ablation, no independent scoring, and one service on one provider - and NO prompt-injection experiment at all
column12: We identify the third as an unaddressed exposure in this class of system, specify the mitigation it requires, and are explicit that the prototype evaluated here does not implement it. (Abstract)
column14: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The abstract names adversary-authored cloud telemetry (attacker-chosen S3 object keys and user-agent strings that CloudTrail records verbatim) as turning any log-to-prompt path into an indirect prompt injection channel that a decoy actively widens, but the evaluation measures only investigation capability and efficiency: scenario-level reconstruction accuracy (event coverage, ordering, IAM attribution, object naming, unsupported assertions) and end-to-end latency. No injection payload is ever planted in a decoy bucket and no injection resistance is measured. This is an unusually honest instance - the authors themselves declare the exposure unaddressed and the prototype non-mitigating - but the marker is still correct: the context-poisoning claim is stated and not measured. DEFENSE-NAMES: Cloud Decoy AI Agent; session aggregation operator over a four-element pivot tuple of provider-derived fields; dynamic prompt generation (two-stage prompt assembly enforcing a stated grounding invariant, Invariant 1). Defense-only paper, so names_registry_technique=no; it coins no attack name, reusing 'indirect prompt injection'. Belongs in the corpus as a clear articulation of a poisoning channel (attacker-controlled fields in provider logs, with the decoy as an adversary-controlled write surface feeding the analysis path) even though it is unmeasured. Other weaknesses the authors admit: self-scored, no baseline, no ablation, one provider. No current registry entry.

column3: When Routine Chats Turn Toxic: Unintended Long-Term State Poisoning in Personalized Agents
column11: ULSPB (350 bilingual instances: 7 interaction scenarios x 5 assistance categories x 5 variants x 2 languages) run on OpenClaw with four backbones (Kimi K2.5, GPT-5.4, MiniMax M2.7, Grok 4.20); routine conversations compared against four matched single-injection counterparts (Injection Tool, Log Replay, Trojan Skill, Web Content); Harm Score (HS) with weight-sensitivity ablation and 40-diff/7-annotator human validation; 50-instance real-seed subset drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M; StateGuard evaluated on HS reduction, false-negative/false-positive rates and overhead
column12: We formalize this risk as unintended long-term state poisoning. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: StateGuard (the paper also names a defense, but it names failure modes too, so names_registry_technique=yes per the rule). Contributions list leads with '(I) New Threat Identification', so proposes_mechanism over benchmark_or_dataset, even though ULSPB and the Harm Score metric are the second contribution. Genuinely non-adversarial core: the headline finding is that routine, benign 24-turn conversations with no injected attacker can shift confirmation boundaries, tool-use defaults and autonomy; the four injection variants are the comparison baseline, not the claim. Claim and measurement line up - the failure mode is measured directly via state diffs (HS over MEMORY.md, memory/, USER.md, AGENTS.md, TOOLS.md) rather than via task scores - so NO claim/evaluation mismatch marker. No current_registry_entry.

column3: MemVenom: Triggered Poisoning of Multimodal Memories in Web Agents
column11: Three web-agent frameworks (SeeAct, LiteWebAgent, ReAct-style web agent) on SeeAct/Mind2Web-style task set, across Qwen3-VL-4B/8B/PLUS and GPT-5.4 backbones; four OWASP-aligned task-substitution goals (Phishing/Redirection, Controlled Privacy Leakage, Unauthorized Financial Operation, Destructive Data Operation); metrics ASR-r, ASR-a, ASR-ra plus benign utility BU/PU; compared against adapted baselines AgentPoison, CPA (Zhong et al. 2023) and BadChain
column12: We propose MemVenom, a unified black-box attack framework that poisons graph-structured external memory with coordinated text-image evidence. (Abstract)
column14: Deliberate adversarial memory poisoning of multimodal graph-structured agent memory; two stages (trigger-conditioned retrieval attack; post-retrieval attack induction with adversarial perturbation and stealthy OCR injection). Claim and evaluation line up: the paper measures recall of poisoned memory and downstream action induction directly, plus benign-utility impact. No mismatch marker. Registry entry was empty; suggested entry attack:MemVenom.

column3: Local LLM Agents as Vulnerable Runtimes:A Source-Code Audit of the Agent Runtime Layer
column11: OpenClawBench (446 GitHub Security Advisories from the OpenClaw repo, temporal split 229 train / 217 held-out test); baselines Semgrep Pro --config auto (~2,815 rules) and CodeQL javascript-security-extended (104 queries); metric advisory-level recall, plus a live HEAD-commit scan for triage/precision cost
column12: We present C LAWAUDIT, a static auditing framework for measuring implementation-level vulnerability exposure in the runtime layer of local LLM agents. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: ClawAudit. Also contributes the OpenClawBench benchmark (446 advisories) and a five-category STRIDE-derived taxonomy (CAT-1..CAT-5: prompt handling, tool/skill execution, permission & isolation, network & communication, authentication & authorization). Coded proposes_defense rather than benchmark_or_dataset because the contributions list leads with the taxonomy and the ClawAudit framework; the benchmark is contribution four and exists to evaluate the rules. Origin invents: the framework is new, though it is instantiated on existing backends (47 Semgrep YAML rules, 30 CodeQL queries). In scope - it audits exactly the runtime components that mediate untrusted input into the prompt (prompt builder, memory writer, tool dispatcher, skill loader), and explicitly positions itself as orthogonal to prompt-injection work (Greshake et al. indirect prompt injection is cited, not proposed). Claim and evaluation line up: recall on disclosed advisories is what the rules are claimed to improve; authors themselves flag low live-code precision. No registry entry to disagree with.

column3: The Injection Paradox: Brand-Level Suppression in Safety-Trained LLM Recommendations via RAG Context Injection
column11: 40-document wireless-earbud RAG corpus (9 brands) with a prompt injection in 1 document (2.5%), four conditions (Baseline, Implicit, Injection, Combined) over seven models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.4; Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6), 4,500+ trials; metric top-2 recommendation hit rate with Fisher's exact test, Wilson CIs and Cohen's h; plus counterfactual brand-propagation, cross-brand replication, trace-level refusal decomposition and a clean-CoT control
column12: In Claude Opus 4.6, the target brand drops from a 54% baseline to zero top-2 recommendations across all 50 trials, even though only 1 of 4 brand documents in the corpus contains an injection. (Abstract)
column14: No registry entry to disagree with. Coded proposes_mechanism because the paper's own lead is a named failure mode of safety training ('a reproducible failure mode ... the Injection Paradox'), not a new attack - although the trigger is an adversarial injection and the paper sketches a derivative reverse-attack (planting injections in a competitor's documents to suppress that competitor), which it does not itself implement or evaluate as an attack. NO MISMATCH MARKER: the failure mode is measured directly and with controls (counterfactual unmodified same-brand documents, cross-brand replication, injection-free clean-CoT control, trace-level evidence that suppression is silent demotion with zero explicit refusals). Scope note: experiments simulate only the generation stage of RAG; retrieval, reranking and chunking are explicitly out of scope, and the agent-loop propagation claim is left to future work. Relevant secondary observation: a recognition-behavior dissociation where the model detects the injection, pledges fair handling, and still drops the brand.

column3: Trace: Unmasking AI Attack Agents Through Terminal Behavior Fingerprinting
column11: 2,028 sessions (1,010 clean + 1,018 DPI) in a Linux CTF container with five planted flags, across 3 scaffolds x 7 frontier model families (Claude Opus, DeepSeek, Gemini 3.1, GLM-5, GPT-5.4, Kimi, Qwen); metrics macro F1 0.981 for fingerprinting, leave-one-scaffold-out generalization 0.815, DPI system-prompt extraction rate 81.9% at 0.736 Sentence-BERT fidelity (plus BERTScore check), verb-only evasion ablation, LLMmap adapted to shell commands as the only baseline, and an in-the-wild test on the blackbox Vulnetic pentest agent (78% family accuracy, full Gemini system prompt recovered)
column12: In this paper, we introduce Trace, a novel multi-stage attribution and forensic framework for AI attack agents using terminal command sequences. (Abstract)
column14: DEFENSE-NAMES: Trace; Defensive Prompt Injection (DPI). No registry entry to disagree with. Role inversion worth recording: here the LLM agent being poisoned is the ATTACKER's pentest agent, and the planted payload (in files the attacker agent reads on a honeypot-style CTF box) is the defender's tool - the paper is still squarely about an agent acting on untrustworthy context it reads from its environment, so it belongs in the corpus. Claim and evaluation line up: fingerprinting accuracy and extraction rate/fidelity are both measured, including a blind-DPI comparison (1.88x more extracted information with fingerprint-guided payload routing) and an in-the-wild blackbox validation. Named attacks/failure modes from other work are cited (LLMmap, CHeaT, HPTSA, PentestGPT, Greshake indirect prompt injection) but not contributed.
